As he broke tackle after tackle, the roar of the Seattle crowd at Qwest Field shook the stands so hard that nearby University of Washington seismographs — the instruments that measure earthquakes — registered the shaking as real ground movement. Fans call the run 'The Beast Quake.' What size quake did the celebration measure?
context: The seismograph that registered the Beast Quake was a station near Qwest Field (now Lumen Field) operated by the UW Pacific Northwest Seismic Network. The magnitude was measured at roughly 2.0 — equivalent to a very small earthquake. The 67-yard run featured Lynch breaking nine tackles, including the famous stiff-arm of Tracy Porter at the 30-yard line. The tradition continues; subsequent Seahawks games have produced their own measurable quakes during big plays.

question: Pete Carroll was hired as head coach of the Seattle Seahawks in January 2010. Before Seattle, he had spent nine years as head coach at the University of Southern California (USC), winning national college football championships with the Trojans in 2003 and 2004. The Seahawks had just finished a losing 5-11 season and fired the head coach they had brought in the year before. Who was the man Carroll replaced in Seattle?
answer: Jim Mora Jr., who lasted only one season as head coach
choices: Jim Mora Jr., who lasted only one season as head coach
Mike Holmgren, who left after the 2008 season
Tom Cable, the interim head coach
Dennis Erickson, who returned for a season
context: Jim Mora Jr was Mike Holmgren's defensive backs coach who was promoted before Carroll arrived. He coached just the 2009 season (5-11). Holmgren left in 2008 after a decade. Carroll became GM and head coach, building the Legion of Boom defense from the ground up.

question: On October 8, 1995, in Game 5 of the American League Division Series (ALDS), Edgar Martinez's series-winning double in the 11th inning scored Joey Cora from third and Ken Griffey Jr. from first base. Dave Niehaus's radio call has become a Mariners legend. What words did Niehaus famously shout as Griffey scored?
answer: 'My oh my!' and 'The Mariners are going to play for the American League Championship!'
choices: 'My oh my!' and 'The Mariners are going to play for the American League Championship!'
'Hot diggity!' and 'They've done the impossible, Seattle's going to the Series!'
'Holy mackerel!' and 'Junior makes it home, Mariners win the West!'
'Goodness gracious!' and 'Griffey scores and Seattle wins it all!'
context: Niehaus's full call: 'Right now the Mariners are going to play for the American League Championship! I don't believe it! It just continues! My oh my!' The call has been played thousands of times at Safeco Field. Niehaus was inducted into the Hall of Fame broadcaster wing in 2008. He died in November 2010 of a heart attack.

question: In January 2016, Ken Griffey Jr. — the Seattle Mariners' legendary center fielder and one of the greatest hitters of the 1990s — was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame at Cooperstown, New York. His election set a then-record for the highest vote percentage in any Hall of Fame class. Junior came just three ballots short of a unanimous vote — three baseball writers, for reasons of their own, refused to check the box next to his name. What exact vote percentage did Griffey receive?
context: Griffey's 99.3% topped Tom Seaver's previous record of 98.84%. The record stood until Mariano Rivera became the first unanimous Hall-of-Famer in 2019. Derek Jeter then missed unanimity by one vote in 2020 (99.7%). The three writers who did not vote for Griffey never revealed themselves publicly.

question: Randy Johnson was a lanky 6-foot-10 left-handed pitcher who would later throw one of baseball's fastest fastballs and win five Cy Young awards. In May 1989 he was still a wild young starter for the Montreal Expos. Seattle Mariners general manager (GM) Woody Woodward called Montreal and worked out a trade, sending one of his own young pitchers north in exchange for Johnson. Which Seattle lefty did Woodward give up to land the future Hall of Famer?
answer: Mark Langston, the Mariners' previous lefty ace
choices: Mark Langston, the Mariners' previous lefty ace
Mike Moore, the staff ace who later won a Cy Young in Oakland
context: The Langston-for-Johnson trade is regarded as one of the most lopsided in baseball history in Seattle's favor. Johnson went on to win four Cy Youngs (the first in 1995). Langston had a solid career but never matched Johnson's dominance. The Mariners also got Brian Holman and Gene Harris in the deal.

question: Ichiro Suzuki spent nine seasons in Japan playing for the Orix BlueWave, then crossed the Pacific in 2001 to join the Seattle Mariners. He kept collecting hits year after year in the American major leagues too. Add his Japanese pro-league hits and his Major League hits together and the combined total stands as a world baseball record no other player has ever matched. About how many career hits did he finish with in all?
answer: 4,367 hits combined — 1,278 in Japan and 3,089 in the United States
choices: 4,367 hits combined — 1,278 in Japan and 3,089 in the United States
4,256 hits combined — to surpass Pete Rose's MLB-only total
4,500 hits combined — to claim the Asian Baseball Federation record
3,772 hits combined — short of Sadaharu Oh's career mark
context: Ichiro reached 4,257 hits in 2016 (passing Pete Rose's MLB record) and continued through the end of his Marlins career. Pete Rose still claims the official MLB record because Ichiro's Japanese hits don't count toward MLB stats. The 4,367 total is commemorated by displays in Cooperstown and at the Orix Buffaloes museum.

question: On August 15, 2012, Felix Hernandez threw a perfect game against the Tampa Bay Rays at Safeco Field — 27 batters up, 27 down. It was the 23rd perfect game in MLB history and the third in 2012 alone. Which other two pitchers threw perfect games that 2012 season?
context: Philip Humber's perfecto came April 21 vs the Mariners; Cain's was June 13 vs Houston. Hernandez's came August 15. Three perfect games in one season is unprecedented. King Felix struck out 12; he became the first AL pitcher to throw a perfecto since David Cone in 1999.

question: MtG's 1993 Beta set was meant to fix Alpha's print errors and reprint the same cards. But a single dual land that had appeared in Alpha was omitted from Beta — apparently due to a print-sheet mistake. It was not reprinted until Revised in April 1994. The omission made the Beta version of this dual land effectively nonexistent, and the Alpha version highly prized. What was the missing dual land?
answer: Volcanic Island, the red-blue dual land
choices: Volcanic Island, the red-blue dual land
Underground Sea, the blue-black dual land
context: Volcanic Island and Circle of Protection: Black were both omitted from Beta. Alpha Volcanic Islands command extreme collector premiums for this reason. The dual lands joined the Reserved List in 1996, so the Alpha printing remains the rarest. Garfield himself credited the duals as the most important non-Power Nine cards for shaping competitive MtG.

question: MtG's Antiquities set from 1994 introduced the Brothers' War story and included Mishra's Workshop. Workshop is a legendary land that produces three colorless mana, but only for artifact spells. It was originally printed at uncommon and never reprinted in the same form. One later reprint set revisited other Antiquities cards but skipped Workshop. Which reprint was that, and in what year?
answer: Chronicles in 1995, which reprinted other Antiquities cards but skipped Mishra's Workshop
choices: Chronicles in 1995, which reprinted other Antiquities cards but skipped Mishra's Workshop
Fifth Edition in 1997, which reprinted other artifacts but skipped Workshop
Anthology in 1997, the gift-set reprint compilation
Battle Royale in 1999, which used Antiquities cards in pre-built decks
context: Chronicles reprinted Atlantic-Nights through The Dark in white-bordered form. Mishra's Workshop was deliberately omitted because Wizards recognized its tournament power. It joined the Reserved List in 1996 and has never been reprinted in any product. Alpha-Beta-Unlimited (1993) Workshops still command thousands of dollars; the Antiquities printing is the only one.

question: MtG's Legends expansion in June 1994 introduced the Elder Dragon cycle: five legendary three-color dragons, including Nicol Bolas (blue-black-red) and Arcades Sabboth (white-blue-green). Each cost 8 mana to cast. They had a notorious design quirk that made them hard to keep on the table despite their power level. What was that quirk?
answer: Each upkeep, you paid 3 mana of their colors or sacrificed them
choices: Each upkeep, you paid 3 mana of their colors or sacrificed them
Each upkeep, you discarded a card from your hand or lost 5 life
Each turn, you skipped your draw step or sacrificed two lands
Each combat, you attacked with them or paid 5 generic mana
context: The upkeep tax of three colored mana made the Elder Dragons unplayable in any deck that wasn't full of mana fixing — by design. The 'must attack' clause was a separate flavor rule on some printings. Their design legacy is enormous: the Elder Dragon Highlander format (later renamed Commander) takes its name from this cycle.

question: MtG's first Pro Tour in February 1996 at the Park Central Hotel in New York City had a $100,000 prize pool — unprecedented for any card game at the time. The 128-player event was won by Michael Loconto. Wizards of the Coast deliberately chose the format to make competitive Magic accessible to players who didn't own the Power Nine. What did that mean for which cards were legal?
answer: The Power Nine and other Alpha-Beta-Unlimited rarities were excluded
choices: The Power Nine and other Alpha-Beta-Unlimited rarities were excluded
Only cards printed in the previous twelve months were eligible
All cards from every printed set were legal, including reserved list
Only cards in current print runs as of January 1996 were allowed
context: The 1996 format limited cards to recent printings — Fourth Edition base set and the most recent expansions. The exclusion of the Power Nine meant decks could not be dominated by Alpha rarities. Loconto won $12,000 with a white aggressive creature deck. The Pro Tour later evolved into a circuit of multiple events per year, including the World Championship.

question: MtG's Reserved List was created in 1996 in response to fan anger over reprints in the 1995 Chronicles set. The Reserved List initially contained over 500 cards. In 2002, Wizards modified the list, removing one specific category of card while leaving the rares intact. What category did they remove from the Reserved List in 2002?
answer: Uncommons and commons from Antiquities, Arabian Nights, Legends, and The Dark
choices: Uncommons and commons from Antiquities, Arabian Nights, Legends, and The Dark
All multicolor cards including the original Legends Elder Dragon cycle
All artifact lands and lands costing more than zero mana to play
All five basic-land variants printed only in early black-bordered sets
context: The 2002 change angered some collectors but allowed reprints of cards like Hymn to Tourach and Land Tax. The Reserved List today contains 569 rare cards and a handful of uncommons that were grandfathered in. Wizards has firmly committed to never modifying the Reserved List again — most recently confirmed in 2010 and 2017.

question: Magic: the Gathering's classic artwork has its own collector subculture. The Alpha card Black Lotus was illustrated by Christopher Rush, the same artist who illustrated Mox Pearl and many other iconic Alpha cards. Rush's distinctive style influenced MtG's visual identity. Rush died in 2016, but had spent his final years signing Alpha cards at MtG conventions. What did fans nickname these specific signed cards?
answer: Rush Lotuses, with PSA Mint 10 signed copies commanding particular value at auction
choices: Rush Lotuses, with PSA Mint 10 signed copies commanding particular value at auction
Rush Stamps, indicating his small phoenix mark next to the signature
Christ Lotuses, since fans nicknamed him 'Christ' Rush
Lotus Sigs, the generic collector term for any signed Alpha lotus
context: Christopher Rush's signed Black Lotuses sell for premiums of $50,000-$200,000+ over unsigned copies. The PSA-graded auction in January 2021 of a signed PSA 10 Alpha Lotus reached $511,000. Rush also illustrated Mox Pearl, Mox Jet, Sengir Vampire, Hypnotic Specter, and Sword of the Ages, among other iconic Alpha cards.

question: MtG's first official novel was published in 1994 — a companion piece for the Arabian Nights expansion. The novel was written by Jeff Grubb and centered on the planeswalker Taysir of Rabiah. Earlier in 1994, Wizards of the Coast had launched a comic book series adapting Magic's lore. What publisher produced the original MtG comics?
answer: Armada Comics, an imprint of Acclaim Comics
choices: Armada Comics, an imprint of Acclaim Comics
DC Comics, with the Magic line edited by Karen Berger
Marvel Comics, under the Epic Comics imprint
Image Comics, alongside the Spawn imprint
context: Armada Comics published the original Magic comics from 1995 to 1997 — a four-arc series featuring different planeswalkers and storylines. The line ended with the Acclaim Comics bankruptcy in 1997. The early novels and comics were the foundation of the MtG storyline before the late-90s revival under Wizards' in-house creative team.

question: Among the rare cards in MtG's June 1994 Legends expansion, one legendary land is consistently considered the most expensive — it makes each creature's controller pay one mana per upkeep or sacrifice them. Played copies command thousands of dollars. What is the card?
answer: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land
choices: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land
Moat, a four-mana enchantment with a flying clause
Mirror Universe, an artifact that swaps life totals
Eureka, a sorcery that puts permanents into play
context: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale taxes every nontoken creature one mana per upkeep. It is brutal in any matchup against creature decks. Played copies often sell for $2,000-$4,000; mint Alpha or Beta copies sell for far more. The Reserved List has guaranteed it will never be reprinted.

question: MtG's 1993 Alpha set was printed on three large uncut press sheets, each containing 121 cards in an 11-by-11 grid. The print sheet positioning created a peculiar effect: certain rares appear at slightly different rates than others, because the print runs for the three sheets weren't identical. Among Alpha's rares, Black Lotus and the five Moxes are the most legendary — but a single Alpha rare is statistically rarer than the others because of a specific print-sheet quirk. What land card was this single rarest Alpha rare?
answer: Volcanic Island, which appeared only on certain print runs
choices: Volcanic Island, which appeared only on certain print runs
Underground Sea, which was misprinted on the rare sheet
Tropical Island, which was misnamed on its initial run
Bayou, which was double-printed on the uncommon sheet
context: Volcanic Island was famously missing from the Beta set due to a printing error and not reprinted until Revised in April 1994. Alpha Volcanic Islands command extreme premiums on the collector market — well above the other dual lands. The other dual lands (Bayou, Tundra, Underground Sea, Tropical Island, etc.) all appeared in both Alpha and Beta. The dual lands joined the Reserved List in 1996.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin's signature 'Austin 3:16' line — delivered after his King of the Ring 1996 win — came together in an unusual way. The 'John 3:16' reference came from his opponent Jake Roberts' overtly Christian post-recovery persona. The numbers '3:16' on Austin's first popular T-shirt were rendered in a distinctive style that became iconic. Specifically, what design choice on Austin's first '3:16' merchandise differentiated it from later Austin shirts?
answer: The original was a black T-shirt with white 'Austin 3:16' block letters and no skull, predating the Smoking Skull logo by months
choices: The original was a black T-shirt with white 'Austin 3:16' block letters and no skull, predating the Smoking Skull logo by months
The original featured a Bible verse reference printed below the 'Austin 3:16' line
The original was a white T-shirt with red 'Austin 3:16' lettering and a Texas star
The original was a tank top with the slogan on the back only
context: The original Austin 3:16 shirt sold ~150,000 units in its first quarter. Austin's Smoking Skull belt (and the related skull logo on later shirts) didn't appear until 1998. The original 3:16 shirt is now a wrestling-merchandise collector's item. Sales peaked in 1998 at over 1 million Austin shirts moved.

question: Mick Foley's first WWF Championship victory aired January 4, 1999 on a taped episode of Raw and became a turning point in the Monday Night Wars. On live Nitro, announcer Tony Schiavone spoiled the ending, reportedly driving 600,000 viewers to flip channels to Raw. Boss Eric Bischoff has said he personally ordered the spoiler. What was his reasoning, according to his own later interviews?
answer: He thought no one would care about Mankind winning and the spoiler would actually retain Nitro's audience
choices: He thought no one would care about Mankind winning and the spoiler would actually retain Nitro's audience
He thought the spoiler would alienate WWF fans into watching WCW long-term
He had been pressured by Ted Turner to attack Vince McMahon directly on-air
He thought the spoiler would draw a lawsuit that would publicize WCW Nitro
context: Bischoff's miscalculation is one of the most-quoted strategic errors in the Monday Night Wars. The flip-over moment is often cited as the night WWF won the war for good. Schiavone later said he had no choice — the spoiler was Bischoff's call. He has expressed regret in multiple later interviews.

question: The Montreal Screwjob on November 9, 1997, was filmed for what became the documentary 'Wrestling with Shadows.' The documentarian Paul Jay was given unprecedented access to Bret Hart in the months leading up to the event. After the screwjob, Bret Hart famously confronted Vince McMahon backstage and connected a punch. The documentary shows the moments leading up to and after the screwjob in real time. The film also captures what specific Bret Hart action during the match itself that telegraphed his suspicion?
answer: Bret spitting on Vince McMahon at the show's table while still in the ring, before Hebner's call
choices: Bret spitting on Vince McMahon at the show's table while still in the ring, before Hebner's call
Bret writing 'WCW' in the air with his finger after Hebner's call
Bret holding his Sharpshooter on Michaels for an extra 30 seconds, refusing to release
Bret breaking out of the Sharpshooter and punching Michaels in the face
context: The 'WCW' fingers-in-the-air moment came after the bell rang. Bret had figured out the screwjob was happening only moments before the bell. Wrestling with Shadows captures the locker-room aftermath including Bret's punch on McMahon. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the 1998 Hot Docs Festival.

question: The first Hell in a Cell match was fought in October 1997 between The Undertaker and Shawn Michaels. The following Hell in a Cell at the June 1998 King of the Ring produced wrestling's most infamous bumps when Mick Foley was thrown off the top of the cell and later crashed through its roof. Foley continued wrestling for several minutes with a real, visible injury. What had happened to him?
answer: His tooth was knocked out and went up his nose, which was later removed with pliers
choices: His tooth was knocked out and went up his nose, which was later removed with pliers
He lost consciousness for 15 seconds, with referees considering stopping the match
He suffered a broken jaw that was wired shut for 6 weeks after
He punctured a lung but continued wrestling to the finish
context: Foley's tooth went through his upper lip and stuck out of his nose. He continued the match — including being thrown into thumbtacks. Vince McMahon famously yelled, 'Will somebody stop the damn match?' on commentary. The bumps are widely considered the two most dangerous spots in wrestling history.

question: The nWo formation at Bash at the Beach 1996 was a months-long buildup. Eric Bischoff brought in former WWF stars Scott Hall and Kevin Nash to pretend they were attacking World Championship Wrestling (WCW) from outside the company. The reveal that Hulk Hogan was the 'third man' came on July 7, 1996. Earlier in 1996, the WWF had filed and lost a legal challenge to WCW. What specific legal issue had WWF raised?
answer: Trademark infringement, because the gimmicks evoked Razor Ramon and Diesel
choices: Trademark infringement, because the gimmicks evoked Razor Ramon and Diesel
Antitrust, alleging WCW had violated talent-poaching agreements
Defamation, claiming Bischoff had falsely promoted Vince McMahon
Copyright infringement on the WWF logo as used in promotional spots
context: WWF sued WCW in summer 1996 over the visual presentation of Scott Hall as 'the Bad Guy' (directly evoking his Razor Ramon character) and Kevin Nash as the WWF-style 'Big Sexy' (his Diesel persona). The case settled with WCW agreeing to certain disclaimers. The disputes are detailed in 'The Death of WCW' by R.D. Reynolds and Bryan Alvarez.

question: The Rock vs Stone Cold WrestleMania X-Seven main event on April 1, 2001, at the Astrodome in Houston is often called the greatest main event in WrestleMania history. The match featured Vince McMahon's interference — Austin's heel turn was the swerve of the night. The exact ending played out with Austin hitting The Rock with a Stunner, McMahon handing Austin chairs, and Austin pinning The Rock. The post-show in-arena celebration featured a key visual moment that was caught on broadcast and became iconic. What did Austin do as the show was ending?
answer: Toasted Vince McMahon with two beer cans on the ring apron as the show went off the air
choices: Toasted Vince McMahon with two beer cans on the ring apron as the show went off the air
Sprayed beer on The Rock's prone body in the center of the ring
Lifted McMahon onto his shoulders as the ramp's pyrotechnics went off
Shared a fist-bump with McMahon as the camera zoomed in
context: The Austin-McMahon beer toast was the visual confirmation of the heel turn. Austin was scripted to wink at the camera and toast Vince as a new alliance forming. The match's WWE Network rating remains exceptionally high among historic matches. Austin's heel run that followed was widely criticized as creatively disappointing, but the WrestleMania match itself stands as a five-star classic.

question: WrestleMania X8 on March 17, 2002, at Toronto's SkyDome marked the official end of World Championship Wrestling (WCW) as separate competition; Vince McMahon had purchased WCW in March 2001. The main event was Hogan vs The Rock — Icon vs Icon. Hogan was scripted as the heel; the Toronto crowd ignored the script and cheered Hogan throughout. This unscripted crowd reaction created what backstage scramble during the match itself?
answer: The Rock and Hogan called audibles to swap multiple key spots so Hogan could absorb the crowd's love as he faced his exit
choices: The Rock and Hogan called audibles to swap multiple key spots so Hogan could absorb the crowd's love as he faced his exit
Vince McMahon ran to the gorilla position to demand Pat Patterson change the finish to a Hogan win
The Rock walked out of the match mid-stride, demanding a script revision before continuing
Hogan tore up the rest of the script and ad-libbed his entire remaining offense
context: The match is widely considered one of the most emotional in WrestleMania history because of the unscripted crowd reaction. Hogan's post-match handshake with The Rock and 'do the right thing' gesture mid-fight created an organic face turn for Hogan. He went on to win his sixth WWF Championship a few weeks later at Backlash 2002.

question: Paul Levesque — the American professional wrestler far better known by his ring name Triple H — first used his signature finishing move, the Pedigree, in 1995. The move was a double-underhook facebuster: a punishing setup meant to look brutal, but its name was chosen to fit his snobby, blue-blooded rich-kid character of that period — Hunter Hearst Helmsley, the socialite from Greenwich, Connecticut. What did the ordinary English word 'pedigree' originally refer to, before wrestling picked it up?
answer: Genealogy showing pure aristocratic ancestry, as in Thoroughbred horses
choices: Genealogy showing pure aristocratic ancestry, as in Thoroughbred horses
The lineage of champions inherited through formal tutoring
The ranking of European nobility by birth-order and title
The selective process of breeding generations for purity
context: Hunter Hearst Helmsley was a snobby Connecticut blueblood character. The Pedigree finisher mocked the idea that he was 'establishing pedigree' on his opponents by humbling them. Levesque adapted the basic move concept from earlier wrestlers but made it his signature. The character softened into D-Generation X's degenerate version in 1997.

question: Extreme Championship Wrestling (ECW) held wild matches with barbed wire and exploding rings. That style came from Japanese deathmatch wrestling. Paul Heyman even brought Japanese stars to ECW shows in Philadelphia. In 1989, one wrestler founded Frontier Martial-Arts Wrestling (FMW), the company that started the deathmatch style. He later appeared in ECW. Who was he?
context: Atsushi Onita founded FMW (Frontier Martial-Arts Wrestling) in 1989. His no-rope barbed-wire and exploding-ring matches stunned audiences. Sabu, Terry Funk, and other ECW stars regularly worked Japanese deathmatch tours. Onita's influence on Heyman's Philadelphia hardcore booking is well documented in the wrestling press.

question: At the World Wrestling Federation (WWF) event King of the Ring on June 28, 1998, in Pittsburgh, the mysterious wrestler known as the Undertaker faced Mick Foley — wrestling as the strange masked character Mankind — inside a Hell in a Cell match. The match takes place under a huge steel-cage roof suspended over the ring, and wrestlers are allowed to climb up onto the flat top of the cage sixteen feet in the air. In the opening moments, the Undertaker did something to Foley that became the most-replayed bump in wrestling history. What did he do?
answer: Threw him off the top of the 16-foot cell, crashing through the Spanish announce table
choices: Threw him off the top of the 16-foot cell, crashing through the Spanish announce table
Chokeslammed him through the steel-mesh top of the cell from inside the cage
Tombstone-piledrove him on the steel floor as the match's opening move
Hit him with a steel chair as Foley climbed in through the top hatch
context: Foley actually took TWO of the most famous bumps in this match. The first (Undertaker throwing him off the top through the table 16 feet below) was the planned spot. The second — when Foley climbed back up after announcers thought he was dead, only for the Undertaker to chokeslam him through the cell roof onto the steel ring below — was a surprise. Foley landed with a chair on top of him. Both bumps are pre-WM18 (March 2002) Attitude Era canon.

question: The Iron Sheik — Khosrow Vaziri — dropped the WWF Championship to Hulk Hogan on January 23, 1984, kicking off Hulkamania. Sheik had won the title from Bob Backlund a month earlier. The original plan, according to multiple later accounts, had been for someone else to be Hogan's first championship victim — and a major WWF deal in late 1983 was specifically structured so Sheik would 'job out' to Hogan. Who was the originally-planned opponent that the WWF replaced with the Iron Sheik?
answer: Don Muraco, the Intercontinental Champion, whom WWF had planned to elevate to the title first
choices: Don Muraco, the Intercontinental Champion, whom WWF had planned to elevate to the title first
Sgt. Slaughter, whose return from AWA was delayed
Big John Studd, who had a clause that prevented him losing on his Garden debut
Roddy Piper, whose contract was still being negotiated in late 1983
context: The booking has been speculated about for years; multiple accounts (including books like 'Sheik' by Page Magen and various Hogan interviews) suggest Bob Backlund's title transition to Hogan was complex and that the Sheik was selected because he could be relied on to do the job correctly. Backlund himself had been a long-running champion (1978-1983) but the WWF wanted a 'foreign menace' transitional champion before the Hogan victory.

question: Super Bowl 49, played February 1, 2015, ended when Patriots rookie Malcolm Butler intercepted Russell Wilson at the goal line. Butler, an undrafted rookie from West Alabama, had studied Seattle's goal-line slant package on film all week before the game. In later interviews, coach Bill Belichick said the tape gave the Patriots confidence Seattle would call that exact play. What had the tape shown?
answer: The Patriots had seen Wilson and Lockette run the same goal-line slant package three times earlier in the playoff run
choices: The Patriots had seen Wilson and Lockette run the same goal-line slant package three times earlier in the playoff run
The Seahawks had used the play in their NFC Championship win and the Patriots had analyzed each formation
Wilson had favored slants over runs in 2014 short-yardage situations 73% of the time
Bevell had used the play as a tendency against goal-line bunch formations
context: Butler's interception is the most-second-guessed playcall in NFL history. The Patriots' goal-line bunch coverage was specifically prepared for the slant the Seahawks ran. Butler's name became permanently associated with the moment. The play won the Patriots Super Bowl XLIX 28-24. Pete Carroll defended the playcall in his post-game press conference and afterwards.

question: Marshawn Lynch's iconic 67-yard 'Beast Quake' touchdown against the Saints on January 8, 2011, was the closing score of a 41-36 Seahawks victory. The run broke at least nine tackles, including a famous stiff-arm of Saints DB (defensive back) Tracy Porter. What specific physical feature of Lynch's running style — used on the Porter stiff-arm — is often cited by analysts as the defining move of the run?
answer: His 'sasquatch' stiff-arm, planted flat-palm into Porter's facemask and lifting him backwards
choices: His 'sasquatch' stiff-arm, planted flat-palm into Porter's facemask and lifting him backwards
His 'spin-cycle' rotation through three would-be tacklers near the line
His 'mountain-goat' jump-hop over the safety cleats at the 35-yard line
His 'jet-ski' lateral cut through the linebacker zone at the 20
context: The Tracy Porter stiff-arm has been singled out by analysts including Booger McFarland on NFL Network. Lynch absorbed eight other tackles on the play. The run remains the single most-replayed Seahawks moment in franchise history. Lynch went on to gain 1,257 yards in 2010 despite arriving from Buffalo midseason.

question: The Seahawks' Legion of Boom defense of the early 2010s — Sherman, Earl Thomas, Kam Chancellor, and Brandon Browner — was statistically dominant for several years. The 2013 season included the all-time NFL passing-defense yards-per-game lowest mark in 16 years. What was that 2013 Seahawks defense's specific yards-per-game allowed?
answer: 172.0 yards per game, the lowest pass-yards-per-game allowed in the NFL since 1997
choices: 172.0 yards per game, the lowest pass-yards-per-game allowed in the NFL since 1997
165.4 yards per game, the lowest pass defense by any modern team
189.3 yards per game, ranking second in NFL pass defense history
203.1 yards per game, the league's best in 2013
context: The 2013 Seahawks led the NFL in fewest yards allowed and points allowed — the rare team to lead both. They allowed 14.4 ppg and 273.6 ypg. Super Bowl XLVIII proved the defense's dominance — they held Peyton Manning's record-breaking offense to 8 points. The Legion of Boom remained largely intact for several more seasons.

question: The Seahawks' draft history includes a 2012 third-round pick of Russell Wilson at 75th overall — at the time, considered a major reach because of Wilson's short height (5'11"). The pick is widely cited as one of the great steals in NFL history. The selection happened despite the Seahawks having signed a $26M free-agent quarterback that same offseason. Who was the QB (quarterback) they had signed?
answer: Matt Flynn, the former Packers backup signed to a 3-year, $26M deal in March 2012
choices: Matt Flynn, the former Packers backup signed to a 3-year, $26M deal in March 2012
Tarvaris Jackson, who had been the previous year's starter
Kevin Kolb, who had been a high-priced free agent
Carson Palmer, who had been a trade target from the Bengals
context: Flynn had set Packers records in the 2012 season finale and was the most-coveted FA QB of 2012. Seattle signed him with the intention to start him; Wilson outperformed him in training camp and beat him out for the starting job. Flynn never started a game for Seattle. Wilson became a two-time Pro Bowler in his first two seasons.

question: Geno Smith's 2022 resurgence in Seattle came after Russell Wilson was traded to Denver in March 2022. Smith — the Seahawks' backup since 2019 — was widely seen as a placeholder. Instead, he had a remarkable season. What was Smith's exact 2022 completion percentage, which led the NFL?
answer: 69.8% — the highest completion rate in the NFL in 2022
choices: 69.8% — the highest completion rate in the NFL in 2022
67.2% — leading the AFC in completion rate but behind Goff in the NFC
71.3% — the highest single-season rate in NFL history
68.7% — second to Joe Burrow in 2022 completion percentage
context: Geno Smith led the NFL in completion percentage in 2022. He made the Pro Bowl as an injury replacement, became the Comeback Player of the Year, and earned a 3-year contract extension. The 2022 Seahawks finished 9-8 and made the playoffs in Carroll's 13th season, snapping a one-year postseason drought.

question: Ichiro Suzuki's record 262-hit 2004 season for the Seattle Mariners broke George Sisler's 84-year-old single-season record of 257. The exact moment of the record-breaking hit was on October 1, 2004, at Safeco Field against Texas Rangers pitcher Ryan Drese. Ichiro had been at the plate eight times in that game, the third game of the season-ending series. Who was the Rangers' catcher who came out from behind the plate to congratulate Ichiro at first base after the historic hit?
answer: Rod Barajas, the Rangers' catcher, who stepped out to congratulate Ichiro at first base
choices: Rod Barajas, the Rangers' catcher, who stepped out to congratulate Ichiro at first base
Ivan Rodriguez, the Hall-of-Famer behind the plate that day
Gerald Laird, the Rangers' backup catcher who replaced Barajas
Pudge Rodriguez, who happened to be umpiring the third-base line
context: Barajas's gesture was a respectful moment from across the league. Members of the Sisler family — George's daughter Frances and granddaughter — were in attendance. Ichiro received a standing ovation that lasted several minutes. The hit was a clean line drive to right; Ichiro's wife Yumiko and his teammates joined him at the plate during the celebration.

question: Ken Griffey Jr.'s controversial 2000 trade from Seattle to Cincinnati came after he requested to be moved closer to his family in Florida. Junior had grown up in Cincinnati — his father Ken Griffey Sr. had been a Big Red Machine outfielder there. The trade sent Griffey to the Reds for which 1999 Mariners players?
answer: Mike Cameron, Brett Tomko, Antonio Perez, and Jake Meyer — collectively worth far less than Griffey
choices: Mike Cameron, Brett Tomko, Antonio Perez, and Jake Meyer — collectively worth far less than Griffey
Pokey Reese and Ryan Anderson — both of whom retired within four years
Sean Casey and Pete Harnisch — both of whom were veterans approaching the end
Aaron Boone and Travis Lee — both of whom became defensive role players
context: The trade was widely considered a steal for Cincinnati at the time but the Mariners got useful talent. Mike Cameron had a multi-year career as a quality outfielder in Seattle. Brett Tomko provided rotation depth. Griffey's Reds career was injury-marred; he never matched his Seattle years. He returned to Seattle in 2009 to finish his career.

question: On October 8, 1995, in the ALDS (American League Division Series) Game 5 'Edgar's Double' play, Ken Griffey Jr. raced from first base all the way to home plate to score the winning run. The Yankees right fielder threw home; catcher Mike Stanley took the relay; Junior slid in just ahead of the tag. The play has been replayed millions of times. Approximately how long did it take Junior to go from first to home?
answer: Around nine and a half seconds, based on broadcast-film analysis
choices: Around nine and a half seconds, based on broadcast-film analysis
Just over eleven seconds, a normal first-to-home pace
Around seven seconds flat, an Olympic-sprinter pace
Just under thirteen seconds, slow for a runner like Junior
context: Junior's slide into home ended in a celebration pile at the plate. The exact time is an estimate; modern Statcast wasn't around in 1995. Joey Cora had scored the tying run on the same hit. Lou Piniella was managing. Dave Niehaus's call defined Mariners baseball lore for a generation.

question: Felix Hernandez's perfect game on August 15, 2012, was the third perfect game in MLB in 2012 — the others by Philip Humber (April 21) and Matt Cain (June 13). 'King Felix' struck out 12 batters. The final out was on a swinging strike by what Tampa Bay Rays player?
answer: Sean Rodriguez, the Rays' utility infielder
choices: Sean Rodriguez, the Rays' utility infielder
Evan Longoria, the Rays' star third baseman
B.J. Upton, the Rays' center fielder
Carlos Pena, the Rays' first baseman
context: Sean Rodriguez swung and missed at a 1-2 changeup for the 27th out. The crowd of 21,889 at Safeco Field erupted as catcher John Jaso threw the ball to Felix and the team mobbed him at the mound. Felix used 113 pitches to retire all 27 Rays. He had thrown the game's first pitch — a fastball strike — at 7:11 PM Pacific.

question: The 2001 Mariners 116-win season was the result of a remarkable mid-1990s organizational rebuild. After Ken Griffey Jr.'s 2000 trade and Alex Rodriguez's 2000 free-agent departure, the team was widely expected to collapse. Instead, GM (general manager) Pat Gillick made several key acquisitions for 2001 — most importantly, signing Ichiro Suzuki from Japan. But Gillick had also signed a veteran second baseman who was the catalyst for the 2001 offense. Who was Seattle's 2001 second baseman who hit .331 with 37 home runs?
answer: Bret Boone, who had a career year with 141 RBI and made his second All-Star team
choices: Bret Boone, who had a career year with 141 RBI and made his second All-Star team
Mark McLemore, who was their reliable veteran
Carlos Guillen, who was their starting shortstop
Mike Cameron, who had been the centerpiece of the Griffey trade
context: Boone signed with Seattle after a 7-year stint with the Reds and Padres. His 2001 season — 37 HRs, 141 RBI, .331 average — earned him MVP votes (finished 3rd). He played second base while John Olerud (also 2001 acquisition) anchored first base. The 116-win team featured Ichiro, Olerud, Boone, Edgar, and Mike Cameron in the everyday lineup.

question: Goku is a spiky-haired boy from another planet with a monkey-like tail, super strength, and a cheerful appetite for fighting. In this famous 1984 manga and anime by the Japanese artist Akira Toriyama, Goku roams Earth searching for seven glowing wish-granting orbs and battles ever stronger enemies as he grows up. What is the whole series called?
context: Toriyama loosely based Goku on Sun Wukong from the 16th-century Chinese novel Journey to the West. Goku's surname Son and the magical staff he carries early on come straight from that source.

question: In this Studio Ghibli film from 1988, two young sisters named Satsuki and Mei move to the Japanese countryside with their father while their mother is sick in a nearby hospital. In the woods behind their new house they meet a huge fluffy gray forest spirit who sleeps in a giant tree, and later they ride a grinning Catbus with fur, whiskers, and glowing paws. What is the movie called?
context: Released in 1988 alongside Takahata's Grave of the Fireflies as a double feature. Hayao Miyazaki wrote and directed it. The Totoro silhouette became the studio's logo.

question: In 2001, director Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli released a movie about a ten-year-old girl named Chihiro. When her family drives into a strange abandoned town, Chihiro's parents are turned into pigs and she is trapped there. To free them, she takes a job scrubbing floors at a huge bathhouse where spirits and gods come to soak. The film later won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature. What is it called?
context: Spirited Away won the Oscar at the 2003 ceremony. It also won the Golden Bear at Berlin, the only hand-drawn film ever to do so. Hayao Miyazaki did not attend the Oscars in protest of the Iraq War.

question: Studio Ghibli, the Japanese animation studio led by Hayao Miyazaki, released a 1989 film about a thirteen-year-old witch. Following witch tradition, she flies off to a new seaside town for a year on her own. With her sarcastic black cat Jiji, she rents an attic above a bakery and starts a broomstick delivery service. The movie is named after her. What is the young witch's name?
context: Kiki's Delivery Service was Miyazaki's first major box-office success in Japan. It was adapted from a children's novel by Eiko Kadono. The Japanese dub of Jiji has the cat speaking; the English dub kept him speaking throughout.

question: Monkey Punch's Japanese manga hero Lupin III is a master thief who steals treasures around the world while wearing a bright red or green jacket. His name comes from his grandfather, a much older character — the suave French gentleman-thief written by novelist Maurice Leblanc in a series of Paris-set adventure novels starting in 1905. Which fictional thief is Lupin III's grandfather?
context: Monkey Punch created the manga in 1967. Arsene Lupin was the protagonist of stories by French author Maurice Leblanc starting in 1905. The Lupin estate periodically objected to the unauthorized grandson; the conflict shaped how Lupin III was credited overseas.

question: Astro Boy is a bright-eyed robot kid built to look like a human boy. He has rocket boots in his feet, machine guns tucked in his hips, and lasers built into his fingers. The Japanese cartoonist who first drew him in 1952 is nicknamed the godfather of manga because so many later artists copied his rounded, expressive style. Who is that pioneering artist?
context: Tezuka's Mighty Atom — Astro Boy in English — debuted in manga form in 1952. The 1963 TV anime adaptation was the first weekly half-hour animated television series in Japan. Tezuka also created Phoenix, Buddha, and Black Jack.

question: Sailor Moon's real name is Usagi Tsukino — a clumsy Tokyo schoolgirl who transforms into a moon-powered warrior in a sailor-suit costume. Her team of Sailor Guardians are each named after a planet, like Sailor Mercury, Sailor Mars, and Sailor Venus. A single Japanese woman first drew this manga back in 1991 and reshaped the whole magical-girl genre. Who is she?
context: Usagi means rabbit; the moon is associated with rabbits in Japanese folklore. The manga ran in Nakayoshi magazine. The 1992 Toei anime adaptation aired internationally and is the show most Western fans grew up with.

question: A shy teen boy named Yugi Mutou lives in the fictional Domino City, where his grandfather Sugoroku runs a small game shop. In the shop, Yugi's grandpa sells packs of a fantasy trading card game full of dragons, wizards, and monsters. Yugi solves an ancient Egyptian puzzle and grows into a champion duelist. What is this long-running Japanese anime called?
context: Kazuki Takahashi created the manga in Weekly Shonen Jump. The Duel Monsters card game in the manga was so popular Konami launched the real-world Yu-Gi-Oh! Trading Card Game in 1999. Takahashi died in 2022 in a snorkeling accident off Okinawa.

question: A modern Japanese schoolgirl named Kagome falls down an old dry well on her family's shrine and lands five hundred years in the past. There she meets a boy with silver hair and pointed dog ears who is half dog demon, half human and carries a giant sword. Together they hunt for the scattered shards of a magic jewel. What is this Rumiko Takahashi manga called?
context: Takahashi is one of the best-selling manga authors of all time. Inuyasha ran in Weekly Shonen Sunday from 1996 to 2008. Kagome Higurashi is the schoolgirl; Inuyasha is the half-demon she ends up shard-hunting with.

question: Cowboy Bebop is a jazzy space-western anime from 1998. The crew of the ship Bebop hunts down criminals through the solar system for bounty money. The team is a lazy gunfighter named Spike, a hard ex-cop named Jet, a con-woman named Faye, a bouncy child hacker called Ed, and one very smart Welsh corgi with genius-level intelligence. What is the corgi's name?
context: Ein is a data dog — a genetically enhanced Pembroke Welsh Corgi smarter than most humans. Cowboy Bebop aired on TV Tokyo in 1998. Shinichiro Watanabe directed it and Yoko Kanno scored it with her band The Seatbelts.

question: In the 1995 anime Neon Genesis Evangelion, huge geometric monsters attack a future Tokyo, and only three teenage pilots strapped inside towering biomechanical mechs called Evangelions can fight them off. Inside the show, no one calls these enemies aliens or monsters — the government and the pilots use a religious name for them instead. What name is that?
context: Each Angel is named after a Judeo-Christian angel — Sachiel, Shamshel, Ramiel, Israfel, Sandalphon. The series aired on TV Tokyo from October 1995 to March 1996 and was created by Hideaki Anno at studio Gainax.

question: Akira is a 1988 Japanese anime film that opens with a huge silent blast leveling Tokyo. The story jumps to 2019 Neo-Tokyo, a neon city rebuilt on the ruins. A biker teen named Tetsuo Shima gets caught in a secret military test and gains scary, unstable psychic powers. The film was directed by the same artist who wrote and drew the massive original manga it is based on. Who is he?
context: Akira's $11 million budget was the highest in anime history at that point. The manga began in Young Magazine in 1982 and continued until 1990; Otomo released the film midway through and altered the manga's ending afterward.

question: Ghost in the Shell is a 1995 Japanese animated cyberpunk film set in a future where people replace body parts with machines. In it, a cybernetic policewoman named Motoko Kusanagi — nearly her whole body is machine, only her brain is still human — hunts a mysterious hacker called the Puppet Master who takes over people's minds through the global network. The film became famous worldwide and later inspired The Matrix. Which director made it?
context: Oshii had previously directed Patlabor. The Wachowskis showed Ghost in the Shell to producer Joel Silver as visual reference when pitching The Matrix. Shirow's manga began in Young Magazine in 1989.

question: Cowboy Bebop is a 1998 Japanese anime about a crew of ragtag space bounty hunters chasing criminals across the solar system. Its opening credits play a loud big-band jazz number written by composer Yoko Kanno and performed by her studio band, The Seatbelts. The music blasts over slick silhouette shots of the crew, and the title of the song flashes on screen in one giant word. What is that opening song called?
context: Tank! is built around a walking bass riff and a horn line that became one of the most-recognized anime themes of all time. Kanno wrote dozens of pieces for the show; the soundtrack was released across four CD volumes plus a film score.

question: Studio Ghibli is the Japanese animation studio behind films like Spirited Away and My Neighbor Totoro. It was founded in Tokyo in 1985 by director Hayao Miyazaki, producer Toshio Suzuki, and one other veteran director — an older friend of Miyazaki's who had mentored him for years. That third founder later made Grave of the Fireflies, a heartbreaking film about two children in wartime Japan. Who is he?
context: Takahata had been Miyazaki's mentor at Toei Animation. The studio name Ghibli comes from an Italian word for a hot Saharan wind — also the name of an Italian World War II scout plane that Miyazaki, an aviation enthusiast, admired.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke came out in 1997 and told the story of a young prince, a wolf-raised girl named San, and a forest god at war with iron-mining humans. It shattered Japan's box-office records that year and became the highest-grossing film ever in Japan up to that point. Later the same year, one American blockbuster came out and finally passed it. Which American film was it?
context: Mononoke was Japan's highest-grossing domestic film until Spirited Away topped it in 2001. Miramax bought the US distribution and Harvey Weinstein famously got told by producer Toshio Suzuki to stop demanding cuts — Suzuki sent him a katana with the message NO CUTS.

question: In the anime Rurouni Kenshin, set in Japan just after the samurai age ended in the 1870s, a wandering swordsman named Kenshin Himura carries a very unusual katana. The sword's sharp edge is flipped to the wrong side of the blade, so it cannot slice — Kenshin has sworn never to kill again after his violent past. What is a reverse-edged katana like this called in Japanese?
context: Sakabato means reverse-blade sword. Kenshin Himura was once the legendary Hitokiri Battosai assassin of the Bakumatsu period. Watsuki later landed in legal trouble in Japan that disrupted the manga's late run.

question: In the anime Trigun, a spiky-blond gunfighter named Vash the Stampede roams a dusty desert colony planet with two suns. He's such a walking disaster area — towns crumble in his wake — that every bounty hunter for light-years wants to catch him. Each episode opens by flashing his bounty poster on screen with an eye-popping cash number in the local currency. How much is Vash's bounty?
context: Vash is nicknamed the Humanoid Typhoon for the devastation that seems to follow him, though he himself refuses to kill. Studio Orange remade the series as Trigun Stampede in 2023 with full-CG animation.

question: Slayers is a 1995 comedy fantasy anime that follows a short red-haired teenage sorceress named Lina Inverse as she and her party bumble across a swords-and-magic world. Lina is famous for casting an incredibly destructive black magic spell that leaves smoking craters where towns used to be — so bad that shopkeepers hide when they see her ride in. What is her signature spell called?
context: Lina Inverse is the sorceress; she can also cast the even more dangerous Giga Slave, which draws from the Lord of Nightmares. Her party includes swordsman Gourry Gabriev, chimera Zelgadis Greywords, and princess Amelia Wil Tesla Saillune.

question: The 1979 anime Mobile Suit Gundam threw out cartoon-style super-robots and imagined giant piloted mechs as gritty military hardware — soldiers pulling levers, machines that overheated, weapons that ran out of ammo. That grounded approach kicked off what fans now call the real-robot style of anime, and the Gundam franchise has run for over four decades. Which director created Gundam and shaped its whole space-war universe?
context: The original series was a ratings flop until reruns and the model kits — Gunpla — turned it into a juggernaut. Tomino is nicknamed Kill 'Em All Tomino for the body counts in his series. Wing in 1995 was the franchise's US Toonami breakthrough.

question: Rumiko Takahashi is one of the most successful manga artists in Japanese history, later famous for Ranma 1/2 and Inuyasha. Her very first big hit ran in a weekly manga magazine from 1978 to 1987. It starred a horned alien princess named Lum who wears a tiger-stripe bikini and floats through the air. When her human fiance Ataru cheats on her, Lum zaps him with lightning. What is the series called?
context: Urusei Yatsura ran in Weekly Shonen Sunday from 1978 to 1987. The title is a pun roughly meaning Those Obnoxious Aliens. Lum's catchphrase darling and her electric shocks became cultural touchstones in Japan.

question: Slam Dunk is a wildly popular Japanese basketball manga written and drawn by Takehiko Inoue between 1990 and 1996. In the story, a red-haired first-year troublemaker named Hanamichi Sakuragi joins his high school's basketball team, mostly to impress a classmate named Haruko who loves the sport. His team wears red jerseys and plays in Kanagawa Prefecture. What is the name of Sakuragi's high school?
context: Inoue is now also famous for Vagabond, the Musashi Miyamoto epic. Slam Dunk is credited with inspiring a generation of Japanese basketball players. Inoue directed The First Slam Dunk, a 2022 animated theatrical film he wrote and storyboarded himself.

question: Berserk is a dark fantasy Japanese manga that Kentaro Miura began drawing in 1988. Set in a medieval European-style world, it follows a huge scarred mercenary swordsman who carries an iron blade the size of a slab. He has been branded for sacrifice and is hunted every night by demons. What is the swordsman's name?
context: Kentaro Miura drew Berserk in Young Animal magazine for over 30 years. Miura died unexpectedly in May 2021 at age 54. The manga has continued since 2022 under his longtime friend Kouji Mori and Studio Gaga.

question: Captain Tsubasa is a Japanese sports manga first drawn in 1981 by Yoichi Takahashi. Its hero is a young athlete named Tsubasa Ozora who dreams of one day playing in a world cup for Japan. Many real professional players — including Lionel Messi, Zinedine Zidane, and Fernando Torres — have said this manga inspired them as kids. What sport does Tsubasa play?
context: Players including Lionel Messi, Andres Iniesta, Alessandro Del Piero, and Fernando Torres have all cited Captain Tsubasa as a childhood inspiration. The series ran in Weekly Shonen Jump.

question: Fist of the North Star is a Japanese manga set in a nuclear-wasteland future after World War Three. Its hero is a stoic seven-star warrior who uses an ancient Chinese-style fighting art called Hokuto Shinken. He hits hidden pressure points on his enemies with lightning-fast jabs, then walks away — and seconds later the foes explode from the inside. What is this warrior's name?
context: Buronson wrote it and Tetsuo Hara drew it. The catchphrase you are already dead — omae wa mou shindeiru — became one of the most-quoted lines in anime. Kenshiro is the successor of the assassination art Hokuto Shinken.

question: Before he founded Studio Ghibli, Japanese director Hayao Miyazaki made a 1984 anime film set in a poisoned far-future world. Its heroine is a kind princess of a small valley kingdom who rides the wind on a glider and befriends the giant armored insects that everyone else fears. The movie is named after her. What is her name?
context: Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind was based on Miyazaki's own manga, which he had begun in 1982. The film's commercial success was what made Studio Ghibli's founding in 1985 possible.

question: Code Geass is a 2006 Japanese anime set in a world where the Britannian Empire has conquered Japan. An exiled Britannian prince, now hiding as a high school student in Tokyo, secretly leads a masked revolt against his own family's empire. He gains a mind-control power called Geass after a deal with C.C., a mysterious green-haired girl who cannot die. What is the prince's name?
context: C.C. is the immortal who grants Lelouch his Geass — the power of absolute obedience in anyone who meets his eyes. Lelouch's masked alter ego is Zero. Goro Taniguchi directed; Ichiro Okouchi wrote the scripts.

question: FLCL (pronounced 'Fooly Cooly') is a wild six-episode Japanese anime released in 2000 by Studio Gainax. It opens with a strange pink-haired alien girl roaring into a sleepy Japanese town on a yellow Vespa scooter. She spots a bored twelve-year-old boy named Naota and smacks him in the head with her blue electric bass guitar. What is the alien girl's name?
context: Haruhara Haruko is the chaos that breaks open the everyday life of Naota Nandaba. FLCL — Fooly Cooly — was directed by Kazuya Tsurumaki. The soundtrack by the rock band The Pillows became iconic on its own.

question: In the hip-hop-scored anime Samurai Champloo, a cheerful teenage waitress named Fuu convinces two rival swordsmen — the wild feral fighter Mugen and the stoic ronin Jin — to travel with her across Edo-era Japan. She is searching for a specific mystery samurai from her childhood memories. He has one very strange trait she uses to identify him. What is it?
context: Mugen is the wild swordsman; Jin is the stoic ronin; Fuu is the teenage waitress who recruited them. Nujabes provided much of the score, including Battlecry. The series ran 26 episodes on Fuji TV.

question: In the quiet, dreamlike anime Mushishi, a soft-spoken white-haired traveler named Ginko wanders old-time rural Japan carrying a wooden medicine chest. He helps villagers who have been hurt or haunted by strange, half-visible spirit creatures that most humans cannot see at all. What does the show call these primal spirit creatures?
context: Mushi are primordial life forms — neither plant nor animal, neither benevolent nor malevolent. Ginko has white hair and a green eye because of his own encounter with them. Hiroshi Nagahama directed the 2005 anime.

question: Before he became world-famous for Dragon Ball, Japanese cartoonist Akira Toriyama drew a 1980 gag comedy manga. It stars Arale Norimaki, a tiny robot girl in round glasses who thinks she is a normal human kid. She was built by a bumbling inventor named Senbei in a strange little place called Penguin Village. What is the manga called?
context: Arale Norimaki is the robot girl; Senbei Norimaki is her inventor. The manga ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1980 to 1984. Toriyama later included Penguin Village cameos in Dragon Ball.

question: Castle of Cagliostro is a 1979 Japanese animated film starring the master thief Lupin III. Lupin sneaks into a tiny European country ruled by a scheming count, hoping to rescue Princess Clarisse, a young woman being forced into marriage. The film was the very first feature movie directed by an animator who would go on to found Studio Ghibli. Who is he?
context: Cagliostro is widely considered the best Lupin III film. Miyazaki had directed TV episodes before but this was his first theatrical feature. Steven Spielberg reportedly cited Cagliostro's car chase as among the greatest action sequences he had ever seen.

question: Digimon started in Japan in 1997 as a line of small handheld virtual-pet keychains — you fed the little digital monster on the tiny screen, trained it, and watched it evolve into stronger forms. They landed on toy shelves right next to another famous digital-pet toy that had come out a year earlier in 1996 and already sold millions of units worldwide. Which competing digital-pet toy did Digimon fight for shelf space with?
context: Bandai released the original Digital Monster virtual pet in 1997, designed by Aki Maita's husband Akiyoshi Hongo as a boys' version of Tamagotchi. The Digimon Adventure anime introduced characters like Tai, Agumon, and Matt.

question: In Dragon Ball Z, Goku and his friends chase seven wish orbs to the alien planet Namek. There the tyrant Frieza — a small icy warlord who has conquered whole galaxies — kills Goku's oldest best friend Krillin right in front of him. Rage floods Goku, his hair explodes upward in gold, his eyes turn green, and his body lights up. This ancient legendary transformation had not been seen in a thousand years. What is this form called?
context: Goku is the first Saiyan to achieve the form in over a thousand years. The transformation became one of the most-referenced moments in anime history. The Frieza arc on Namek famously lasted dozens of episodes despite the in-universe planet exploding in five minutes.

question: Neon Genesis Evangelion is a 1995 Japanese anime by director Hideaki Anno. Teenagers pilot giant biomechanical robots called Evangelions, or Evas, to defend Tokyo-3 from monsters called Angels. Anxious Shinji Ikari pilots Eva Unit 01. Fiery redhead Asuka Langley pilots Eva Unit 02. A quiet, pale, blue-haired girl called the First Child pilots the prototype Eva Unit 00. What is her name?
context: Rei has blue hair and red eyes and a flat affect — at least early in the series. Character designs were by Yoshiyuki Sadamoto, who also drew the manga adaptation. Rei's quiet presence and visual design became wildly influential on subsequent anime.

question: Studio Ghibli released a 1992 film directed by Hayao Miyazaki, set on the sunny Adriatic coast between the World Wars. A gruff former World War I flying ace works as a bounty hunter, chasing sky pirates from the cockpit of his crimson seaplane. Years earlier, a strange curse turned his human face into that of a talking pig. The movie is named after him. What is the film called?
context: Marco Pagot was the human pilot before the curse; Porco Rosso means Red Pig in Italian. Miyazaki, an aviation obsessive, drew the planes himself. The film originated as an in-flight short for Japan Airlines that grew into a feature.

question: Akira is a 1988 Japanese anime film set in 2019 Neo-Tokyo, a neon city rebuilt after a mysterious blast. A teen biker named Tetsuo Shima crashes his motorcycle, is dragged into a secret military lab, and returns with huge, unstable psychic powers. His best friend, the leader of their motorcycle gang, chases him across the city trying to stop the destruction. What is that friend's name?
context: Shotaro Kaneda rides the iconic red motorcycle whose long sliding stop became an instant cinema-shorthand for cyberpunk anime. The slide was hand-animated frame by frame. Mitsuo Iwata voiced Kaneda in Japanese; Cam Clarke voiced him in the original Streamline dub.

question: Dragon Ball Z is the 1990s sequel to Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball, following the grown-up Goku and his fighter friends. The American company Funimation made the popular English-language dub. Voice actor Sean Schemmel played the hero Goku. A single other Funimation actor voiced most of the big male co-stars — proud Prince Vegeta, the green warrior Piccolo, ex-desert-bandit Yamcha, and old Master Roshi. Who was he?
context: Sabat voices Vegeta, Piccolo, Yamcha, Mr. Popo, Burter, Recoome, Korin, Shenron, King Vegeta, and dozens of others. Schemmel voices Goku, Goten, King Kai, and Nail. Both actors started at Funimation in Texas and continued the roles for decades.

question: Berserk is Kentaro Miura's dark fantasy Japanese manga about mercenaries in a medieval world. Griffith, the beautiful golden-haired leader of the mercenary Band of the Hawk, is captured, tortured, and left crippled in a dungeon. In despair he clutches a small red bead-like stone he has carried for years. It opens a portal, and he strikes a bargain with five dark gods called the God Hand, launching the massacre known as the Eclipse. What is the red stone called?
context: The Behelit is sometimes called the Egg of the King. The five beings Griffith contracts are the God Hand. Kentaro Miura drew the Eclipse arc as some of the most intense art in manga history; he kept refining the panels long afterward.

question: Cowboy Bebop is a 1998 anime about a crew of bounty hunters flying through the solar system on the ship Bebop. In the closing two-part finale, the moody swordsman-turned-gunslinger Spike learns that his old crime-syndicate lover Julia has been killed. Alone and grieving, Spike walks back into the Red Dragon syndicate's tower for one last showdown with the crime boss Vicious. What is the final episode of the series called?
context: The series was originally planned for 26 episodes but several stations only aired 13. The full run aired in Japan via WOWOW satellite. The 2001 theatrical film Knockin' on Heaven's Door is set between episodes 22 and 23 of the series.

question: Monkey Punch's Japanese manga Lupin III, first drawn in 1967, follows a master thief named Arsene Lupin III, grandson of the classic French gentleman burglar. Wherever Lupin travels stealing famous treasures, one tired police inspector from Japan, working for the international police agency Interpol, chases him around the globe. The two have been playing cat-and-mouse for decades, and the inspector always seems just one step behind. What is the inspector's name?
context: Koichi Zenigata is named for Heiji Zenigata, a fictional Edo-period police detective. The Castle of Cagliostro gave Zenigata the dignity of being the moral heart of Miyazaki's Lupin film. He has been voiced in Japanese by Goro Naya, Kiyoshi Kobayashi, and others.

question: Mobile Suit Gundam Wing is a Japanese anime that first aired in 1995. In the late 1990s it became one of the first big hits on Toonami, the Cartoon Network afternoon anime block. Set in the year After Colony 195, it follows a small group of teenage boys sent from the space colonies down to Earth as pilots of powerful mecha called Gundams, aiming to break the war with the Earth Alliance. How many teen Gundam pilots are there?
context: The five Gundam pilots are Heero Yuy, Duo Maxwell, Trowa Barton, Quatre Raberba Winner, and Chang Wufei. Wing aired in the US on Cartoon Network's Toonami in March 2000 and ran as the kick-off to that block's anime mainstreaming.

question: Studio Ghibli released a 2008 animated film directed by Hayao Miyazaki and loosely inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's The Little Mermaid. A goldfish-like sea creature escapes her wizard father, gets stuck in a jar on a beach, and is rescued by a five-year-old boy named Sosuke. He keeps her in a bucket, feeds her ham, and gives her a name. The movie is named after her. What is the fish-girl's name?
context: Sosuke is the boy. Ponyo is the daughter of the sea-wizard Fujimoto and the sea-goddess Granmamare. Miyazaki personally hand-drew the film's distinctive wave sequences and reportedly threw out CGI experiments to keep the animation hand-drawn throughout.

question: Howl's Moving Castle is a 2004 Studio Ghibli film directed by Hayao Miyazaki, based on a novel by British writer Diana Wynne Jones. A shy young hat-maker named Sophie is cursed by a jealous witch to look like a ninety-year-old woman. She wanders off and hides inside a huge walking mechanical castle owned by the wizard Howl. Inside the castle's hearth burns a talkative fire demon who secretly powers the whole castle and has an old bargain with Howl. What is the demon's name?
context: Calcifer powers the castle by burning Howl's heart. Sophie's curse can be broken if she breaks the contract. Christian Bale voiced Howl and Billy Crystal voiced Calcifer in the English dub. Miyazaki took the directing job over from Mamoru Hosoda after the latter departed the project.

question: In Dragon Ball Z's Cell saga, the bio-android Cell achieves his perfect form by absorbing Android 17 and Android 18. The arc climaxes at the Cell Games, where Cell, displeased by Android 16's peace-preaching, crushes the peaceful android mid-speech. This shatters Gohan's psychological control. What does Gohan ascend to?
context: Super Saiyan 2 is distinguished by Gohan's spikier hair, electric aura, and dramatic increase in power. Goku could not achieve it during the Cell saga; SSJ2 first manifested in the franchise via Gohan at the Cell Games. Mystic Gohan and Ultimate Gohan are later forms achieved during the Buu saga via the Elder Kai's unlocking ritual. Goku's sacrifice (Instant Transmission with Cell to King Kai's planet) happens AFTER Gohan's transformation, not before.

question: Neon Genesis Evangelion is a 1995 Japanese mecha anime directed by Hideaki Anno at Studio Gainax. It shows teenage pilots defending Tokyo-3 from monsters, and it is packed with Christian iconography — the monsters are called Angels, a spear from the crucifixion story shows up as the Lance of Longinus, and the Tree of Life diagram appears on a wall. Anno himself was raised in a non-Christian Japanese household. In interviews he later gave his real reason for choosing these symbols. Why did he pick them?
answer: Because it looked cool and was visually distinct from typical Japanese motifs
choices: Because it looked cool and was visually distinct from typical Japanese motifs
Because Anno had been studying Christian theology at Tokyo University seminary
Because the studio's American distributor required Western religious imagery
Because Gainax founder Toshio Okada was a devout Catholic theologian
context: Anno has repeatedly said in interviews that he and the staff found Christian imagery exotic and visually striking. The Tree of Life motif on the wall of NERV headquarters and the angel-name conventions are aesthetic choices, not statements of religious meaning. The Rebuild tetralogy began in 2007 and concluded in 2021 with Thrice Upon a Time.

question: In 1997 Hayao Miyazaki finished Princess Mononoke, a dark Studio Ghibli film about a girl raised by wolves and a boy caught between forest gods and human miners. When Miramax boss Harvey Weinstein tried to trim its grim scenes for the 1999 American release, the English-dub writer fought hard to keep every tough theme intact. Which British fantasy novelist wrote that dub script?
context: Gaiman has said the experience was difficult — Weinstein wanted the dub simplified for American audiences. Producer Toshio Suzuki famously sent Weinstein a katana with the message NO CUTS. Billy Crudup voiced Ashitaka and Claire Danes voiced San.

question: Katsuhiro Otomo's 1988 anime Akira is a landmark Japanese film about biker gangs in a ruined future Tokyo. The Japanese ensemble Geinoh Yamashirogumi composed its whole score BEFORE most of the film was drawn, and the animators then cut the visuals to fit the music. Which three unusual sounds did Geinoh Yamashirogumi build the score from?
answer: Taiko drums, Indonesian gamelan, and traditional Japanese noh chanting
choices: Taiko drums, Indonesian gamelan, and traditional Japanese noh chanting
Synthesizer pads, jazz fusion, and Bulgarian women's choir
Traditional Chinese erhu, electronic ambient, and Korean folk drumming
Tibetan throat singing, sitar drones, and modern Tokyo street percussion
context: Ohashi's chorus was a real performing group composed of his university colleagues and amateur singers. The famous opening of the film — Kaneda's motorcycle headlight in the dark, then the title slamming on with the drums — was set to a piece called Kaneda from the score.

question: Berserk is a long-running dark-fantasy manga by Japanese artist Kentaro Miura, set in a medieval European-style kingdom torn by endless war. In the story's Golden Age arc, the huge orphaned swordsman Guts is hired as a mercenary by a rising private army called the Band of the Hawk. Their beautiful young commander dreams of building his own kingdom one day, and his second-in-command — a swordswoman named Casca — is quietly in love with him. What is the commander's name?
context: Griffith carries a small egg-like talisman called a Behelit. After his torture and crippling by the Midland king, he uses it to summon the God Hand in the Eclipse. Kentaro Miura drew the Golden Age arc across volumes 3 through 14 of the manga and considered it the manga's central story.

question: Yoko Kanno, the composer of Cowboy Bebop and many other anime scores, frequently fronts the studio band that performs the music live. The band's name is also a recurring inside joke — it shares its name with a safety device drivers should use. What is the band called?
context: The Seatbelts include guitarist Tsuneo Imahori and a roster of session players Kanno has worked with for decades. Kanno also scored Macross Plus, Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex, and Wolf's Rain. Her vocalist of choice for many Bebop tracks was Mai Yamane.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's 1986 Studio Ghibli film Castle in the Sky was originally titled Laputa: Castle in the Sky, borrowing the flying-island name from Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels. When Disney prepared its English release in 2003, the studio quietly shortened the name to just Castle in the Sky. Why was the word Laputa considered a problem for Spanish-speaking audiences?
answer: It is a vulgar Spanish slang word meaning a female prostitute
choices: It is a vulgar Spanish slang word meaning a female prostitute
It conflicted with a 1980s Italian fantasy film of similar title
It was the name of a Disney competitor's animated franchise
It triggered objections from Jonathan Swift's literary estate
context: Miyazaki took the name directly from Gulliver's Travels, where Swift apparently coined it without knowing the Spanish meaning. In Spanish-speaking countries the film has been released as El Castillo en el Cielo or Laputa: El Castillo en el Cielo despite the connotation.

question: Rurouni Kenshin is a Japanese manga and anime set in the early Meiji era of the 1870s. The wandering hero, Kenshin Himura, is a former imperial assassin who has sworn off killing. In the story's Kyoto arc, Kenshin travels to the ancient capital of Kyoto to stop the master assassin who replaced him — a man now plotting to overthrow the young Meiji government with a private army of loyal killers. The villain's face and body are wrapped in bandages after severe burns nearly killed him. What is his name?
context: Shishio was Kenshin's successor as Hitokiri Battosai during the Bakumatsu. The Meiji government tried to assassinate him by setting him on fire. The Kyoto arc was adapted as a beautifully animated 1996-1998 TV arc and again in the 2014 live-action film Rurouni Kenshin: Kyoto Inferno starring Takeru Satoh.

question: In the Majin Buu saga of Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball Z, the round pink demon Fat Buu is sent to assassinate the world's phony martial-arts champion Mr. Satan (called Hercule in the English dub). Instead of killing him, Buu becomes best friends with Mr. Satan and with his loyal little dog. Name the dog.
context: Bee was originally Mr. Satan's (Hercule's) dog, taken in after Hercule rescued him from Buu. Fat Buu's bond with Bee leads to one of the saga's emotional pivots — when Buu thinks Bee has been killed, his rage triggers his splitting into Good Buu and Evil Buu. Puar is a magical companion to Yamcha from earlier Dragon Ball. Korin (Karin) is the cat-sage at the top of the Tower. Mimi is not a Dragon Ball character.

question: Dragon Ball Z is the huge Japanese anime that ran from 1989 to 1996, based on Akira Toriyama's manga about warriors like Goku and Vegeta. In 2009, to celebrate the series' 20th anniversary, the same Japanese studio that made the original rebooted it as Dragon Ball Z Kai. Kai cut the 291 old episodes down to about 167 by trimming filler, re-recorded the voice acting, and re-edited the pacing. Which studio and team made Kai?
answer: Toei Animation in-house, with new dubbing and a re-edit by Kazuhiro Furuhashi
choices: Toei Animation in-house, with new dubbing and a re-edit by Kazuhiro Furuhashi
Studio Pierrot, with new music by Yasuharu Takanashi and Konami sponsorship
Tokyo Movie Shinsha, with re-edits by Production I.G's Mamoru Oshii
Sunrise, with mecha-art consulting from Yoshiyuki Tomino and Bandai
context: Kai was originally aired in Japan from April 2009 to March 2011 and from 2014 to 2015 for the Buu saga. Funimation's English Kai dub featured most of the original DBZ cast — Sean Schemmel, Christopher Sabat, Sonny Strait — but tightened the dialogue and removed many of the original dub's added punchlines.

question: The 1979 Mobile Suit Gundam anime stars rookie teenage pilot Amuro Ray, who stumbles into piloting a top-secret Federation mobile suit during a Zeon attack. His rival across the series is a Zeon ace who wears a half-mask. What name does this rival go by?
context: Char's red mobile suit established the trope that ace pilots get a custom-colored unit three times faster than standard. His real name is Casval Rem Deikun. The Char-versus-Amuro rivalry runs through the original series, Zeta Gundam, Char's Counterattack, and decades of Universal Century continuity.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's 1997 Studio Ghibli film Princess Mononoke is set in medieval Japan, where a girl named San was abandoned as a baby and raised by wolves in the deep forest. She fights on the wolves' side against humans clear-cutting the woods for iron. In every battle, she rides on the back of the massive white wolf-god who took her in and raised her as her own. What is this wolf-god's name?
context: Moro is voiced in Japanese by actress Akihiro Miwa and in the English Miramax dub by Gillian Anderson. Okkoto is the elder boar-god. Lady Eboshi runs Irontown. Yakul is Ashitaka's loyal red elk. The film's eponymous mononoke is San herself — the wolf princess.

question: Yasuhiro Nightow's 1998 anime Trigun is set on a desert planet where the peaceful gunfighter Vash the Stampede has a huge bounty on his head. Vash carries a long-barreled silver revolver, but his prosthetic left arm — built by his twin brother Knives — secretly hides a very different, far more destructive weapon. What is hidden inside Vash's arm?
context: Vash and his villain brother Knives are Plants — humanoid beings grown from the same biological-technology Plants that power the desert planet's cities. The angel arm appears late in the series. Yasuhiro Nightow's manga ran in Shonen Captain then Young King OURs from 1995 to 2008.

question: In Hayao Miyazaki's 1984 anime Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind, Princess Nausicaa lives in a small kingdom on the edge of a poisonous forest called the Sea of Decay, where giant insects roam. She scouts the toxic jungle from the air, riding a tiny one-seater jet-powered glider that lets her land almost anywhere. What is her glider called?
context: Mehve comes from the German word Mowe, meaning seagull. The Mehve is jet-powered with a small engine slung beneath the wing. Studio Ghibli built a working flying replica in 2013 for engineering enthusiast Kazuhiko Hachiya's OpenSky project.

question: Studio Ghibli's 1988 film Grave of the Fireflies, directed by Isao Takahata, tells the story of two siblings struggling to survive in Kobe during the final months of World War II. The two main characters are a teenage boy and his much younger sister. What are their names?
context: Takahata adapted Akiyuki Nosaka's 1967 semi-autobiographical novel. Nosaka had lost his own younger sister to malnutrition during the war. The film was released as a double feature with Miyazaki's My Neighbor Totoro on April 16, 1988 — a contrast that astonished audiences.

question: Cowboy Bebop is Shinichiro Watanabe's 1998 Japanese science-fiction anime about a ragged crew of bounty hunters chasing criminals across the solar system in the year 2071. One crew member is a wild-haired barefoot kid computer hacker known simply as Edward, or Ed.
