question: Death Note, by writer Tsugumi Ohba and artist Takeshi Obata, pits high schooler Light Yagami — the notebook-wielding killer known as Kira — against the world's greatest detective, L. In chapter 58 of the manga, Light figures out that L has him under close surveillance. As he thinks through his options, his internal narration walks the reader through six lettered contingency plans, A through F. Which of those plans did Light actually execute?
answer: Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page
choices: Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page
Plan A, the primary intended approach with no contingency
Plan E, the doomsday option with a Watari-targeting clause
Plan F, the only one Light actually rehearsed in advance
context: Chapter 58 of the manga is widely cited as one of Death Note's tightest-written sequences. Light's internal monologue — listing six lettered plans, executing the contingency, and silently saying 'just as planned' — was animated by Madhouse in the 2006 anime with iconic effect. The 'just as planned' moment became one of anime's most-quoted phrases, alongside 'I'll take a potato chip... AND EAT IT.'

question: Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball Z's Trunks arc (1991-1993) introduced a future timeline where Goku has died of a heart virus and the Androids 17 and 18 have killed all the Z fighters. The arc's centerpiece is the visit of teenaged future Trunks from that timeline, traveling back to warn the present-day Z fighters. Trunks gives Goku a specific medicine to take when he develops the same heart virus. What is the medicine?
answer: A specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle
choices: A specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle
A sample of Dr. Gero's android-engineering blueprints in microfilm format
A Saiyan-bloodline immunity injection developed by Bulma's lab in the future
A serum from a senzu-bean cross-bred with synthetic immune-system tissue
context: The future-Trunks visit kicks off the Cell Saga; Trunks is the son of Bulma and Vegeta in a future where Goku died and the Z fighters were destroyed. Toriyama's careful work to keep both timelines coherent (the future Trunks's birth, the present-day Trunks's birth, the medicine plot point) became a model for shonen time-travel structures. Trunks's red Capsule Corp jacket and his sword (passed down from Tapion in the films) became iconic franchise looks.

question: Tite Kubo's Bleach features a recurring 'zanpakuto release' command structure: each Soul Reaper's sealed sword has a unique release command-phrase that activates its Shikai form. Captain Toshiro Hitsugaya's command 'Souten ni Zase, Hyorinmaru!' translates loosely to 'Reign over the frozen heavens, Hyorinmaru!' His released zanpakuto becomes a long-bladed ice-dragon-themed sword. Hitsugaya is which Squad's captain?
choices: Squad 13, the Western Rukongai recruitment-and-protection squad
Squad 6, the noble Kuchiki-family squad of intellectual warriors
Squad 4, the medical and recovery squad led by Unohana
context: Hitsugaya is the youngest captain in the Gotei 13, having attained his rank as a child prodigy. His Bankai, Daiguren Hyorinmaru, is one of the most-rendered shows of bankai in the anime. The character's design — short, silver-haired, with a perpetually-scowling face — made him a fan favorite immediately. His relationship with his squad's lieutenant Rangiku Matsumoto is one of Bleach's most-loved character pairings.

question: In Eiichiro Oda's One Piece, the Wano arc confirmed the 'Joy Boy' legend from the Void Century. The Void Century is a 100-year gap in history, about 800 years ago, when an ancient kingdom was wiped out by 19 other kingdoms — the ancestors of today's World Government. What is the erased kingdom called?
answer: The Great Kingdom (the Ancient Kingdom of D., never given a public name in-canon)
choices: The Great Kingdom (the Ancient Kingdom of D., never given a public name in-canon)
The Kingdom of Lulusia, the central island-nation of the One Piece world
The Holy Kingdom of God Valley, where the original Celestial Dragons originated
The Atlantean Crown, the underwater nation Joy Boy's people ruled
context: The Great Kingdom's destruction is the foundational event of One Piece's worldbuilding. The 'Will of D.' inheritance system (Luffy's middle name, Roger's middle name, Blackbeard's middle name) is a remnant of the lost kingdom's bloodline. The Marines and World Government have suppressed all knowledge of the kingdom's name and history for 800 years. The truth of the Void Century is set to be revealed in One Piece's final saga.

question: Demon Slayer, Koyoharu Gotouge's manga about demon-hunting swordsmen in Taisho-era Japan, ended in 2020. Its final chapter jumps roughly a hundred years into the future and shows the whole cast reincarnated as ordinary high schoolers in modern Tokyo. One of those reborn characters is drawn sitting alone at a cafe, reading a book. Which reincarnated hero is it?
answer: Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe
choices: Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe
Tanjiro's reincarnation, reading a children's storybook on a train
Kanroji Mitsuri's reincarnation, reading a Greek mythology textbook
Zenitsu's reincarnation, reading a music magazine in the school library
context: The modern-Tokyo epilogue runs from chapters 200 to 205 of the manga. The reincarnations are mostly cousins or descendants of the original cast, with a few exceptions (Kanao herself appears slightly older). The manga's final beat is a quiet, peaceful Tokyo scene contrasting against the demon-fighting violence of the main story. Gotouge was clear in interviews that this 100-years-later setting was intentional.

question: In Masashi Kishimoto's manga Naruto, the Fourth Great Shinobi World War brings enemies back from the dead with a forbidden jutsu called Edo Tensei — 'Impure World Reincarnation.' The technique drags a dead warrior's soul back into a nearly-invincible clay body under the caster's control. Edo Tensei was invented long before the war by one of the Hidden Leaf Village's own past Hokages — the village's supreme leaders — who was later branded a war criminal for the horror the jutsu unleashed. Which Hokage invented it?
answer: The Second Hokage Tobirama Senju, brother and successor to Hashirama
choices: The Second Hokage Tobirama Senju, brother and successor to Hashirama
The First Hokage Hashirama Senju, the founder of the village
The Third Hokage Hiruzen Sarutobi, the Professor of Konoha
The Fourth Hokage Minato Namikaze, the Yellow Flash
context: Tobirama created Edo Tensei to bind the dead to living-tissue vessels — the technique is universally banned, but Orochimaru and Madara revive it for war purposes. The reanimated ninja include the previous four Hokage, Itachi, the Akatsuki, and dozens of others. The reanimation scenes were the manga's longest and most spectacle-driven sequences. Tobirama's status as inventor of multiple forbidden jutsu (including Edo Tensei and the original Flying Thunder God) became defining.

question: Hajime Isayama's manga Attack on Titan features a soldier unit called the Survey Corps, whose members scout beyond the walls to fight giant titans. Their green uniforms carry a crossed-wings badge — one white wing over one blue wing — nicknamed the Wings of Freedom. In interviews, Isayama told fans that he based the badge on a real-world military unit he had researched. Which real squadron did he copy?
answer: The British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII
choices: The British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII
The Imperial Japanese Army's Tokkotai (Special Attack Unit) of WWII
The German Luftwaffe's Schnellbomber squadron of the early Battle of Britain
The Soviet Union's Yak-9 aerial-superiority wing of the Eastern Front
context: Isayama studied multiple Western military traditions for AOT's visual design. The Survey Corps's crossed-wings emblem, the boot-and-trouser uniform style, and the cavalry-rank organization all draw from real WWII-era European militaries. The German-language naming convention for characters (Eren, Mikasa, Armin, etc.) similarly draws from Isayama's research. The Pathfinder squadron's role — finding enemy territory in the dark — fits the Survey Corps's narrative function.

question: In Hirohiko Araki's manga JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5 — Vento Aureo, or Golden Wind — the story moves to Italy in 2001 and follows a fifteen-year-old mafia recruit named Giorno Giovanna. Giorno's father is the vampire Dio Brando from Part 1, who fathered him in the late 1980s while wearing the stolen, stitched-on headless body of his old rival, the English gentleman Jonathan Joestar. Who is Giorno's living human mother?
answer: Yuhko, a Japanese woman impregnated by the vampire while he wore Jonathan Joestar's stolen body in 1989
choices: Yuhko, a Japanese woman impregnated by the vampire while he wore Jonathan Joestar's stolen body in 1989
Erina Pendleton, Jonathan's widow returned for a brief Italian vacation
Tonpetty's daughter, a Wamuu-Pillar-Man bloodline character
Caesar Zeppeli's mother, returned mysteriously after Part 2's events
context: The Giorno-paternity reveal is one of JoJo's signature lore details. Giorno inherits the Joestar bloodline through his father (the vampire who wore Jonathan's body) and the JoJo family of Stand users through his Joestar inheritance. His blond hair, golden eyes, and his Stand (Gold Experience) all reference his particular dual-bloodline status. Part 5 is set in Naples, Italy, and is heavily influenced by Italian fashion-and-film aesthetics.

question: Death Note by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata ran in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2003 to 2006. Partway through the manga, the world's greatest detective L is killed, and he is replaced by a young albino boy named Nate River, whom his handlers call Near. Near plays with toys and dice on the floor while cracking cases. Every time he sits down to think, he does one signature nervous habit. What does Near always do while he thinks?
answer: He twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger
choices: He twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger
He arranges a chess match between miniature figures on a desk
He cracks his knuckles in a specific six-finger pattern
He counts dice and arranges them in pyramidal stacks on the floor
context: Near's hair-twisting habit is one of the manga's most-replicated character tics. Obata's drawings show the gesture frequently — close-ups of the finger in the curl of white hair became standard Near framing. The character is meant to be even more reclusive than L, with anxieties about social contact. Near's eventual confrontation with Light, ending the manga's main arc, is structured as a deliberate parallel-mirror to L's earlier confrontation.

question: Hiromu Arakawa's manga Fullmetal Alchemist was so beloved that when the 2003 anime adaptation ran out of manga and invented its own ending, fans complained for years. Studio Bones finally made a second anime in 2009 — Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood — that stuck to Arakawa's manga faithfully all the way to the end. The very first opening song, a fast rock number called 'Again,' was performed by a Japanese artist known for pop-rock singles in the 2000s. Which artist?
answer: Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc
choices: Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc
Asian Kung-Fu Generation, whose 'Rewrite' opened the 2003 series instead
The High Wide and Handsome, an indie group used for opening rotations
L'Arc-en-Ciel, whose 'My Heart Draws a Dream' was used for Episode 50
context: Yui's 'Again' became one of the most-recognized anime opening themes of the late 2000s. Her solo work was characterized by acoustic guitar-driven J-rock with strong vocal melodies. The Brotherhood adaptation by Studio Bones is widely considered the better adaptation of the manga, with five different opening themes across its run. Asian Kung-Fu Generation's 'Rewrite' is iconic but belongs to the 2003 series.

question: Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball first showed the Super Saiyan form during the Frieza fight. The form requires a Saiyan hitting a breaking point of rage. Toriyama's editor at the time was Kazuhiko Torishima. How did Torishima react when Toriyama pitched the transformation?
answer: Torishima loved it and reportedly told Toriyama 'this is the breakthrough'
choices: Torishima loved it and reportedly told Toriyama 'this is the breakthrough'
Torishima resisted, calling the idea derivative of Berserk's behavior shift
Torishima requested major design changes including different hair color
Torishima initially rejected the idea, suggesting a power-up sword instead
context: Toriyama and Torishima had a famously productive working relationship. The Super Saiyan design — gold hair, teal eyes, glowing aura — emerged from Toriyama's own preference for high-contrast color palettes and was approved with minimal editorial intervention. The transformation became one of anime's most-imitated tropes, with countless other shonen series featuring similar 'breakthrough power-up' sequences. The Saiyan-rage trigger remained part of the franchise's core canon through Dragon Ball Super.

question: In Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball Z, during the Buu Saga, a loud, muscle-bound world-tournament champion named Hercule — 'Mr. Satan' in the Japanese version — struts around claiming he defeated the villain Cell, when it was really the teenage hero Gohan. Toriyama plays the boast for laughs. Later, Hercule redeems himself by shouting Earth's people into raising their arms and pouring their life energy into Goku's massive Spirit Bomb. What kind of real-world figure was Toriyama parodying with Hercule?
answer: A bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan
choices: A bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan
A Japanese sumo grand champion (yokozuna), of late-1980s celebrity status
A 1980s American bodybuilding magazine cover star, in the Lou Ferrigno mold
An Italian motorcycle daredevil of the Evel Knievel tradition
context: The Hercule / Mr. Satan name choice was a deliberate Toriyama joke. The character's hairstyle, his boastful interview style, his merchandising-heavy fame — all reference the pro-wrestling celebrity culture of the late 1980s. Hercule's redemption arc in the Buu Saga — convincing humanity to save Goku, befriending Majin Buu — turned what was a comic-relief satire into one of the franchise's most-loved characters. The dub's name 'Hercule' was a licensing-driven change from his Japanese 'Mr. Satan.'

question: Eiichiro Oda's One Piece introduced the Pirate King concept in chapter one with the words of the executed Pirate King Gol D. Roger: 'My treasure? If you want it, it's yours. I left everything I had in One Piece.' These were the public final words spoken by Roger on the execution platform at Loguetown. The execution started 22 years before Luffy's chapter-one departure. Roger's final words and their public broadcast kicked off what's referred to in the franchise as what era?
choices: The Golden Age of the Sea
context: The Great Pirate Era is the active framing the World Government uses for the post-Roger period. Twenty-two years of pirate activity were directly enabled by Roger's final words; the four Yonko (Whitebeard, Big Mom, Kaido, and later Blackbeard) are the present-day equivalents of the older 'Rocks Pirates.' One Piece's narrative tension between law-and-pirate-freedom is the foundational genre-mechanic of the entire manga. Luffy's stated goal — to find One Piece and become King of the Pirates — directly continues Roger's announced legacy.

question: Yoshihiro Togashi's manga Hunter x Hunter opens with the Hunter Exam — a brutal multi-stage test that turns ordinary applicants into licensed Hunters, elite roving agents with world-class privileges. The stages include a marathon run through poison-swamp, cooking a bizarre wild animal to a fussy chef-judge, and a survival tournament aboard an airship. The whole exam is run by a tiny, wizened old master who chairs the Hunter Association itself. Who chairs the first-arc exam?
answer: Netero, the chairman of the Hunter Association
choices: Netero, the chairman of the Hunter Association
Hisoka, the freelance examiner who'd taken the test years prior
Bisuke (Biscuit Krueger), in disguise as a child examiner
Kurapika, who's actually a fellow applicant taking it for the first time
context: Netero himself organized and oversaw the year-one Hunter Exam in which Gon, Killua, Kurapika, and Leorio participated. His chairmanship would later become important in the Chimera Ant arc when he personally challenges Meruem. The Hunter Exam is a recurring narrative device in the franchise; it's been remade in five different forms across Togashi's various story arcs. The Hunter Association's secret 'Zodiacs' inner circle is one of HxH's most-imitated worldbuilding elements.

question: When the Pokemon anime launched in Japan in April 1997, the production team had to choose the hero's partner Pokemon. In the story, ten-year-old Ash Ketchum oversleeps his big day, so the three Red-and-Blue video-game starters — Bulbasaur, Charmander, and Squirtle — are already taken, and he ends up stuck with a stubborn electric mouse named Pikachu instead. That choice ignored the game's starter lineup on purpose. Who inside the production team pushed hardest for Pikachu to be the star?
answer: Producer Takemoto Mori at Shogakukan, citing Pikachu's plush-toy potential and child-recognition data
choices: Producer Takemoto Mori at Shogakukan, citing Pikachu's plush-toy potential and child-recognition data
Series director Junichi Masuda, in disagreement with Satoshi Tajiri who'd preferred Bulbasaur
Animator Sayuri Ichiishi, who'd designed the Pikachu's anime-specific facial expressions
Marketing executive Junichi Nishioka, who'd run focus groups on the original Red/Blue cover art
context: The Pikachu-as-starter decision was a marketing-driven one rather than a creative-team choice. Producer Mori's bet on Pikachu — partly based on the character's friendliness and cute design, partly based on early plush-toy sales data — became the most consequential anime-marketing decision of the late 1990s. Within two years of the anime's premiere, Pikachu was the most-recognized cartoon character among American children under 10 years old, even ahead of Mickey Mouse for a brief period in 1999.

question: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4: Diamond Is Unbreakable is a 1992 manga arc by Hirohiko Araki, set in the fictional Japanese town of Morioh. Its main villain is Yoshikage Kira, a quiet salaryman by day and a hand-obsessed serial killer by night. In interviews, Araki said he modeled Kira on a real Japanese criminal whose Tokyo-area murder case had shocked the whole country a few years before the manga began. Who was that real killer?
answer: Tsutomu Miyazaki, the Tokyo-area 1988-1989 child murderer known as the 'Otaku Murderer'
choices: Tsutomu Miyazaki, the Tokyo-area 1988-1989 child murderer known as the 'Otaku Murderer'
Shoko Asahara, leader of the Aum Shinrikyo cult behind the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack
Akihabara Massacre perpetrator Tomohiro Kato, from a 2008 case that postdated the manga
Hiroshi Maeue, the Internet-suicide-club serial killer of mid-2000s Osaka
context: Araki's research into the Miyazaki case is documented in his author's notes. The 'normal-looking salaryman' aspect of Kira's character design — his desire for a quiet life, his collection of body-part trophies, his methodical evasion — closely mirrors aspects of the Miyazaki case. The Kira character became one of the most-imitated 'banality of evil' antagonist designs in shonen manga. Yoshikage Kira's specific 'I just want a quiet life' speech is among the franchise's most-quoted villain monologues.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride, a poor farm boy named Westley works for a beautiful farm girl named Buttercup on her family's little country farm. Whenever she asks him for anything at all, whether to fetch a bucket, pass a pitcher, or chase down a stray sheep, he answers with the exact same three-word reply, said quietly with a small smile. Buttercup slowly figures out those three words really mean 'I love you.' What are the three words?
context: Westley's catchphrase is revealed to mean 'I love you.' Cary Elwes played Westley; Robin Wright played Buttercup. William Goldman wrote both the 1973 novel and screenplay.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride, a short, bald, loudmouth Sicilian mastermind named Vizzini leads a trio of kidnappers up the sheer Cliffs of Insanity with the kidnapped Princess Buttercup. Every time one of his plans goes wrong, or the mysterious black-masked Man in Black keeps climbing after them no matter what, Vizzini shouts one big fancy word (the same word every time) as if repeating it will bend reality back into shape. What is that word?
context: Inigo Montoya finally responds: 'You keep using that word. I do not think it means what you think it means.' The line became one of the most-quoted in 80s film history.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels and Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, a scrawny Toronto slacker bass-player named Scott Pilgrim falls in love with a pink-haired American delivery girl named Ramona Flowers. Before Ramona will date him for real, Scott must fight and defeat each and every one of her former partners, one by one, in over-the-top video-game-style duels. How many evil exes must Scott defeat in total?
context: The League of Evil Exes is led by Gideon Graves, the seventh and final boss. Bryan Lee O'Malley's six graphic novels (2004-2010) inspired Edgar Wright's 2010 film and the 2023 Netflix anime.

question: In the 2023 animated blockbuster The Super Mario Bros. Movie, the giant koopa king Bowser has captured Mario and imprisons him aboard his flying airship castle. Between battles, Bowser sits down at a grand piano in his throne room and belts out a heartfelt love ballad to Princess Peach, voiced with full commitment by the real-life actor Jack Black. The song became a chart-hit outside the movie and got Bowser more fans than the movie itself. What is the song called?
context: Jack Black voiced Bowser and performed the song, which became a viral hit and was Oscar-shortlisted. The Illumination film was directed by Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic.

question: In Robert Zemeckis's 1985 film Back to the Future, the wild-haired scientist Doc Brown builds the world's first working time machine. Instead of putting it in a laboratory booth, he wires his 'flux capacitor' into a real 1980s American stainless-steel sports car with gullwing doors that lift up like wings. The car must reach exactly 88 miles per hour before it can jump through time. What kind of car did Doc convert into a time machine?
context: Director Robert Zemeckis chose the DeLorean for its iconic gull-wing doors that would look like a UFO when people first saw it. Christopher Lloyd played Doc Emmett Brown; Michael J. Fox replaced Eric Stoltz as Marty after several weeks of filming.

question: In the 1984 comedy Ghostbusters, four New York City parapsychologists (Peter, Ray, Egon, and Winston) climb a Manhattan skyscraper to trap a Sumerian demon-god named Gozer. Gozer commands them to choose the form of their destructor, and Ray accidentally pictures a friendly white cartoon mascot from a marshmallow bag. Seconds later, a hundred-foot version of that grinning mascot, in a sailor hat and a blue neckerchief, stomps down 5th Avenue crushing taxi cabs. What is this giant marshmallow monster called?
context: Ray Stantz (Dan Aykroyd) accidentally chose the form by thinking of 'the most harmless thing.' Ivan Reitman directed; the screenplay was by Aykroyd and Harold Ramis.

question: In Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future trilogy (1985 through 1990), the wild-haired scientist Doc Brown reacts to every huge shock, whether the DeLorean time machine actually working, a paradox in the timeline, or his dog Einstein vanishing into thin air, by clutching his frizzy white hair and yelling the same old-fashioned two-word exclamation. He shouts it in 1985, in 1955, in the future of 2015, and in the Old West of 1885. What is Doc Brown's two-word catchphrase?
context: Christopher Lloyd ad-libbed the phrasing on set; it appears repeatedly in all three films (1985, 1989, 1990). The 'Doc Brown' character was inspired by physicist Jack Parsons and conductor Leopold Stokowski.

question: In the 1984 martial-arts film The Karate Kid, the teenage Daniel LaRusso trains under the gentle old handyman Mr. Miyagi and enters the All-Valley Karate Tournament. In the championship final match, injured in one leg and standing on the other, Daniel raises his arms wide like a bird stretching its wings, hops on his good leg, and unleashes a flying front-kick that catches his bully rival Johnny square in the face. What is this signature move called?
context: Mr. Miyagi (Pat Morita) taught Daniel the crane kick by demonstration on the beach. John G. Avildsen directed; Ralph Macchio played Daniel. The crane kick is technically illegal under tournament rules in the film.

question: In Tony Scott's 1986 action film Top Gun, a cocky young U.S. Naval aviator named Pete Mitchell reports to the elite fighter-pilot school in Miramar, California, where he flies F-14 Tomcat jets and plays shirtless volleyball on the beach. Every Navy pilot has a nickname (called a call sign) that other pilots radio each other by. Pete's call sign fits his reckless, rule-breaking, hot-shot flying style. What is Pete Mitchell's call sign?
context: Tom Cruise played Maverick. Director Tony Scott was Ridley Scott's brother. The Navy got a recruitment boom from the film and reportedly opened recruiting stations near theaters.

question: In Richard Donner's 1985 adventure film The Goonies, a gang of Oregon kids follow a pirate treasure map into a network of underground caves under their coastal town. Deep in the basement of the criminal Fratelli family's hideout they find a huge, gentle, deformed man chained to a wall by his own cruel mother and brothers. Once the kids free him, he shares a Baby Ruth candy bar and quickly bonds with the plump kid nicknamed Chunk. What is the deformed prisoner's own nickname?
context: John Matuszak played Sloth, the deformed brother of the Fratelli crime family. Director Richard Donner and producer Steven Spielberg developed the story together. Sean Astin played Mikey.

question: In Steven Spielberg's 1982 film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, a lonely California boy named Elliott finds a stranded alien with a glowing fingertip hiding in his family's backyard tool shed. To coax the frightened alien out of the shed and up into his suburban house, Elliott lays down a trail of a real orange-and-brown peanut-butter candy across the lawn and up the stairs to his bedroom. The candy company got so much free advertising the film turned the brand into a national hit. What brand of candy did Elliott use?
context: Mars Inc. famously turned down product placement for M&Ms; Hershey paid $1 million for Reese's Pieces. Sales tripled within two weeks of the film's release. Steven Spielberg directed.

question: In Steven Spielberg's 1981 adventure film Raiders of the Lost Ark, the archaeology professor and adventurer Indiana Jones (played by Harrison Ford) races the Nazis in 1936 to find a golden box the ancient Israelites once carried through the desert. The box supposedly held the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments given to Moses at Mount Sinai, and Adolf Hitler believes owning it will make his armies unstoppable. What is this holy golden box called?
context: Steven Spielberg directed; George Lucas produced. Harrison Ford was cast as Indy after Tom Selleck dropped out due to Magnum P.I. commitments. The Ark's opening melts Nazi faces in the climax.

question: In the 1984 movie The Terminator, Arnold Schwarzenegger plays a killer cyborg sent back from the future. He goes to a Los Angeles police station hunting his target, Sarah Connor. A desk clerk tells him he cannot come in. Arnold says one short line and walks out. Minutes later he crashes a car right through the front doors. What did he say to the clerk?
context: James Cameron wrote and directed. Schwarzenegger originally objected to the line, suggesting 'I will be back,' but Cameron insisted. The phrase became Arnold's signature.

question: In the Indiana Jones movies from Steven Spielberg and George Lucas, Harrison Ford plays a college professor of archaeology named Dr. Indiana Jones. When Indy leaves campus to hunt lost treasures, he always wears the same outfit — a brown leather jacket, a bullwhip on his belt, and one particular kind of hat pulled low over his eyes. What kind of hat is it?
context: The hat became so iconic that the production team had a strict 'never lose the hat' rule on set. Harrison Ford wore it across all four films from 1981 to 2008. Originally inspired by old serial-adventure heroes.

question: In the 1987 movie Predator, Arnold Schwarzenegger plays Major Dutch Schaefer, the leader of a special-forces team trapped in a Central American jungle. An invisible alien hunter is picking them off one by one. When a rescue helicopter finally lifts through the trees, Dutch turns and shouts at his surviving team to run for it. What does he yell?
context: John McTiernan directed. Arnold's character Major Dutch Schaefer leads a special forces team hunting an extraterrestrial big-game hunter. Jesse Ventura plays a teammate; he later became Governor of Minnesota.

question: In James Cameron's 1991 movie Terminator 2: Judgment Day, a shape-shifting cyborg is sent back in time from the future to kill young John Connor, the boy who will one day lead humanity's war against the machines. This new cyborg is made of liquid metal — it can flow through bars and form its arms into blades. What is this new model of Terminator called?
context: Robert Patrick played the T-1000. The liquid-metal effects by ILM cost the film much of its $102 million budget — the most expensive film made up to that point. James Cameron returned to direct.

question: The 1982 movie Conan the Barbarian stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as the young warrior Conan. A snake-cult wizard named Thulsa Doom murders Conan's parents, and grown-up Conan spends the film hunting him down for revenge. Thulsa Doom is played by the deep-voiced American actor who also voiced Darth Vader in the Star Wars films. Who plays Thulsa Doom?
context: John Milius directed; Arnold Schwarzenegger played Conan. The film opens with Conan's father teaching him the 'riddle of steel.' Carlos Palomino played Thulsa Doom with James Earl Jones providing the voice.

question: In George Lucas's 1977 movie Star Wars, Princess Leia of the Rebel Alliance has stolen the Empire's most guarded military secret. Right before Darth Vader captures her ship, she hides the stolen files inside a little astromech droid named R2-D2 and jettisons him down to a nearby desert planet. Luke Skywalker and Han Solo then risk their lives to get those files to the Rebels. What has Leia hidden inside R2-D2?
context: The technical readout of the Death Star — stolen by Rebel spies on Toprawa in events later expanded by Rogue One (2016) — is hidden in R2's memory along with Leia's hologram message: 'Help me, Obi-Wan Kenobi. You're my only hope.' R2 escapes the captured Tantive IV, lands on Tatooine, and the rest is the plot of A New Hope. The Death Star plans reveal the vulnerable exhaust port Luke later exploits.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim comics and Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, Scott is a broke 23-year-old in Toronto who plays bass in a garage-rock band with his friends Stephen Stills and Kim Pine. To date the American delivery girl Ramona Flowers, he has to defeat her seven evil exes in video-game-style fights. What is the name of Scott's band?
context: Sex Bob-omb is named after Mario's Bob-omb enemy. The band's songs for the 2010 film were written by Beck. Bandmates are Stephen Stills 'the talent' and drummer Kim Pine.

question: In the 2023 animated Super Mario Bros. Movie from Illumination and Nintendo, Mario finds himself in the Mushroom Kingdom and meets Princess Peach, its ruler, who is raising an army to stop Bowser. Peach takes Mario through a punishing obstacle course of spinning saws and fireballs on Mt. Plumb to test whether he is tough enough to help. Which actress provides Peach's voice?
context: Chris Pratt voiced Mario, Charlie Day voiced Luigi, Jack Black voiced Bowser, Seth Rogen voiced Donkey Kong, and Keegan-Michael Key voiced Toad. The film grossed over $1.36 billion worldwide.

question: In Ridley Scott's 1982 movie Blade Runner, Harrison Ford plays Rick Deckard, a burnt-out detective in a rainy, neon-lit Los Angeles of the future. Deckard's job is to hunt down artificial humans — bio-engineered beings built by the Tyrell Corporation for hard labor in off-world colonies. Four of them have escaped and come back to Earth. What are these artificial humans called?
context: Ridley Scott directed. Harrison Ford played Deckard. Based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel 'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?' The Tyrell Corporation manufactures the replicants.

question: The Princess Bride is Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy movie, based on William Goldman's novel. In one scene, the hero Westley and his love Buttercup run through the Fire Swamp. They face three hazards there: patches of lightning sand, sudden flame spurts, and packs of rodents of unusual size. What short acronym do fans use for those giant rats?
context: Westley famously denies their existence — 'Rodents of Unusual Size? I don't think they exist' — right before being attacked by one. The practical-effect ROUSes were stuntmen in rat suits set on fire (carefully).

question: In Steven Spielberg's 1989 movie Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, Harrison Ford returns as archaeologist Indy on a quest to find the Holy Grail. Along the way he teams up with his own father, Dr. Henry Jones Sr., a grumpy medieval-history professor who has spent his whole life hunting the Grail too. A very famous older actor — best known for playing James Bond in the 1960s — was cast as Indy's dad. Who is he?
context: Connery was only 12 years older than Harrison Ford. Steven Spielberg directed; the film's MacGuffin was the Holy Grail. Critics widely consider it the best of the original three Indy films.

question: In the 1993 Western Tombstone, Kurt Russell plays the lawman Wyatt Earp and Val Kilmer plays his tuberculosis-ridden friend Doc Holliday. The movie is set in the Arizona silver-mining town of Tombstone in 1881. Early on, the Earp brothers and Doc face off against a gang of red-sashed outlaws called the Cowboys in a thirty-second shootout in a narrow lot behind a livery stable — the most famous gunfight in the American Old West. What is this real gunfight called?
answer: The Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
choices: The Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
context: The historical gunfight happened on October 26, 1881, in Tombstone, Arizona Territory. Kurt Russell played Wyatt Earp; Val Kilmer played Doc Holliday. Wyatt Earp lived until 1929 in Los Angeles.

question: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is Edgar Wright's 2010 movie, based on Bryan Lee O'Malley's comic. Scott Pilgrim is a broke 23-year-old bass player living in Toronto. He can't afford his own apartment, so he crashes with a roommate who is openly gay, gives him snarky advice, and even shares his bed. What is that roommate's name?
context: Kieran Culkin played Wallace in the 2010 film. Wallace is consistently the smartest character in the room and gets the best deadpan lines. Bryan Lee O'Malley confirmed Wallace based on real friends in Toronto's queer arts scene.

question: In the 2023 animated Super Mario Bros. Movie, Mario and Luigi are two Italian-American brothers who have just started their own plumbing business in New York City. They live in a small apartment together with their loud extended family. One night they crawl into the sewers to fix a broken water main and get sucked through a warp pipe to the Mushroom Kingdom. Which borough of New York City is their home?
context: The film opens with the Mario Brothers as struggling plumbers in their Brooklyn apartment. The 'Super Mario Bros. Plumbing' commercial was directly recreated for the film. The brothers fall down a warp pipe under the city.

question: In George Lucas's 1977 movie Star Wars: A New Hope, we first meet Luke Skywalker on a hot, dry world with two suns hanging in the sky. Luke lives with his Uncle Owen and Aunt Beru on a moisture farm, doing chores and staring at the horizon, dreaming of leaving to fight for the Rebellion. Sand people and scavenging Jawas roam the wastes. What is the name of this desert planet?
context: Tatooine scenes were filmed in Tunisia. Owen and Beru Lars raise Luke on the moisture farm. The name was inspired by Tataouine, an actual town in southern Tunisia.

question: In James Cameron's 1986 movie Aliens, a warrant officer wakes up from decades of frozen sleep and joins a squad of Colonial Marines heading back to LV-426, a colony overrun by the toothy black creatures called xenomorphs. At the film's climax she straps herself into a walking industrial forklift — a Caterpillar-yellow power loader — and squares off against the massive alien queen to save a little girl. What is her name?
context: Sigourney Weaver played Ripley across four Alien films (1979, 1986, 1992, 1997). Her power-loader vs. xenomorph queen fight is one of cinema's most-imitated practical-effect sequences. Cameron also wrote the screenplay.

question: In Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride, the swordsman Inigo Montoya and the giant Fezzik carry their friend Westley — who is only mostly dead — to a witch doctor named Miracle Max, played by Billy Crystal. Max sells them a magic chocolate-coated pill that revives Westley enough to storm Prince Humperdinck's castle and rescue Princess Buttercup. As the three set out, Max's wife Valerie (played by Carol Kane) cheerfully shouts a farewell after them. What does she shout?
choices: Try not to die out there!
context: Billy Crystal played Miracle Max; Carol Kane played Valerie. The pair were married only seven days of shooting but their improvised banter became some of the film's most-quoted material.

question: Rob Reiner's beloved 1987 film The Princess Bride, starring Cary Elwes and Robin Wright, is based on a 1973 fantasy novel of the same name. Very unusually, the same American writer wrote both the original novel and the movie's screenplay himself. He was also famous in Hollywood for the line 'Nobody knows anything' — his blunt summary of how the movie business really worked. Who was this writer?
context: Goldman also wrote Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) and All the President's Men (1976), winning two Oscars for screenwriting. He framed The Princess Bride as a faux-abridgement of a fictional 'S. Morgenstern' classic.

question: The friendly giant Fezzik in Rob Reiner's 1987 fantasy film The Princess Bride was played by the French wrestler Andre the Giant, who stood 7 feet 4 inches tall. His enormous size wasn't natural — it was caused by a rare medical condition that made his body keep pumping out growth hormone long after childhood. The same condition wore out his heart and killed him in 1993 at just 46. What was the condition called?
context: Acromegaly is a pituitary disorder causing excess growth hormone in adulthood. Andre's real name was Andre Roussimoff. He won WrestleMania III against Hulk Hogan in 1987 and feuded with Hogan in the WWF for years.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is a video-game-flavored comedy based on six graphic novels by Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley (2004-2010). Michael Cera stars as awkward Toronto bassist Scott Pilgrim, who has to defeat the seven evil ex-boyfriends of his mysterious purple-haired dream girl Ramona Flowers to earn the right to date her. Which actress played Ramona Flowers in the film?
context: Winstead (American, from Rocky Mount NC) had previously starred in Final Destination 3 (2006). Anna Kendrick played Scott's sister Stacey; Aubrey Plaza played the foul-mouthed Julie Powers.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie is a 2023 Illumination animated film based on the Nintendo game series. In one scene near the end, Mario races along Rainbow Road on a Mario Kart-style track chase. As he pulls ahead, a famous blue-shelled homing weapon from the Mario Kart video games rockets in and knocks him clean off the track. What is that infamous knock-out item called?
context: The Blue Shell debuted in Mario Kart 64 (1996) and is famous for homing in on the first-place racer. Donkey Kong (Seth Rogen) drives in the same race; the sequence ends with the Rainbow Road bridge collapsing.

question: When Robert Zemeckis started shooting his 1985 time-travel comedy Back to the Future, he cast a serious young actor named Eric Stoltz as the wisecracking teen hero Marty McFly. After a few weeks of filming, Zemeckis realized Stoltz was too dramatic for the comedy — so he fired Stoltz, threw out weeks of footage, and reshot almost every Marty scene from scratch with a Canadian television sitcom star instead. Which actor took over the role?
context: Stoltz was reportedly too dramatic for the comedy. Fox was committed to Family Ties and shot the film at night and on weekends, sleeping in his car between sets. Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment produced.

question: In September 1979, senior Disney animator Don Bluth quit Walt Disney Animation and walked out with a group of fellow animators, angry that Disney's cartoons had lost their old hand-drawn craft. He set up his own studio and in 1982 released his first independent feature — a dark fantasy about a widowed field mouse desperately seeking help for her sick child before a farmer's plow destroys her home. What was Bluth's 1982 debut feature called?
context: Based on Robert C. O'Brien's 1971 novel Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH. Bluth's defection took 17 Disney animators with him, leaving the studio scrambling on The Fox and the Hound. NIMH stands for National Institute of Mental Health.

question: Released by Cinematronics in 1983, the laserdisc arcade game Dragon's Lair was created by Don Bluth and his team using full-cel-animated cartoon footage. Players guide a knight named Dirk the Daring through a dragon's castle to rescue a princess. What was the princess's name?
context: Dragon's Lair was so popular at $0.50 per play (double the standard quarter) that machines had to be reset constantly. The game won several industry awards in 1983 and inspired the Space Ace follow-up in 1984.

question: Ghostbusters is the 1984 comedy directed by Ivan Reitman, starring Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, and Harold Ramis as three parapsychology professors chasing ghosts in New York City. Their team of Peter Venkman, Ray Stantz, and Egon Spengler gets a fourth member named Winston Zeddemore, an ordinary guy hired later on. Which American actor played Winston Zeddemore?
context: The role was originally written for Eddie Murphy. Hudson was paid significantly less than Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, and Harold Ramis. He reprised the role in Ghostbusters II (1989) and the 2021 Afterlife sequel.

question: In 1968, American science fiction writer Philip K. Dick published a novel about a bounty hunter named Rick Deckard who tracks down escaped androids in a bleak future Earth. Real animals had nearly vanished from the planet, so people kept electric fakes as pets to feel less lonely. In 1982, director Ridley Scott turned Dick's book into the famous rainy neon-lit film Blade Runner. What was Dick's original novel called?
answer: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
choices: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
context: Dick died in March 1982, three months before Blade Runner's June 25 release. The novel features Mercer-ism, mood organs, and the empathy box — most cut from the film. Hampton Fancher wrote the original screenplay; David Peoples did rewrites.

question: The 1982 movie Blade Runner is set in a rainy, neon-drenched future Los Angeles, and its dreamy electronic score was composed by the Greek musician Vangelis, who had just won an Oscar for the Chariots of Fire theme. Vangelis built most of the Blade Runner sound on a single giant polyphonic synthesizer — a rare Japanese keyboard weighing around 200 pounds. Which synthesizer did he mostly use?
context: Vangelis (Evangelos Papathanassiou) used the CS-80 for nearly every iconic Blade Runner cue. The synthesizer cost around $7,000 in 1982 dollars and had a polyphonic keyboard with ribbon-controlled pitch bend.

question: John Milius's 1982 fantasy film Conan the Barbarian, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger as the Cimmerian warrior Conan, opens with a thundering choral piece called 'Anvil of Crom' — pounding drums, chanting horns, blaring brass, and cracking whips. The Greek-American composer behind that score also wrote music for The Hunt for Red October and RoboCop. Who was he?
context: Poledouris's score is widely considered one of the greatest in fantasy-film history. He also scored RoboCop (1987) and Starship Troopers (1997). Director John Milius wanted the score 'as though Wagner had written it from a Mongol's perspective.'

question: For his 1977 movie Star Wars, George Lucas wanted a big, old-fashioned symphonic score instead of the electronic synthesizer music that was fashionable in the 1970s. He hired the American composer John Williams, who wrote the blaring brass-fanfare main theme every kid can hum. Williams recorded the score not in Hollywood but in England, with one of the world's most famous orchestras. Which orchestra played the Star Wars soundtrack?
context: Williams recorded the score at Anvil Studios in Denham, England across two weeks in March 1977. The Star Wars score won the Oscar that year. Williams used Wagnerian leitmotifs — assigning specific themes to specific characters (Vader, the Force, Princess Leia).

question: Sean Astin, who would later play Samwise Gamgee in the Lord of the Rings movies, first became famous as the asthmatic kid hero Mikey in Richard Donner's 1985 adventure The Goonies. Sean's real-life mother was also a Hollywood star — she had won an Oscar at age 16 for playing the young Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker back in 1962, and later had her own hit TV sitcom. Who was Sean's actress mother?
context: Sean later starred in Rudy (1993) and as Sam Gamgee in The Lord of the Rings (2001-2003). His Goonies co-star Josh Brolin was 17 during filming and went on to play Thanos in the MCU.

question: Steven Spielberg's 1989 adventure Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade sends archaeologist Indy and his crusty medievalist father, played by Sean Connery, chasing the Holy Grail across Europe. Standing in their way are the same jackbooted totalitarian villains who chased Indy for the Ark of the Covenant eight years earlier in 1981's Raiders of the Lost Ark. Who are those returning villains?
context: Steven Spielberg famously called the Nazis 'the bad guys nobody minds seeing punched.' Last Crusade earned $474M worldwide. Temple of Doom (1984) used the Thuggee cult to avoid repeating Nazis.

question: The Goonies was a 1985 kid-adventure movie about a gang of friends hunting pirate treasure to save their neighborhood from being bulldozed. Its theme song 'Good Enough' was written and sung by American pop star Cyndi Lauper. Two years earlier, in 1983, Lauper had exploded onto the music scene with her first solo album — packed with hits like 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun' and 'Time After Time.' What was that breakout album called?
choices: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
context: She's So Unusual sold over 6 million copies and produced four top-5 singles including 'Time After Time' and 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun.' Lauper's 'The Goonies 'R' Good Enough' music video featured cameos from WWF wrestlers including The Iron Sheik.

question: The 1990 action movie Total Recall stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as Douglas Quaid, an ordinary construction worker who starts to suspect his memories are all fake — that he is really a secret agent on Mars whose mind was wiped clean. The film was adapted from a 1966 short story by American science fiction writer Philip K. Dick. What was Dick's original story called?
answer: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale
choices: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale
The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
The Man in the High Castle of Time
Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said
context: Dick's 1966 story is much shorter than the film and lacks the Mars setting. Verhoeven had directed RoboCop three years earlier. The famous three-breasted Martian mutant appears in both the 1990 original and 2012 remake.

question: In the 1987 sci-fi action film Predator, Arnold Schwarzenegger leads a squad of commandos through a Central American jungle where an invisible alien hunter picks them off one by one. The towering alien was played by a 7-foot-2 American actor whose face was hidden under the mask. That same year, the very same tall performer suited up in a different costume to play the friendly Bigfoot named Harry, in the family comedy Harry and the Hendersons. Who was this actor?
context: Hall played the Predator in both 1987 and 1990. He also played Harry in Harry and the Hendersons (1987). Hall died in 1991 at age 35 from AIDS-related complications. Jean-Claude Van Damme was originally cast as the Predator but was replaced after just two days of filming.

question: The British director Tony Scott — younger brother of Ridley Scott — made the 1986 fighter-pilot blockbuster Top Gun starring Tom Cruise. Nine years later, in 1995, Scott directed a tense underwater thriller in which Gene Hackman and Denzel Washington play a nuclear-submarine captain and his executive officer who violently disagree over whether to launch their missiles at Russia. What was that submarine movie called?
context: Crimson Tide starred Denzel Washington and Gene Hackman. Tony Scott also directed True Romance (1993), Enemy of the State (1998), and Man on Fire (2004). He was Ridley Scott's younger brother.

question: In Richard Donner's 1985 film The Goonies, a group of kids from Astoria, Oregon go looking for buried pirate treasure to save their neighborhood from being demolished. In the abandoned seaside restaurant above the treasure caves, a hideout is being used by a rough Italian-American crime family — Mama, her sons Jake and Francis, and their monstrous-looking brother Sloth. What is this criminal family's last name?
context: Anne Ramsey played Mama Fratelli; Robert Davi played Jake; Joe Pantoliano played Francis. Sloth was their imprisoned brother (John Matuszak). The setting was Astoria, Oregon — also the filming location.

question: In 1989, the American animator Don Bluth — a former Disney artist who had already made The Land Before Time and An American Tail — released a hand-drawn animated musical set in 1930s New Orleans. Its main character is a German Shepherd gangster dog named Charlie B. Barkin, voiced by Burt Reynolds, who is murdered by his business partner and sneaks back to Earth from the afterlife. What is the movie called?
context: The film opened the same day as The Little Mermaid (November 17, 1989) and was crushed at the box office by Disney's hit. Dom DeLuise voiced Charlie's friend Itchy. Bluth's NIMH was 1982; American Tail 1986; Land Before Time 1988.

question: In 2010, British director Edgar Wright released Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, a movie about a 22-year-old bass player who must defeat his new girlfriend Ramona's seven evil exes in video-game-style fights. It was based on a graphic novel series by Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley, and both the books and the film are set in the same snowy Canadian city where O'Malley wrote them. Which city is that?
context: The film features Toronto landmarks: the Honest Ed's discount store (now demolished), Casa Loma castle, the St. Lawrence Market, and the Bathurst Street subway station. O'Malley grew up in London, Ontario but set the story in Toronto where he lived in his 20s.

question: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World is a 2010 movie and graphic novel series about a Canadian rock bassist named Scott who lives in Toronto. Before he meets his real love Ramona Flowers, Scott is dating a starry-eyed 17-year-old Catholic high-school girl — she comes to all his band's concerts, thinks he is the coolest guy alive, and is brutally heartbroken when he dumps her for Ramona. What is this high-school girlfriend's name?
context: Ellen Wong played Knives in the 2010 film. She's introduced as 'Knives Chau, 17 years old.' Knives's story arc — discovering Scott's douchebaggery and finding her own strength — is one of the comic's most-loved subplots.

question: The Super Mario Bros. Movie came out in 2023 and made over a billion dollars at the box office. In one of its biggest scenes, actor Jack Black voices the villain Bowser and sings a lonely piano ballad called 'Peaches' about his crush on Princess Peach — a song that later got nominated for the Critics Choice Best Song award. The full musical score for the whole rest of the film was written by an American composer. Who wrote the score?
context: Tyler also composed for the Fast and Furious franchise. The score arranges classic Mario themes by Koji Kondo (the original Nintendo composer) throughout. Kondo received a 'thematic material by' credit on the film.

question: The 1993 Western Tombstone dramatizes real events in 1881 Arizona, where Kurt Russell's Wyatt Earp and his brothers clashed with a gang of cattle rustlers known as the Cowboys, who wore red sashes to signal each other. The gang's brutal ringleader in the film shoots the town's marshal Fred White in an opium daze near the start. This character is based on a real historical outlaw. Who was the leader of the Cowboys?
context: Curly Bill was historically the unofficial leader of the Cowboys, though Johnny Ringo (Michael Biehn in the film) was also iconic. Powers Boothe played Curly Bill. After Morgan Earp's murder, Wyatt led a vendetta ride that hunted the Cowboys across the Arizona Territory.

question: American director Rob Reiner is best known for the 1987 fairytale comedy The Princess Bride, with its famous sword fights and 'inconceivable' line. Three years earlier, in 1984, Reiner made his first film — a mock-documentary (a movie that pretends to be a real documentary but is actually a comedy) about a fictional British heavy metal band on a disastrous American tour. Fans still quote it, and its amps famously 'go up to eleven.' What was that earlier film called?
context: Reiner co-wrote Spinal Tap with Christopher Guest, Michael McKean, and Harry Shearer (who all starred). Reiner also played the director Marty DiBergi. His other 80s hits: Stand By Me (1986), Princess Bride (1987), When Harry Met Sally (1989), Misery (1990).

question: The 1984 adventure film Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom stars Harrison Ford as archaeologist Indiana Jones. His young sidekick is a spunky Chinese kid nicknamed Short Round, who drives Indy's getaway car through the streets of Shanghai. The Vietnamese-born child actor who played Short Round disappeared from Hollywood for decades — then, in 2023, made a stunning comeback and won an Oscar. What is his real name?
context: Ke Huy Quan also played Data in The Goonies (1985). He stepped away from acting in the 1990s and worked as a stunt coordinator. He made a major comeback as Waymond Wang in Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), winning the Oscar.

question: In the early 1980s, Canadian filmmaker James Cameron wrote a science-fiction script called The Terminator — about a killer robot sent back in time to murder a young waitress named Sarah Connor. The producers loved the script but wanted a more experienced director. Cameron refused to give up the job. He agreed to sell them the entire script for one tiny fee, on the condition that he got to direct it himself. What did he take for the whole script?
context: Cameron sold the script to Hemdale Pictures for $1 in exchange for the director's chair. The Terminator made $78M on a $6.4M budget and launched both Cameron's and Arnold Schwarzenegger's A-list careers.

question: Ridley Scott's 1979 space-horror film Alien, starring Sigourney Weaver as warrant officer Ellen Ripley aboard the towing ship Nostromo, was advertised with the chilling tagline 'In space no one can hear you scream.' The nightmarish creature stalking the crew — a skeletal black beast with a second inner mouth — was designed by a Swiss surrealist painter whose airbrushed art book Necronomicon had caught Ridley Scott's eye. Who designed the alien?
context: Giger was a Swiss surrealist whose 1977 art book Necronomicon (no relation to Lovecraft) caught Scott's eye. The 'biomechanical' aesthetic — fusion of skeletal and machine forms — defined the franchise. Giger won the Oscar for Visual Effects.

question: The 1981 adventure movie Raiders of the Lost Ark opens with archaeologist Indiana Jones — played by Harrison Ford — sneaking into a booby-trapped Peruvian temple to steal a small golden idol from the top of a stone pedestal. Indy knows the pedestal is weight-triggered: lift the idol and deadly traps will fire. So he brings something with him to place onto the pedestal the instant he grabs the idol. What did he swap onto the pedestal?
context: Indy underestimates the weight; the trap triggers anyway. The giant rolling boulder sequence followed. The opening was inspired by old Republic Pictures Saturday-morning serials Lucas and Spielberg loved as kids.

question: In the climactic confrontation at Tannhäuser Gate in Ridley Scott's 1982 Blade Runner, Rutger Hauer's replicant Roy Batty delivers a final monologue ending 'All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.' Most of those famous final lines were not in David Peoples's shooting script. Hauer reportedly cut the original speech down to its iconic length. When did he write his version?
answer: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
choices: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
During the table read three weeks before filming
On set between takes with Scott approving each line
Two months after wrap, for the redubbed director's cut
context: Hauer cut Peoples's longer speech down and added the 'tears in rain' image. The film crew reportedly applauded after the take. Roy Batty had been hunting Deckard but spares him at the moment of his own death — one of cinema's most-studied scenes.

question: The opening of Rob Reiner's 1987 The Princess Bride shows young Fred Savage in bed playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga computer while his grandfather (Peter Falk) arrives. Savage was already cast in another show that would air the same year and run six seasons. What was the show?
context: The Wonder Years premiered on ABC in January 1988 (filmed late 1987). Savage played Kevin Arnold with Daniel Stern's voiceover as the adult narrator. He was 11 during The Princess Bride filming.

question: Andre the Giant (Andre Roussimoff) played Fezzik in The Princess Bride. The 7-foot-4 wrestler famously could not properly read the script due to dyslexia, so co-star Mandy Patinkin would help him memorize lines. Andre also worked with another famous filmmaker years later. What 1987 film did Andre appear in besides Princess Bride?
context: Andre had played a 'Bigfoot' character in The Six Million Dollar Man (1976) and the title role in a Hulk Hogan Saturday-morning cartoon. He died January 27, 1993 in Paris from congestive heart failure at age 46. His pre-Princess Bride wrestling fame had peaked with WrestleMania III (1987) vs. Hulk Hogan.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, published as six volumes between 2004 and 2010, Ramona Flowers is the American delivery girl Scott Pilgrim falls for. A running visual joke is that Ramona dyes her hair a new color for each book — the reader can tell which volume they are in just by looking at her head. Across volumes 1, 2, and 3, what order do her hair colors go in?
context: O'Malley said the hair-color changes signal Ramona's emotional state and the relationship's phases. In the 2010 film, Mary Elizabeth Winstead wore wigs to match. The 2023 Netflix anime brought back the color sequence more closely than the film could.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World climaxes with a rock-concert battle inside a Toronto music club modeled on the real-life venue Lee's Palace on Bloor Street. In the six-volume comic that the film adapts, cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley gives the venue a different, more villainous name — it's the private concert hall of Ramona's seventh and worst evil ex, the record-label mogul Gideon Graves. What does the comic call the venue?
context: Gideon Graves is Ramona's seventh evil ex and the leader of the League. Jason Schwartzman played him in the 2010 film. The Chaos Theatre fight features the famous 'Power of Love' sword vs. the 'Power of Self-Respect' sword sequence.

question: Don Bluth's first independent film after quitting Walt Disney Animation in 1979, The Secret of NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health), came out in 1982. It's the story of a widowed field mouse named Mrs. Brisby who discovers a colony of super-intelligent rats living in the farmer's rosebush — rats that escaped from a real government mental-health laboratory that had experimented on them. The film is based on a 1971 children's novel that won that year's Newbery Medal. Who wrote the book?
context: O'Brien (pen name for Robert Leslie Conly) died in 1973 before seeing the film. The novel was titled 'Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH.' Bluth changed Frisby to 'Brisby' to avoid trademark conflict with the Wham-O flying disc.

question: Released in 1983, the arcade game Dragon's Lair let players guide the knight Dirk the Daring through a wizard's castle to rescue Princess Daphne, using pre-rendered cartoon animation drawn by former Disney animator Don Bluth. The game stored all those cartoons on a laserdisc inside each cabinet. At 50 cents a play — double the normal quarter — Dragon's Lair pulled huge crowds. Yet arcade owners still ended up losing money on the cabinets. Why?
answer: The laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair
choices: The laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair
Players completed the game in ten minutes so cabinets couldn't generate enough revenue
Nintendo's Donkey Kong released the same month and dominated arcade floor space
The cabinets weighed 600 pounds, requiring two-person installation in most arcades
context: The Pioneer laserdisc players were never designed for the constant-load arcade environment. Cinematronics replaced thousands of laserdiscs and players. Dragon's Lair sequels (Space Ace 1984, Dragon's Lair II: Time Warp 1991) attempted to recapture the magic. The original was the first video game in the Smithsonian.

question: In 1984's Ghostbusters, the team confronts a giant marshmallow monster in the climactic battle. The Stay-Puft Marshmallow Man was an entirely practical-effect creation directed by which Hollywood special-effects veteran whose other 1980s work included E.T. and Poltergeist?
answer: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
choices: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
Stan Winston and his creature shop in Van Nuys
Phil Tippett and his stop-motion animation team
Rob Bottin and his The Thing prosthetics company
context: Stay-Puft was a suit worn by stuntman Bill Bryan, filmed at miniature scale to make him look 100 feet tall against tabletop New York buildings. Edlund had been ILM's visual-effects supervisor on the Star Wars OT before founding Boss Film. The Stay-Puft sequence cost more than the rest of the film's effects combined.

question: In 1981, the AT-AT (All Terrain Armored Transport) walkers in The Empire Strikes Back's Hoth sequence were filmed using stop-motion animation. The lead animator who pioneered the 'go-motion' blur technique on those scenes (and on E.T. the same year) went on to design the iconic alien dinosaurs in Jurassic Park. Who is he?
context: Tippett's go-motion technique used motion-controlled rods to slightly blur each frame, eliminating the jerky look of pure stop-motion. He was set to do Jurassic Park's dinosaurs in stop-motion until Spielberg switched to CGI. Tippett's quote: 'I think I'm extinct.' He got 'Dinosaur Supervisor' credit instead.

question: Tony Scott's 1986 blockbuster Top Gun stars Tom Cruise as the hotshot Navy pilot Maverick at the elite Miramar fighter-weapons school in California. Because the film needed real F-14 Tomcat jets for its dogfight scenes, the US Navy loaned the aircraft — but only on the condition it could approve the script. Scott agreed, and the Navy signed off on almost every scene. It vetoed exactly one major story change. What did the Navy prohibit?
answer: Maverick was originally supposed to die at the end (instead of just losing Goose)
choices: Maverick was originally supposed to die at the end (instead of just losing Goose)
The Russian MiGs were originally identified as specifically being Soviet aircraft
Maverick's romantic interest was originally a Naval officer instead of a contractor
The Top Gun school was originally based at Miramar but moved to fictional Coronado
context: The Navy was thrilled with the recruitment boost the film provided — applications jumped 500% in some markets. Charlie (Kelly McGillis) was originally a Naval flight officer; the Navy insisted she be a civilian to avoid fraternization optics. Top Gun school actually existed at NAS Miramar (now relocated to NAS Fallon).

question: In 1989's Ghostbusters II, the team confronts a sentient river of pink slime flowing beneath Manhattan. The slime is fed by negative emotions, and the climactic battle uses the Statue of Liberty as a giant ghost-busting weapon. What animates the Statue of Liberty in the film?
answer: The team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions
choices: The team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions
Egon's modified proton pack uses neutron-charged ectoplasm to walk the statue
The Statue of Liberty's flame ignites the slime through chemical pyrokinesis
Peter Venkman's slimer pet drags the statue via psychokinetic ectoplasmic feedback
context: Ghostbusters II features Janosz Poha (Peter MacNicol), the Carpathian art restorer being manipulated by the 16th-century painted villain Vigo the Carpathian. The film grossed $215M worldwide. Bobby Brown's 'On Our Own' was the theme song.

question: In Robert Zemeckis's 1985 time-travel comedy Back to the Future, teenage Marty McFly borrows Doc Brown's DeLorean and accidentally travels back to the year 1955 wearing a bright red down-filled puffer vest. The 1955 townsfolk have never seen a modern puffer jacket — the design didn't exist yet — and they mistake his vest for a completely different kind of garment. (Later, seeing his 'Calvin Klein' underwear label, they even start calling him Calvin Klein.) What do the 1955 locals think Marty's puffer vest is?
answer: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
choices: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
A fireman's life vest from the local volunteer station
A Russian air-force flight survival vest from the Eisenhower era
A cowboy-inspired buoyancy aid worn by 1955 rodeo participants
context: The famous Calvin Klein joke wasn't accidental — Calvin Klein launched his eponymous brand in 1968 and had become a household name by the 1985 production. Robert Zemeckis specifically wrote the gag to land with 1985 audiences. The puffer vest itself was a then-current style.

question: In 1985's The Goonies, the film's iconic 'truffle shuffle' scene features Chunk (Jeff Cohen) lifting his shirt and shaking his belly to gain entry to Mikey's house. Cohen was famously typecast by the role. He grew up to be a successful Hollywood professional in what field — not acting?
answer: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
choices: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
Film direction (he directed three indie thrillers in the 2010s)
Restaurant ownership (he opened a Beverly Hills steakhouse)
Real-estate development (he built a luxury hotel chain)
context: Jeff Cohen graduated from UCLA Law School and became founding partner of Cohen Gardner LLP, representing major Hollywood talent and studios. He stopped acting in his teens, calling the experience formative but unsustainable. He maintains friendly relationships with co-stars Sean Astin and Corey Feldman.

question: Released in 1982, John Milius's Conan the Barbarian opens with Conan's father teaching him the riddle of steel before being killed by Thulsa Doom. The opening text-on-screen quote is famously attributed to Nietzsche but actually from a different source. What's the quote and source?
answer: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
choices: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
'In steel a man's soul finds its purest test' — fictional, written by John Milius himself
'The sword is mightier than the kingdom' — from Robert E. Howard's Conan stories
'Crom counts the slain, not the conquests' — from L. Sprague de Camp's pastiches
context: The Nietzsche quote is genuine — from Twilight of the Idols (1888), aphorism 8 of Maxims and Arrows. Milius was a self-confessed Nietzschean. The riddle of steel — 'what is steel compared to the hand that wields it' — is Milius's own invention for the film, not from Howard.

question: In 1983, George Lucas released Return of the Jedi, the third Star Wars film. The Ewoks were furry, teddy-bear-like forest warriors who lived on the moon of Endor and helped the Rebels beat the Empire. A young British actor named Warwick Davis played Wicket W. Warrick, the little Ewok scout who befriends Princess Leia in the woods. Standing only two feet eleven inches tall, Davis was cast for his height in what was his very first movie role. How old was Warwick Davis when he took on the part of Wicket?
context: Davis later starred in Willow (1988), Leprechaun (1993), and Harry Potter (as Professor Flitwick + Griphook the goblin). He was originally cast as a different Ewok and only got the Wicket role when Kenny Baker fell ill. His daughter Annabelle has the same condition (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita).

question: In the 1987 fairytale film The Princess Bride, actors Cary Elwes and Mandy Patinkin fight a long, witty sword duel on the edge of a cliff — and they performed most of the swordplay themselves. Their teacher was Bob Anderson, a former British Olympic fencer who spent decades secretly choreographing movie duels around the world. Anderson also helped train the sword-fighting cast of another huge film franchise. Which series did he work on?
answer: Star Wars (he was Darth Vader's swordsman in the OT)
choices: Star Wars (he was Darth Vader's swordsman in the OT)
Indiana Jones (he choreographed the Petra sword fight in Last Crusade)
James Bond (he taught Roger Moore the For Your Eyes Only sequences)
The Three Musketeers (the 1973 Richard Lester version)
context: Anderson was an Olympic fencer (1952 GBR) who became Hollywood's go-to sword choreographer. He wore the Darth Vader costume in the lightsaber duels of Empire and Jedi (with David Prowse acting elsewhere and James Earl Jones voicing). He also choreographed the 1973 Three Musketeers.

question: In 1985, Disney released an animated fantasy called The Black Cauldron, based on Lloyd Alexander's Prydain Chronicles book series. The film featured the terrifying Horned King raising an undead army of skeleton warriors — much scarier material than Disney's usual princess tales. Because of the frightening scenes, this movie broke a decades-long streak: it was the very first Disney animated feature to carry a rating stronger than G. Which Disney animated film was the first to be rated PG?
choices: The Hunchback of Notre Dame, in 1996
context: The Black Cauldron was Disney's most-expensive animated feature at the time ($44M) and bombed. The Horned King's army of cauldron-born undead earned the PG. Don Bluth was NOT involved despite often being credited — he had defected six years earlier.

question: The 1988 animated film The Land Before Time follows a young dinosaur named Littlefoot on a dangerous journey to find safety after his mother's death. It was directed by American animator Don Bluth and co-produced by Amblin Entertainment, the studio Steven Spielberg had founded. Two years earlier, in 1986, Bluth and Amblin had teamed up on another beloved animated film — a story about a family of mice traveling across the ocean to America. Which film was it?
answer: An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America
choices: An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America
Anastasia (1997), about the orphaned Russian princess
Rock-a-Doodle (1991), about a rooster who can stop the sun
All Dogs Go to Heaven (1989), about a Louisiana gambler dog
context: American Tail's Fievel character was inspired by Spielberg's grandfather. Spielberg never produced Anastasia (Fox Animation) or All Dogs (Goldcrest Films) — those were post-Spielberg Bluth projects. Land Before Time was meant to be a quiet meditative film; the eventual 14 direct-to-video sequels were not Bluth's work.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, the climactic gunfight at the O.K. Corral is historically inaccurate — the real 1881 gunfight lasted approximately 30 seconds and was actually in a narrow vacant lot near, but not in, the O.K. Corral. The real fight killed three of the Cowboys faction. Who was NOT among the dead?
answer: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
choices: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
Tom McLaury (shot by Doc Holliday's shotgun)
context: Ike Clanton had instigated the fight by drunkenly threatening the Earps the night before but ran when shooting started. Tom McLaury, Frank McLaury, and Billy Clanton were killed. Virgil and Morgan Earp were wounded. Wyatt was untouched. Doc Holliday took a graze. The real fight is now reenacted in Tombstone, Arizona for tourists.

question: In Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the climactic battle with Gideon Graves uses a 'Power of Love' sword Scott earns from defeating Todd Ingram, the third evil ex. What special-ability tag does the Power of Love sword have in the game's UI (user interface) text on screen?
context: The sword appears with a Final Fantasy-style item-acquisition screen showing the stats. Scott also earns a Power of Self-Respect sword when fighting his Nega-Scott self. Both swords appear in the climactic Chaos Theatre battle against Gideon Graves.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, Scott's third evil ex Todd Ingram has vegan powers. When he violates his vegan diet, the Vegan Police arrive to strip him of his abilities. What two specific items does Todd eat to trigger the Vegan Police visit in the film?
answer: Half-and-half in his coffee, then chicken parmigiana
choices: Half-and-half in his coffee, then chicken parmigiana
Milk in cereal, then a hamburger from Wimpy's
Cheese on a pizza, then ice cream at Honest Ed's
Butter on toast, then beef chow mein takeout
context: Brandon Routh played Todd in the 2010 film. The Vegan Police agents are played by Thomas Jane and Clifton Collins Jr. Todd's powers include super-strength, telekinesis, and bowl-cut hair. After being de-veganed, he's reduced to a regular bassist who Scott easily defeats.

question: In Edgar Wright's Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the band Sex Bob-omb performs throughout the film. The film's music was overseen by Nigel Godrich (Radiohead's producer), with original songs written by which musician known for his 1990s solo career and his work in the band Beck?
choices: Jack White of The White Stripes
context: Beck wrote 'Garbage Truck' and 'We Are Sex Bob-omb' for the film. Broken Social Scene's Brendan Canning and Kevin Drew also contributed. The Clash at Demonhead's songs (Envy Adams's band) were written by Metric's Emily Haines.

question: In the 2023 animated Super Mario Bros. Movie, Donkey Kong's grumpy old father is Cranky Kong, the ape who rules Kong Island from his throne. Cranky wasn't invented for the movie though — he first showed up way back in 1981 in Nintendo's original Donkey Kong arcade game, the one where Mario, then called Jumpman, climbed girders to rescue a woman named Pauline. In that first cabinet, Cranky wasn't called Cranky yet. Which arcade character was he originally?
answer: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
choices: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
King Kong from a separate Universal Studios franchise
Diddy Kong's grandfather from the SNES Donkey Kong Country games
An entirely new character invented for Donkey Kong 64
context: Cranky's identity as the original DK was established in Donkey Kong Country (1994). The film's Donkey Kong is technically Donkey Kong Jr., who appeared in the 1982 arcade game. The Donkey Kong Country reference in the movie includes a brief snippet of the iconic 1994 banana theme.

question: The 1988 animated film The Land Before Time follows a young dinosaur named Littlefoot and his friends after Littlefoot's mother is killed by a T-Rex. Test audiences of children found the mother's death scene so upsetting that director Don Bluth had to cut about ten minutes of scary footage from the finished movie. Littlefoot was voiced not by a movie star but by a real American child actor — a twelve-year-old boy who spoke every one of the little dinosaur's lines. Who did his voice?
choices: Pat Hingle, the famous voice of the original Bluto
Brian Doyle-Murray, brother of Bill Murray
Macaulay Culkin, before his Home Alone breakout
context: Damon's other notable credit was Newsies (1992). The Land Before Time spawned 13 direct-to-video sequels (1994-2016) without Bluth's involvement. The original is widely considered the only one worth watching by fans.

question: In 1989's Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, the Holy Grail is hidden in the temple of the Sun in Petra, Jordan. The 'cup of a carpenter' test at the end has Indy choosing between dozens of grails. What's the actual line the Grail Knight delivers when Donovan (Julian Glover) drinks from the wrong one?
choices: He picked the cup of pride
context: Robert Eddison played the immortal Grail Knight. The drinking-from-the-wrong-cup effect (Donovan rapidly ages and disintegrates) was Industrial Light & Magic's most-complex prosthetic-and-puppet sequence to that point. The line is a near-perfect mirror of 'he chose wisely' moments later.

question: The 1984 movie The Karate Kid tells the story of Daniel LaRusso, a bullied New Jersey teenager who moves to California and secretly trains in karate under his apartment building's handyman, Mr. Miyagi.
