It was directed by American filmmaker John G. Avildsen. Eight years earlier, in 1976, Avildsen had won the Academy Award for Best Director for another underdog sports film — this one about a poor Philadelphia boxer given one shot at the heavyweight title. Which film was that?
context: Rocky won Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing in 1977. Karate Kid's emotional structure mirrors Rocky's — the unlikely mentor, the romantic subplot, the climactic tournament. Pat Morita's performance as Mr. Miyagi earned a Best Supporting Actor nomination.

question: John McTiernan's 1987 action-horror film Predator drops Arnold Schwarzenegger's commando squad into the Central American jungle to be picked off one by one by an invisible alien hunter — later fans learn the species is called the Yautja. The Predator hunts by heat rather than by sight, and to show what the alien sees on screen, the filmmakers refused to fake the effect in post-production. They shot with a real, then-cutting-edge machine that turned heat into false-color video. What was it?
answer: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
choices: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
Stop-motion overlays composited frame-by-frame in post-production
False-color time-lapse photography exposed through dichroic filters
A custom video feedback loop with chromatic separation lenses
context: The Inframetrics 525 cost approximately $80,000 in 1986. The Predator's thermal POV had to be filmed separately and then matted in. The technology had previously been used to identify roof leaks and electrical equipment failures.

question: The 1990 action film Total Recall stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as a construction worker who may — or may not — really be a spy on Mars with fake memories. Dutch filmmaker Paul Verhoeven directed the finished movie, full of exploding heads and Martian mutants. But years before Verhoeven took the job, a completely different director had been attached to the project. He worked on it for a while before quitting over big creative arguments with the producers. Who was that first director?
answer: David Cronenberg, who left over creative differences with the producers
choices: David Cronenberg, who left over creative differences with the producers
Bruce Beresford, who was attached for two years in pre-production
Patrick Duncan, who wrote an early draft but never directed
Russell Mulcahy, who was set to direct after Highlander's success
context: Cronenberg's vision was reportedly much closer to Philip K. Dick's original short story — psychological-horror-focused rather than action-blockbuster. He left in 1985. The project then went through many directors before Carolco Pictures hired Verhoeven post-RoboCop.

question: The 1986 science-fiction film Aliens is director James Cameron's sequel to Ridley Scott's Alien. Sigourney Weaver returns as Ellen Ripley, who wakes up from 57 years of hibernation drifting in space and joins a squad of tough Colonial Marines heading to check on a lost human colony. When they arrive, they find every single colonist dead or missing — except one terrified little girl who has been hiding alone in the air ducts. What is that girl's name?
context: Carrie Henn played Newt; this was her only film role. Newt's family had named her Rebecca but her brother called her Newt because she could 'fit into all the small places.' In Alien 3 (1992), Newt dies in the opening sequence — a creative decision that infuriated Cameron, who had final-cut authority on Aliens but not Alien 3.

question: In 1984, director James Cameron was casting his sci-fi thriller The Terminator. He almost gave the muscular Austrian actor Arnold Schwarzenegger the role of the hero Kyle Reese, not the killer cyborg. Then Cameron and Schwarzenegger met for lunch, and by the end of that meal Cameron had switched him over to the villain — the unstoppable Terminator itself. What meal supposedly changed Cameron's mind?
answer: There was no specific dish; Cameron just realized Arnold's bulk and accent fit the Terminator better
choices: There was no specific dish; Cameron just realized Arnold's bulk and accent fit the Terminator better
Arnold ordered steak rare and ate aggressively, suggesting the cold cyborg
Arnold's hostess insisted on Italian, which Cameron found revealingly mild
The lunch was at Schatzi's, Arnold's Austrian-themed Santa Monica restaurant
context: The screenplay had originally Arnold as Reese (the human soldier sent back to protect Sarah Connor). Cameron later said Arnold's physical presence and the Austrian accent made him ideal for the unstoppable cyborg. Lance Henriksen had been considered for the T-800 and got the role of Detective Vukovich instead.

question: Andre the Giant played the friendly giant Fezzik in 1987's The Princess Bride. The 7-foot-4 wrestler was at the peak of his fame after his April 1987 WrestleMania III match against Hulk Hogan at the Pontiac Silverdome — a match that drew 93,173 fans and ended with Hogan body-slamming the 520-pound Andre. By 1987, Andre's acromegaly was advancing rapidly. During Princess Bride production, Rob Reiner had to accommodate which specific medical issue?
answer: Andre's back was failing; many of his scenes required hidden rigs to support his weight during lifts
choices: Andre's back was failing; many of his scenes required hidden rigs to support his weight during lifts
Andre's eyesight was deteriorating; he needed his lines read aloud right before each take
Andre needed dialysis treatment three times during production at a Surrey hospital
Andre's hands were so swollen he couldn't grip Westley's leg in the cliff-climbing scene
context: Andre had back surgery just before Princess Bride filming. The famous 'rhyming' scene where Fezzik recites poetry with Vizzini reportedly took multiple takes because Andre would lose his place. Reiner has said working with Andre was one of his life's great honors. The wrestler died January 27, 1993 in Paris.

question: From 2004 to 2010, Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley wrote and drew the Scott Pilgrim graphic novels. They were small, black-and-white paperbacks that looked and read like Japanese manga. British director Edgar Wright — the guy who had just made Shaun of the Dead — snapped up the film rights in 2005, before book two had even hit shelves. What was that second book called?
choices: Scott Pilgrim and the Infinite Sadness
context: The six volumes: Precious Little Life (2004), vs. the World (2005), and the Infinite Sadness (2006), Gets It Together (2007), vs. the Universe (2009), Finest Hour (2010). Wright's film took the title of volume 2 and adapted plot beats from all six. O'Malley drew the final volume's color art in part because the Netflix anime announcement had created industry curiosity.

question: The 2023 Mario Movie's Brooklyn opening uses a recreation of the original 1981 Donkey Kong arcade level as a literal training course. Mario climbs through industrial Brooklyn rooftops while construction crews throw barrels. The sequence is filled with deep-cut Nintendo Easter eggs. The 'Super Mario Bros. Plumbing' commercial that opens the film is a direct shot-for-shot recreation of a real Nintendo print ad from what era?
answer: 1989, when Nintendo had Mario and Luigi appear in a Super Mario Bros. 2-era promotional cassette tape
choices: 1989, when Nintendo had Mario and Luigi appear in a Super Mario Bros. 2-era promotional cassette tape
1995, in a Nickelodeon-style cable TV ad introducing Mario 64
1985, in the original Famicom-era Japanese commercials for Super Mario Bros.
2003, in the GameCube launch advertising campaign for Mario Sunshine
context: The 'Plumbing Service' commercial was hand-animated to match late-80s home-video tape quality. Easter eggs in the Brooklyn opening include the Punch-Out!! gym sign, the Mario Movie 2 logo on the Plumbing van rear, and references to the Wrecking Crew. The commercial's website (supermariobrosplumbing.com) was actually registered as a real domain by Universal Studios.

question: In 1986, animator Don Bluth and producer Steven Spielberg released the cartoon film An American Tail. It followed Fievel, a young Russian-Jewish mouse who gets separated from his family sailing to America in the 1880s. It became the biggest cartoon hit not made by Disney. Spielberg named Fievel after his own grandfather, a real man he had loved as a boy. What was that grandfather's last name?
context: Phillip 'Fievel' Posner emigrated from Ukraine to America in the early 20th century. The film's central song 'Somewhere Out There' (sung by Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram) was a top-5 hit. American Tail spawned a sequel (Fievel Goes West, 1991) and a TV series. Bluth left the franchise after the first film.

question: In 1985's Back to the Future, the role of Marty McFly was originally cast with a different actor who filmed for four to five weeks before being replaced. The Amblin team realized the chemistry wasn't working, paid out the original actor, and brought in Michael J. Fox to refilm everything. Who was the original Marty?
context: Eric Stoltz had just come off the Oscar-buzzy Mask (1985, where he played a young man with cranial dysplasia). The BTTF team felt he was too dramatic for the comedic tone the film needed. Michael J. Fox was the original first choice but had been unavailable due to his Family Ties shooting schedule. After the swap, Family Ties producer Gary David Goldberg let Fox shoot BTTF during Family Ties production gaps — Fox filmed late nights and weekends for months. Stoltz was paid in full for his weeks of work and went on to a strong indie-film career.

question: The original 1979 Don Bluth defection from Walt Disney Animation took 17 animators with him. Bluth had been at Disney since 1955 (working on Sleeping Beauty as a 17-year-old in-betweener) and was the lead animator on The Rescuers (1977). He left because of his frustration with what specific corporate trend at the studio?
answer: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
choices: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
Disney was outsourcing in-between animation work to a studio in Tokyo
Disney was about to license its characters to a kids' meal partnership at McDonald's
Disney was reorganizing its Burbank studio to share space with the theme parks
context: Bluth specifically named the loss of inking-by-hand and the elimination of multi-plane camera shots. Xerography (the photocopy-style process pioneered on 101 Dalmatians in 1961) gave a rougher line quality. Bluth's later films restored multi-plane and hand-inking. The Disney Renaissance starting with The Little Mermaid (1989) partly addressed his original grievances.

question: In 1983, Cinematronics released Don Bluth's Dragon's Lair as an arcade laserdisc game. The cabinet sold for $4,300 — roughly double a standard arcade cabinet's price. Players paid 50 cents per play (double the standard quarter). One year later, Sega Games released a Bluth follow-up using similar laserdisc technology with a space-opera theme. What was the 1984 follow-up called?
context: Space Ace starred Dexter, the lasso-wielding space hero who transforms via the 'Infanto Ray.' Both Dragon's Lair and Space Ace ran on Pioneer LD-V1000 laserdisc players and used digital frame addressing for gameplay branching. American Laser Games later attempted live-action laserdisc games (Mad Dog McCree, 1990) that flopped.

question: Released June 25, 1982, Blade Runner had a famously troubled theatrical release. Test screenings in Denver and Dallas in May 1982 received hostile responses from audiences confused by the film's pacing and lack of narration. Warner Bros. forced Ridley Scott to add a Harrison Ford voiceover before the theatrical release. Ford reportedly delivered the voiceover badly on purpose, hoping it would be cut. What was added besides the voiceover?
answer: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
choices: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
An opening expository newsreel explaining the off-world colonies
A new scene where Deckard explicitly states he's a replicant himself
A live-action prologue with Edward James Olmos's Gaff explaining the case
context: The aerial footage flying over forests was originally shot by Kubrick for The Shining's opening but unused. Scott borrowed the footage for the 1982 theatrical 'happy ending.' The 1992 Director's Cut and 2007 Final Cut removed both the voiceover and the happy ending, restored the unicorn dream sequence, and clarified Deckard's possible replicant identity.

question: The 1982 movie Conan the Barbarian starred Arnold Schwarzenegger. Basil Poledouris wrote the score in Rome. Director John Milius told him to make it sound like Wagner mixed with a Mongol horseman. What sound anchors the famous 'Anvil of Crom' opening?
answer: A choir over hammer-on-anvil percussion with timpani and brass underneath
choices: A choir over hammer-on-anvil percussion with timpani and brass underneath
Solo cello over a string section playing the main theme in counterpoint
A brass-and-bone-flute fanfare over taiko drums
A Hungarian zither over a string ensemble in minor pentatonic
context: Poledouris hired blacksmiths to physically pound anvils on the studio floor for the percussion track. The choir sang in Latin (specifically: 'Doom upon all things, doom and woe' translated). The score became one of the most-licensed fantasy themes for film trailers in the next 40 years. Poledouris died in 2006 at age 61.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday was widely considered the film's standout performance, eclipsing star Kurt Russell. Kilmer reportedly stayed in character with consumptive coughing for months. The film's original director was George P. Cosmatos, but Russell has long claimed he was the uncredited true director. The original director who was fired before filming began was the screenwriter himself. Who?
answer: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
choices: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
John Carpenter, who left over budget disputes with Disney's Hollywood Pictures
Andy Garcia, in his first attempted directorial debut after a delayed Godfather Part III
Steve Beck, the visual-effects supervisor who had directed second-unit work
context: Jarre was fired three weeks into shooting because the production was running behind. He had written a much longer epic screenplay; Cosmatos cut it considerably. Russell has said publicly that he 'ghost-directed' the film with Cosmatos as a paper-only credit. Jarre's screenplay credit remained intact. He died in 2011 at age 56.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World was a financial disappointment on release ($47M on a $90M production+marketing budget) but became a cult favorite on home video. The film features Brandon Routh as Todd Ingram, Chris Evans as Lucas Lee, and Brie Larson as Envy Adams. Two of those cast members went on to play other comic-book heroes in the following decade. Which roles?
answer: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)
choices: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)
Larson played Captain Marvel (2019) and Routh played Atom on CW's Legends of Tomorrow
Evans played the Human Torch (Fantastic Four, 2005) and Routh played the Atom on CW
Larson played Squirrel Girl on a Marvel pilot and Evans played Captain America
context: All four answers are partially true. Routh played Superman in 2006 and the Atom on CW Arrowverse shows. Evans had played the Human Torch in 2005's Fantastic Four before becoming Cap in 2011. Larson played Captain Marvel starting in 2019. The Scott Pilgrim casting was prescient about which young actors would dominate the next decade.

question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner, who had earlier made The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). The film's plot involves the kids finding the treasure map of a 17th-century pirate named One-Eyed Willy. What real-world pirate was Willy loosely based on?
answer: No single specific pirate; the character was original to writer Chris Columbus
choices: No single specific pirate; the character was original to writer Chris Columbus
Blackbeard (Edward Teach), with the eye-patch motif transposed from another period
Henry Morgan, the Welsh privateer turned governor of Jamaica
Anne Bonny's husband Calico Jack Rackham, executed in Jamaica in 1720
context: Chris Columbus wrote the screenplay based on Spielberg's story outline. Columbus later directed Home Alone (1990) and the first two Harry Potter films (2001, 2002). One-Eyed Willy's ship 'The Inferno' was a full-scale practical-effect ship constructed for the climax — Donner refused to destroy it after filming, and crew members have said it sat in a warehouse for years.

question: The Canadian director James Cameron made Aliens in 1986, the action-heavy sequel to Ridley Scott's 1979 horror film Alien. His Aliens earned Sigourney Weaver an Oscar nomination for Best Actress and became one of the most celebrated sequels in cinema. Fans expected Cameron to jump straight into Alien 3, but he did not. Instead Cameron went deep underwater, writing and directing a completely different science-fiction film released in 1989 before he touched any franchise again. What did Cameron actually do next?
answer: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
choices: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
Cameron immediately directed Alien 3 (1992) before The Abyss
Cameron directed Aliens 4 in 1995 before True Lies
Cameron made a Working Title Aliens 2.5 between Aliens and T2
context: Alien 3 (1992) was directed by David Fincher (his directorial debut, an experience he has called a 'horror story'). The Abyss followed Aliens for Cameron. Cameron and Sigourney Weaver were both deeply disappointed by Alien 3's killing of Newt and Hicks. Weaver's involvement in Alien 3 was strange — she was a producer.

question: Director John McTiernan had one of the greatest three-year runs in action-movie history. In 1987 he directed Predator, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger as a commando hunted through the jungle by an alien. Then, back-to-back, he made two more iconic action films before 1990 was out — one starring Bruce Willis, the other starring Sean Connery. What were those two films?
answer: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
choices: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
Die Hard (1988) and Last Action Hero (1993)
Lethal Weapon (1987) and The Russia House (1990)
RoboCop (1987) and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989)
context: McTiernan's Die Hard-Predator-Hunt for Red October trio is one of the great action-director runs in cinema. He later went to prison briefly in 2013 for lying to the FBI about a wiretapping incident involving a private investigator. His daughter Annaliesa Henrik McTiernan is also a filmmaker.

question: In the 1990 science-fiction film Total Recall, Dutch director Paul Verhoeven built a rowdy Martian bar full of strange mutants. One of the movie's costliest special-effects scenes featured a mutant dancer named Mary — a red-dressed woman with three breasts. The American actress who played Mary later left acting entirely and became a working newspaper and magazine journalist, covering serious real-world stories. What is her name?
answer: Lycia Naff, who later played the Three-Breasted Whore (her IMDB credit) and went on to journalism
choices: Lycia Naff, who later played the Three-Breasted Whore (her IMDB credit) and went on to journalism
Sharon Stone, who had a similar bit role here before Basic Instinct (1992)
Roxann Dawson, who played B'Elanna Torres on Star Trek Voyager (1995-2001)
Mel Johnson Jr., the cabbie character actor's daughter playing a mutant niece
context: Lycia Naff appeared in three scenes total in the film. The three-breasted effect was a practical prosthetic, not CGI. Verhoeven famously delights in inserting transgressive imagery in commercial films (RoboCop's ED-209 boardroom shooting, Starship Troopers's flesh-eating brain bug). Naff later worked as an entertainment journalist for the National Enquirer.

question: In 1986, Tony Scott directed Top Gun on a $15M budget, which was high for a non-effects-driven film at the time. The Navy provided the F-14 Tomcats but required script approval. Tom Cruise nearly drowned during one stunt scene that was eventually cut from the final film. What was the cut sequence?
answer: An underwater ejection-seat training drill at the NAS Miramar pool
choices: An underwater ejection-seat training drill at the NAS Miramar pool
A high-altitude bailout sequence over the Mojave Desert salt flats
A submarine-deck landing simulation in the Pacific off San Diego
A water-survival exercise in San Francisco Bay near Alcatraz
context: Cruise was reportedly fine but the producers cut the sequence due to liability concerns. Cruise's later fame for doing his own stunts (notably the helicopter sequence in Mission: Impossible — Fallout) descends partly from his Top Gun experience. The 2022 sequel Top Gun: Maverick brought back the underwater stunt theme with Cruise actually performing G-force flight in real Navy aircraft.

question: In 1986's Top Gun, the famous beach volleyball scene was added at the last minute by producer Don Simpson. The scene's homoerotic subtext has been widely discussed by film critics. Tony Scott reportedly resisted including it. What real-life element of Cruise's career did the scene contribute to?
answer: It established Cruise's shirtless-action-star image that would dominate the next decade of his filmography
choices: It established Cruise's shirtless-action-star image that would dominate the next decade of his filmography
It introduced his Scientology recruiting pitch to younger actors in early on-set rehearsals
It started his publicly known feud with co-star Val Kilmer (Iceman) over creative direction
It led to his marriage to Nicole Kidman, whom he met at a Top Gun production party
context: The volleyball scene was added by producer Don Simpson against Scott's wishes. Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer were known for adding 'beefcake' shots to their films. Cruise's subsequent shirtless scenes in The Color of Money (1986), Cocktail (1988), and Mission: Impossible (1996) reinforced the look. He met Nicole Kidman on Days of Thunder (1990), not Top Gun.

question: The 1984 comedy Ghostbusters was first written by Dan Aykroyd for himself and three friends: John Belushi, Eddie Murphy, and John Candy. Belushi died of a drug overdose in 1982, before filming ever started, so Bill Murray took over Belushi's part — the wisecracking parapsychologist Peter Venkman. Aykroyd later said Venkman's whole loose, mischievous vibe was a direct tribute to Belushi's roles in which two earlier films?
answer: Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman
choices: Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman
Continental Divide (1981) and Neighbors (1981) — Belushi's late-career romantic-lead attempts
1941 (1979) and Goin' South (1978) — Spielberg/Nicholson-era serious roles
Saturday Night Live's Samurai sketches (1976-1979) — the deadpan-anarchist character type
context: Belushi died of a drug overdose on March 5, 1982 in Hollywood's Chateau Marmont. Aykroyd had developed the Ghostbusters concept partly as a Belushi vehicle. Eddie Murphy declined because of Beverly Hills Cop conflict; the role became Winston Zeddemore (Ernie Hudson). Aykroyd's brother Peter Aykroyd had inspired the idea via the family's interest in spiritualism.

question: In 1985, director Ron Howard — the redheaded kid who had grown up playing Opie on The Andy Griffith Show — made the sci-fi drama Cocoon. In it, a group of retirement-home men swim in a pool full of glowing alien pods and suddenly feel young and strong again. Don Ameche won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for it. What Disney movie, released the year before Cocoon, had Howard directed too?
answer: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
choices: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
Night Shift (1982), with Henry Winkler and Michael Keaton
Gung Ho (1986), with Michael Keaton at the Japanese auto plant
Willow (1988), with Warwick Davis and Val Kilmer in the lead roles
context: Splash was Touchstone Pictures' first release — Disney's adult-oriented label. Howard's career took off after Splash. He had been Opie on The Andy Griffith Show and Richie on Happy Days before transitioning to directing in the late 1970s. His next big hit was Backdraft (1991).

question: In Princess Bride, William Goldman's 1973 novel famously frames itself as the abridgement of a fictional classic by 'S. Morgenstern.' Many readers wrote to Goldman asking for the 'unabridged' version. Goldman's introduction included a real publisher offer that became famous. What did he promise readers who wrote in?
answer: He'd send them the unabridged 'reunion scene' between Westley and Buttercup, but the publisher legally couldn't reproduce it
choices: He'd send them the unabridged 'reunion scene' between Westley and Buttercup, but the publisher legally couldn't reproduce it
He'd send them a corrected manuscript page from S. Morgenstern's original text
He'd send them a Florinese-language certificate of completion from the abridgement
He'd send them his personal copy of the original Morgenstern hardback for inspection
context: Goldman's gag was elaborate — readers who wrote to the publisher (Harcourt Brace) received an apologetic form letter explaining that 'the Morgenstern estate had refused permission' for the reunion scene to be reproduced. The book has a real publisher's-introduction-style apparatus throughout. Goldman never wrote a real Morgenstern manuscript; the joke continues.

question: Released in 1983, Don Bluth and Sega's Dragon's Lair laserdisc arcade game features Princess Daphne being held by the dragon Singe. The game was so frame-by-frame animated that the 22-minute game length contained more individual hand-drawn animation than most full feature films. How many cels did Bluth's team draw for the game?
answer: Approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature
choices: Approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature
Approximately 12,000 cels — comparable to a single Looney Tunes short
Approximately 250,000 cels — comparable to The Lion King (1994)
Approximately 8,000 cels — heavily reusing animation across branches
context: Bluth's team worked for 7 months on the project. The non-linear branching structure meant scenes that the player might or might not see depending on choices. The original arcade laserdiscs are now considered collectible artifacts of arcade history. Don Bluth himself estimated the cel count in interviews.

question: In 1989's Ghostbusters II, the team's main antagonist is a 16th-century Carpathian tyrant whose spirit is trapped in a self-portrait at a Manhattan art museum. The character is named Vigo the Carpathian. The actor playing Vigo was a 6-foot-9 Croatian giant who was a former bodybuilder and Mr. Yugoslavia. What was his name?
answer: Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe)
choices: Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe)
Bill Bixby (best known as the original TV Hulk's Bruce Banner)
Ernie Reyes Sr. (the martial-arts coach who choreographed the Karate Kid)
Tor Johnson (the Plan 9 from Outer Space wrestler who died in 1971)
context: Homburg's German accent was so thick that director Ivan Reitman dubbed all his lines using Max von Sydow. Homburg had been a pro wrestler before becoming an actor. He died in 2004 at age 63. His one-time girlfriend was actress Romy Schneider.

question: In 1985, Back to the Future's iconic Twin Pines Mall location (used for the DeLorean's first time-jump) was actually a real Burbank, California shopping center called Puente Hills Mall. The 'Twin Pines Ranch' joke (Marty knocks down one pine, so it becomes 'Lone Pine Mall' on his return) was an inside joke about the location's real name. What was the real name?
answer: Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank)
choices: Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank)
Hollywood Mall, a since-demolished shopping center on Sunset Boulevard
Northridge Fashion Center, the locations team's alternate-day backup
Universal CityWalk, before its later 1990s development
context: Puente Hills Mall has hosted multiple BTTF reunions. The Twin Pines / Lone Pine joke is one of the film's many small payoffs from Marty's brief 1955 actions affecting 1985. The mall's actual location is in the city of Industry, southeast of Los Angeles. Universal-themed Marty's Cafe operated at the mall for years.

question: In 1984, director John G. Avildsen — who had already won a Best Director Oscar for the 1976 boxing film Rocky — made The Karate Kid, about a bullied teenager named Daniel LaRusso learning karate from an elderly Japanese-American gardener named Mr. Miyagi. The script was originally set in Florida but Avildsen moved the whole story to Los Angeles. One reason was simple production logistics. What was the other reason?
answer: The crane kick stance required a beach with sunset lighting that Florida couldn't reliably provide
choices: The crane kick stance required a beach with sunset lighting that Florida couldn't reliably provide
The script's reference to Daniel's late father required California's specific car-culture imagery
Mr. Miyagi's character was rewritten as a Japanese-American gardener fitting Los Angeles demographics
The Cobra Kai dojo's biker aesthetic required the San Fernando Valley's specific scenery
context: Miyagi's backstory includes Manzanar internment during WWII — a California-specific element. Pat Morita's Oscar-nominated performance was widely credited with humanizing Japanese-American history for 1980s audiences. The crane-kick scene was filmed at Leo Carrillo State Beach in Malibu. Avildsen passed away in 2017.

question: The 1987 sci-fi film Predator, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, needed a terrifying alien hunter to menace his commando squad in the Central American jungle. The first Predator suit looked like a skinny insect with a long red neck, and it was worn on set by a young Jean-Claude Van Damme. Schwarzenegger and director John McTiernan both hated the design and demanded a full redo. The redesign was handed to a legendary special-effects sculptor who had also built the creatures for Aliens and The Thing. Who was he?
context: Stan Winston Studio became the go-to creature-effects shop in the 1980s and 90s — also doing Terminator (1984), Aliens (1986), Predator (1987), Jurassic Park (1993), and Edward Scissorhands (1990). Winston died of multiple myeloma in 2008 at age 62. Jean-Claude Van Damme had originally been cast as the Predator but quit after one day.

question: In 1991's T2, James Cameron pushed CGI (computer-generated imagery) to new heights with the liquid-metal T-1000. Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) spent months developing the morphing software, dramatically expanding what was possible in film effects. The breakthrough was made possible by a custom 'morph' program written by an ILM engineer. What was that engineer's name?
answer: Doug Smythe, who later won an Academy Award for the morphing technology
choices: Doug Smythe, who later won an Academy Award for the morphing technology
John Knoll, the inventor of Photoshop while at ILM
Dennis Muren, the special-effects supervisor on the OT Star Wars films
Phil Tippett, fresh from his go-motion T-Rex work at the time
context: Doug Smythe led the morphing-software team at ILM. The T-1000's effects took several minutes of screen time to render per second. The technology was reused on Death Becomes Her (1992) and helped enable Jurassic Park (1993). The morph effect became so culturally iconic that Michael Jackson's Black or White music video (1991) immediately copied it.

question: Released in 1986, James Cameron's Aliens famously used a Cat called Jonesy — but with multiple cat actors playing the role across scenes. The film also featured the famous Power Loader exoskeleton used in the climactic fight against the Alien Queen. The Power Loader was a practical-effects build. How tall was the Queen costume?
answer: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
choices: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
Twelve feet, with rod puppeteers controlling only the upper body
Eighteen feet, with hydraulics controlled by joystick offstage
Sixteen feet, with three suit performers stacked vertically inside the costume
context: The Queen costume was designed by Stan Winston and operated by 14-16 people total when the rod-and-puppet team was counted. Sigourney Weaver insisted on doing her own Power Loader stunts after a few rehearsals. The cat Jonesy was played by four trained cats.

question: The 1993 Western film Tombstone tells the story of legendary lawman Wyatt Earp and his friends facing down outlaws in the 1880s Arizona town of Tombstone. American actor Val Kilmer plays Doc Holliday, a tubercular gambler and gunfighter who coughs blood and drinks whiskey between duels. In one tense scene, Doc stares down his rival Johnny Ringo and mutters an old Latin proverb: 'in vino veritas.' What does that Latin phrase mean in English?
context: Doc Holliday was historically a Georgia dentist who turned to gunfighting after his tuberculosis diagnosis. He died at age 36 in Glenwood Springs, Colorado in 1887. Val Kilmer's performance is widely considered one of the greatest portrayals of the historical character. The film also features Bill Paxton as Morgan Earp.

question: The 1990 gangster film Goodfellas was directed by American filmmaker Martin Scorsese and stars Ray Liotta as Henry Hill — a real New York mobster who spent decades inside the Lucchese crime family before turning informant for the FBI. The screenplay was adapted from a 1985 non-fiction book by American journalist Nicholas Pileggi, drawn from hundreds of taped interviews Pileggi had done with the real Hill himself. What was Pileggi's book called?
answer: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
choices: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
The Goodfella's Tale: Henry Hill's Story
The Mob: A Made Man's Memoir
context: Pileggi co-wrote the screenplay with Scorsese. The title 'Goodfellas' was changed because of an unrelated TV series called Wiseguy (1987-90). Henry Hill, the real-life informant subject, died in 2012. The film's improvised dinner scenes (especially Joe Pesci's 'Funny how?' bit) became iconic.

question: Released in 1985, Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future earned $381M worldwide on a $19M budget. The film famously features a Pepsi product placement in 1985 and 1955. What other beverage did Marty try to order in 1955 that wasn't yet available, becoming a famous gag?
answer: Tab and Pepsi Free, both Pepsi-brand variants that didn't exist in 1955
choices: Tab and Pepsi Free, both Pepsi-brand variants that didn't exist in 1955
Diet Coke and Sprite Zero, Coca-Cola products from later decades
Mountain Dew and Sunkist, brands that hadn't yet been launched
Coca-Cola Classic and New Coke, distinguishing the 1985 confusion
context: Marty asks for a Tab — the soda clerk responds 'I can't give you a tab unless you order something.' Marty then asks for a Pepsi Free — the clerk says 'You want a Pepsi, pal, you're gonna pay for it.' Tab and Pepsi Free were both real Pepsi/Coca-Cola products in 1985 (diet variants). The gag plays on 1955 versus 1985 vocabulary differences.

question: In 1987 the American comedy director Mel Brooks released Spaceballs, a movie that spoofed Star Wars. The hero Lone Starr piloted a Winnebago spaceship across the galaxy with his best friend Barf, a big lovable half-man, half-dog creature Brooks called a Mawg. Barf had floppy ears, a wagging tail, and a huge appetite. He was played by a warm-hearted, heavyset Canadian comedy actor famous for movies like Uncle Buck and Planes, Trains and Automobiles. Who played Barf the Mawg in Spaceballs?
context: Candy died in 1994 at age 43 from a heart attack. Rick Moranis played Dark Helmet (the Vader parody). Bill Pullman played Lone Starr (the Han Solo parody). Spaceballs took Star Wars to task for marketing itself through merchandise — the 'Spaceballs the Lunchbox' running gag was prescient.

question: The 1987 movie The Princess Bride opens with a boy playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga. His grandpa comes to read him a story. The game shown was published by Accolade in 1985. Many fans got it wrong and thought it was a 1989 sequel. What was the real title?
answer: Hardball! (the 1985 original, not Hardball II from 1989)
choices: Hardball! (the 1985 original, not Hardball II from 1989)
World Series Baseball by Atari Ages
context: Hardball was Accolade's first hit, programmed by Bob Whitehead. The Amiga prop in the film was a Commodore Amiga 1000 (released 1985). Fred Savage was 11 during filming and was already cast in The Wonder Years pilot that same year. Norman Reynolds had production-designed Star Wars (1977) and Empire Strikes Back (1980) before Princess Bride. The video-game prop is one of the most-Googled details of any 80s film opening.

question: In Canadian cartoonist Bryan Lee O'Malley's six-volume Scott Pilgrim graphic novel series, hero Scott must defeat the seven evil exes of his girlfriend Ramona Flowers one by one to keep dating her. Ramona's fourth evil ex is the only female fighter Scott has to face — a katana-wielding young woman Ramona briefly dated during college. What is this fourth ex's name?
context: Roxie Richter is Ramona's fourth evil ex and only female ex. Mae Whitman played her in the 2010 Edgar Wright film. The 'L-word' chapter title alludes to Ramona's revelation of her 'little bi-furious phase in college.' Whitman is also famous as Katara's voice in Avatar: The Last Airbender. Envy Adams (Brie Larson) is Scott's heartbreaking ex-girlfriend. Knives Chau is Scott's then-current 17-year-old high school girlfriend. Kim Pine is Sex Bob-omb's drummer.

question: The original 1985 NES Super Mario Bros. famously contains a glitch in World 1-2 that lets players warp into a 'Minus World' (World -1) — actually a corrupted underwater Water Level 7 that loops with no exit. The Japanese Famicom Disk System version had a DIFFERENT result for the same glitch sequence. What happens on the Famicom Disk version?
answer: The Minus World is three different glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position, and one is even completable
choices: The Minus World is three different glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position, and one is even completable
The Minus World plays back the title screen in distorted color, freezing the console
The Minus World becomes World 0, an inverted version of 1-1 with reversed gravity
The Minus World contains the developer Easter egg crediting Shigeru Miyamoto by name
context: The cartridge ROM version's Minus World loops because the corrupted tile is read as Water Level 7's start. The Famicom Disk version stores level data slightly differently in RAM, so the result varies. SMB's Minus World is one of the most-studied glitches in video-game history. The 1-2 warp pipe was intended to send Mario to Worlds 2-4; the glitch hijacks the warp routine.

question: The 2023 Mario Movie's 'Penguin King' sequence is set in a Snow Kingdom where the King of Penguins (voiced by Khary Payton) tries to defend his realm from Bowser's attack. The sequence's snowball-fight scene is loaded with Mario-game references. The Snow Kingdom is partly inspired by which specific Mario game world from Super Mario 64 (1996)?
answer: Cool, Cool Mountain — the snowy peak with the cabin and the slide level
choices: Cool, Cool Mountain — the snowy peak with the cabin and the slide level
Snowman's Land — the wider Mario 64 ice level with the big snowman
Sherbet Land — from Mario Kart 64, not Super Mario 64
Freezeflame Galaxy — actually from Super Mario Galaxy (2007), post-N64
context: Cool, Cool Mountain features a baby penguin lost on the slope that Mario can rescue. The level appeared in Super Mario 64 (Nintendo 64, 1996), one of the most-celebrated 3D platformers ever. The 2023 film's Snow Kingdom design directly evokes the Cool, Cool Mountain cabin and slide aesthetic. The Khary Payton casting for the Penguin King is itself a deep cut — he voiced Cyborg on Teen Titans for years.

question: In 1985's Back to the Future, the clock-tower lightning strike scene was filmed at the courthouse on the Universal Studios backlot — the same set used for To Kill a Mockingbird (1962). The film's production used a specific stunt-double for Christopher Lloyd in the cable-swinging climax. What was unusual about the stunt setup that allowed for the famously dangerous-looking shot?
answer: The cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion
choices: The cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion
Lloyd performed the stunt himself with no harness, and ILM digitally added the cable in post-production
The clock tower was a half-scale forced-perspective miniature, and the stunt was filmed sideways
The scene was filmed using bluescreen, with the cable swing entirely added via matte painting
context: The Universal Studios courthouse was actually built for To Kill a Mockingbird in 1962. The clock face was added for BTTF and remained a Universal Studios tour stop for years. The original Back to the Future Part II (1989) revisited the scene from a different angle. Zemeckis's commitment to practical effects on the trilogy gave it a tactile quality CGI sequels often lack.

question: Released in 1982, Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial featured Reese's Pieces as the candy used to lure E.T. After Mars Inc. famously turned down product placement for M&Ms, Hershey signed a $1 million deal with Universal. Within weeks of release, Reese's Pieces sales jumped dramatically. By what factor did sales increase in the months following the film's release?
answer: Sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history
choices: Sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history
Sales doubled, restoring Hershey's market share against M&Ms briefly
Sales quadrupled in the first month, then settled to a 50% lift
Sales increased tenfold, leading Hershey to triple production capacity
context: The Mars Inc. rejection of M&Ms is one of the most-cited examples of poor marketing decision-making. Hershey's $1M deal was modest by today's standards but groundbreaking in 1982. E.T. grossed $359M domestically, holding the all-time record until 1997's Titanic. Spielberg's son Mikaela was born around the time of the film's production, partly influencing its child-centric perspective.

question: John Williams's 1977 score for Star Wars: A New Hope was performed by the London Symphony Orchestra at Anvil Studios in Denham, England. Williams used Wagnerian leitmotifs — assigning specific themes to specific characters. The famous 'Imperial March' (Darth Vader's theme) does NOT actually appear in the original 1977 film. When did it debut?
answer: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
choices: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
Return of the Jedi (1983), where it premiered in the throne-room confrontation
The original 1977 film, in a slower, less-recognizable form during the Death Star scenes
The 1997 Special Edition rerelease, which added the Imperial March to several Vader scenes
context: The Imperial March (technically 'The Imperial March/Darth Vader's Theme') premiered in The Empire Strikes Back (1980). The original 1977 Star Wars used the Main Title theme for Vader's appearances. Williams composed the leitmotif specifically for the Empire score. The London Symphony Orchestra has now recorded Williams's Star Wars scores for every theatrically released film through the entire saga.

question: Released in 1989, Don Bluth's All Dogs Go to Heaven famously released the same day as Disney's The Little Mermaid — November 17, 1989. The Disney film crushed it at the box office. Bluth's Charlie B. Barkin character was voiced by Burt Reynolds. Reynolds reportedly took the role for a specific personal reason. What was it?
answer: His pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss
choices: His pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss
His agent forced the role to fulfill a three-picture deal with United Artists
He needed quick income while waiting for the Cannonball Run III project to greenlight
He wanted to learn animation voice-work for a planned cartoon based on his career
context: Reynolds was at the peak of his Hollywood power in the late 1980s but had begun the steep decline that defined his 1990s. All Dogs Go to Heaven was his only major animated voice role. He died in 2018 at age 82. Bluth has spoken in interviews about Reynolds being deeply committed to the part despite the film's box-office disappointment.

question: Released in 1982, John Carpenter's The Thing was a financial disappointment at $19.6M against an $11M budget — partly because it opened against E.T. (June 25, 1982 Carpenter; June 11, 1982 E.T.). The film's practical effects by Rob Bottin pioneered creature transformation imagery. The most-iconic transformation sequence involves a character's head detaching and growing spider legs. The shot has a specific cultural nickname. What's it called?
answer: The Norris head-spider, named after the character (Charles Hallahan) whose head transforms
choices: The Norris head-spider, named after the character (Charles Hallahan) whose head transforms
The Bennings split, named for the first character to obviously transform in the film
The Blair monster, the basement creature's first reveal moment
The Palmer transformation, the most-quoted body-horror scene in the kennel
context: The Norris head-spider scene features the head growing spider legs and walking across the floor. The famous line: 'You've gotta be fucking kidding.' Rob Bottin was 22 when he supervised the effects. Stan Winston also contributed (the dog-thing transformation). The Thing has been reassessed as one of the greatest horror films ever made, its initial commercial failure attributed to E.T.'s family-friendly competition.

question: Released in 1984, Ghostbusters had its iconic theme song written by Ray Parker Jr. The song became one of 1984's biggest hits — but immediately triggered a famous copyright-infringement lawsuit. Who sued Parker for plagiarism, and what was the disputed song?
answer: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
choices: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
Lionel Richie sued for similarity to 'All Night Long' (1983); won damages on appeal
Tina Turner sued for similarity to 'What's Love Got to Do With It' (1984); was dismissed
Prince sued for similarity to 'When Doves Cry' (1984); settled for publishing royalties
context: The settlement included a non-disclosure clause. Lewis later spoke about it in interviews, costing him a confidentiality-violation lawsuit from Parker. The Ghostbusters theme spent three weeks at #1 on Billboard Hot 100 in September 1984. Ray Parker Jr. was also a respected session guitarist who had played on records by Stevie Wonder and Barry White.

question: Released in 1987, Predator was filmed in the jungles around Mismaloya and Palenque in Mexico. The brutal production conditions — heat, humidity, dysentery — led to multiple cast members losing significant weight. Arnold Schwarzenegger was reportedly the only major cast member who didn't get sick. The film's iconic 'tribal chief' final-act scene features Schwarzenegger covered in mud to mask his heat signature from the Predator's thermal vision. The mud sequence had a specific real-world inspiration. What?
answer: Vietnam War-era veterans had reportedly used mud to evade NVA night-vision optics, inspiring the script choice
choices: Vietnam War-era veterans had reportedly used mud to evade NVA night-vision optics, inspiring the script choice
African elephant-hunting tribes had used mud to mask their scent from elephants, per anthropologist consultants
Camo-pattern mudding was a then-current US Army Ranger field training technique
Schwarzenegger improvised the mud move during a take, and McTiernan kept it in
context: John McTiernan had researched military jungle-warfare tactics for the film. The mud-covering scene became Predator's most-iconic visual. Carl Weathers (Apollo Creed from Rocky) played Dillon, the CIA contact. Bill Duke and Jesse Ventura played other commandos. Ventura's catchphrase 'I ain't got time to bleed' was reportedly ad-libbed by him on set.

question: Released in 1986, James Cameron's Aliens was filmed at Pinewood Studios in England. Cameron clashed extensively with the British crew over American versus British filmmaking practices. The most-famous on-set incident involved Cameron firing the entire British crew on the first day. What did he do?
answer: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made
choices: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made
He brought in his own American crew from The Terminator after the British crew walked out
He hired Stanley Kubrick's longtime first AD to manage the British team
He made a deal with the union to let Sigourney Weaver be technically a producer to satisfy quotas
context: Cameron's reputation for being demanding came partly from Aliens. He has said in interviews that the crew was unaccustomed to working at the pace he wanted. Sigourney Weaver was famously paid $1M for Aliens (a then-record for a female lead in an action film). The film's $18M budget was modest by 1980s standards. Aliens received seven Oscar nominations and won two.

question: The 1985 science-fiction film Cocoon is about a group of Florida retirees who sneak into a neighbor's swimming pool and discover alien pods that make them feel young again. American actor Don Ameche plays retiree Art Selwyn and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the role. In one show-stopping scene, seventy-seven-year-old Ameche crashes a nightclub dance floor and pulls off a real breakdance move — spinning on his upper back and shoulders while his legs point straight at the ceiling. Which breakdance move did Ameche perform?
answer: A backspin (the move where the body rotates on the upper back/shoulders)
choices: A backspin (the move where the body rotates on the upper back/shoulders)
A windmill (the legs swing in a vertical circle while the back stays on the floor)
The moonwalk (Michael Jackson had popularized it in March 1983)
context: Ameche was 77 when he won the Oscar — at the time the second-oldest recipient of the Best Supporting Actor category. He had been a major film star in the 1930s and 40s and Cocoon revitalized his career. The breakdancing scene was performed by a stunt double for the actual spinning moves, but Ameche performed all the dance footwork himself. The 1988 sequel Cocoon: The Return reunited most of the original cast.

question: Released in 1988, Don Bluth's Land Before Time was originally going to be a much darker film. Universal Studios and producers Steven Spielberg and George Lucas reportedly forced significant cuts after test audiences with children expressed distress. The release version is 69 minutes long. How much footage was reportedly cut from Bluth's original?
answer: Approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother
choices: Approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother
Approximately 3 minutes, mostly Bluth-favorite dialogue between Cera and Littlefoot
Approximately 18 minutes, including an entire subplot about Petrie's missing father
Approximately 6 minutes, focusing on Ducky's separation from her family early in the film
context: Bluth has been ambivalent about the cuts in subsequent interviews. The death of Littlefoot's mother was reportedly so traumatic in the original cut that test-screening parents complained Universal had screened a horror film. The cuts gave the film a tighter pace at the cost of much of its emotional depth. Bluth left the franchise after the original; the 13 direct-to-video sequels are widely considered inferior.

question: Released in 1986, Don Bluth's An American Tail featured the song 'Somewhere Out There' — a duet between Fievel and his sister Tanya at opposite ends of the New York night sky, longing to find each other. The song was a top-5 hit on Billboard. The film's musical sequence was animated using a specific Bluth-pioneered technique that gave it visual depth. What technique?
answer: A multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection
choices: A multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection
Rotoscoping over live-action performers in costume for the song's choreography
Computer-assisted 'tweening' on a Cray supercomputer that ILM had loaned to Bluth
Inverse-kinematic limb animation, an early version of the modern 3D rigging technique
context: Multi-plane camera (invented by Disney's Iwerks in 1937) involved multiple glass planes of artwork being filmed through a camera that focused on each at different depths. Bluth's commitment to the technique was central to his break from Disney. The 'Somewhere Out There' sequence in An American Tail features at least 5 planes of moving artwork. Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram's recording of the song reached #2 on Billboard.

question: Released in 1990, Paul Verhoeven's Total Recall featured a transgressive approach to violence that was typical of Verhoeven's RoboCop-era Hollywood work. The film's Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) rating fight was famous. Verhoeven and the studio submitted the film a total of 8 times before getting an R rating. What was the specific scene that gave the MPAA the most trouble?
answer: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
choices: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
The three-breasted Martian mutant Mary's brief topless scene
Sharon Stone's character being shot in the head and the explicit aftermath
Quaid's eye-popping scene as the Mars atmosphere reaches him
context: The subway scene shows Schwarzenegger holding a dead body in front of him as bullets riddle it. The MPAA initially gave it an X rating. Verhoeven darkened the lighting and slightly trimmed the frame count to get the R. Total Recall earned $261M worldwide. Verhoeven's career trajectory continued with Basic Instinct (1992), Showgirls (1995), and Starship Troopers (1997) before he returned to European cinema.

question: Released in 1989, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade featured Sean Connery as Indy's father Henry Sr. Connery was only 12 years older than Harrison Ford (born 1930 vs. Ford 1942). Spielberg cast Connery partly because of a specific role Connery had played as a literary action hero. Which role?
answer: James Bond, since Spielberg wanted to evoke 'James Bond as the father of Indiana Jones'
choices: James Bond, since Spielberg wanted to evoke 'James Bond as the father of Indiana Jones'
King Arthur in Excalibur (1981), which had been Connery's other recent prestige fantasy role
Robin Hood in Robin and Marian (1976), where Connery had played an aging hero
King Agamemnon in Time Bandits (1981), Connery's Terry Gilliam fantasy outing
context: Spielberg's quote was: 'I always thought of James Bond as the inspiration for Indiana Jones, so why not have James Bond actually BE Indy's father?' Connery had famously played Bond from 1962-1971 (six films) and again in 1983's Never Say Never Again (a non-EON Bond). The casting brought 1980s audiences full-circle on the action-hero archetype.

question: Released in 1984, the original Karate Kid features Mr. Miyagi's wartime backstory — interned at Manzanar War Relocation Center during World War II (WWII) while his wife and child died there. Pat Morita's Oscar-nominated performance gave the scene exceptional emotional weight. Morita had himself been interned as a child during WWII. Where was the real Pat Morita interned?
answer: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
choices: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
Manzanar, California (the same camp his Karate Kid character was set at)
Heart Mountain, Wyoming (the highest-altitude camp in the system)
Topaz, Utah (where Morita's family had owned a Sacramento Valley restaurant)
context: Morita was born in Isleton, California in 1932 to immigrant parents. He had spinal tuberculosis as a child and spent nine years in a Sacramento hospital. After the war, his family ran restaurants. He moved into stand-up comedy in the 1960s as 'The Hip Nip' and broke into TV with Happy Days. The Karate Kid (1984) was his career-defining role. He died in 2005 at age 73.

question: Released in 1993, Tombstone went through a famously chaotic production. Director Kevin Jarre was fired three weeks into shooting. George P. Cosmatos was hired as a paper director — Kurt Russell has long claimed Russell himself was the de facto director, with Cosmatos a credit-only figurehead. Cosmatos's son Panos confirmed his father's role on a 2018 podcast. What did Panos confirm?
answer: His father George had been a paid 'frontman' director; Kurt Russell did most of the directorial work
choices: His father George had been a paid 'frontman' director; Kurt Russell did most of the directorial work
His father had a longer cut that was never released by Hollywood Pictures
Val Kilmer had directed all his own consumption-coughing scenes via improvisation
Wyatt Earp's grand-niece had been a behind-the-scenes consultant for historical accuracy
context: Panos Cosmatos directed Mandy (2018) and Beyond the Black Rainbow (2010). His confirmation matched what Kurt Russell had publicly claimed since 2006. George P. Cosmatos directed Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985) and Cobra (1986) for Sylvester Stallone, who had similar paper-director arrangements. Tombstone went on to become a Western canon classic despite the production chaos.

question: Released in 1989, Jim Henson's character Yoda from Star Wars (1980) gets a brief 'Empire Strikes Back' Easter-egg appearance in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) during the Berlin book-burning scene. The two characters share a creator connection. Which puppeteer's vocal style links Yoda to the Last Crusade gag?
answer: Frank Oz performed Yoda's voice and puppetry for ESB and the Last Crusade scene used the same Oz vocal style for a brief gag
choices: Frank Oz performed Yoda's voice and puppetry for ESB and the Last Crusade scene used the same Oz vocal style for a brief gag
Stuart Freeborn designed both Yoda's makeup and a Nazi officer's prosthetic for Last Crusade
Industrial Light & Magic built both Yoda's puppetry rig and Last Crusade's Holy Grail effect
The hidden Yoda appears as a ghost on a flag in the Berlin book-burning crowd scene
context: Stuart Freeborn was the legendary Empire makeup designer who built Yoda's original puppet. He also worked on Star Wars (1977) doing the Mos Eisley aliens. Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade has many Easter eggs — Indiana Jones's name on a Yale University football team list, the Lucasfilm 'C-3PO' relief carving in the Petra temple, and the Mickey Mouse on Indy's tie in the airport scene. Star Wars cameos in Indy films had been a tradition since Raiders.

question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner. Donner had directed The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). The Goonies featured a young Sean Astin (Mikey), Josh Brolin (Brand), Corey Feldman (Mouth), Jonathan Ke Quan (Data), Jeff Cohen (Chunk), and Martha Plimpton (Stef). The film's emotional climax has the kids discovering One-Eyed Willy's pirate ship. The ship was built as a full-scale practical effect. What happened to the ship after filming?
answer: Donner refused to destroy it; it sat in a warehouse for years before being scrapped in the early 2000s
choices: Donner refused to destroy it; it sat in a warehouse for years before being scrapped in the early 2000s
It was sold to Universal Studios theme park and became part of the Earthquake ride decoration
It was donated to the Astoria Maritime Museum in Astoria, Oregon (the filming location)
It was burned for the Goonies' 20th-anniversary 2005 ceremony with Donner's blessing
context: Donner reportedly hated destroying built sets. The Goonies' ship 'The Inferno' was constructed at a major budget cost. Donner has said in interviews that the ship was scrapped reluctantly years later. The Astoria, Oregon film locations have become a tourist attraction; the Goon Docks (Mikey's house) was vandalized so frequently that the city eventually moved the original mailbox to City Hall.

question: In 1986, Tony Scott's Top Gun was a financial massive ($357M worldwide on $15M budget). The film's iconic 'Danger Zone' theme by Kenny Loggins became one of the decade's most-licensed songs. Loggins recorded the song at a specific California studio that had previously produced what other major 1985 hit album?
answer: The 'Brothers in Arms' Dire Straits album, at A&M Records Studios in Hollywood
choices: The 'Brothers in Arms' Dire Straits album, at A&M Records Studios in Hollywood
Bruce Springsteen's 'Born in the U.S.A.' at the Power Station in New York
Madonna's 'Like a Virgin' album at Sigma Sound in Philadelphia
Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' tracks recorded at the same time as Loggins
context: Kenny Loggins's 'Danger Zone' was rejected by several artists before Loggins picked it up. Toto, REO Speedwagon, and Bryan Adams all reportedly passed. Loggins also recorded 'Footloose' (1984) and 'I'm Alright' for Caddyshack (1980). The song's distinctive synth-and-guitar arrangement was crafted by producer Giorgio Moroder. The 2022 sequel Top Gun: Maverick had Loggins re-record the song for the film's release.

question: The 1991 action film Terminator 2: Judgment Day was directed by James Cameron and starred Arnold Schwarzenegger as a reprogrammed protector robot. Its villain, the shape-shifting liquid-metal T-1000, was one of the first big Hollywood uses of computer-generated imagery (CGI). The film's rebellious teenage hero John Connor was played by a total unknown named Edward Furlong, cast at the very last minute. How was Furlong first discovered by the film?
answer: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him at a Pasadena YMCA, where he was 13 years old and hanging out with friends
choices: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him at a Pasadena YMCA, where he was 13 years old and hanging out with friends
He was a child model who had appeared in Sears catalogs and was already on Cameron's shortlist
His mother sent his school photo to the production office along with thousands of others
His uncle was a stunt coordinator at Stan Winston Studios who recommended him
context: Mali Finn had been the casting director for Cameron's The Abyss (1989). Furlong had no prior acting experience. T2 was Furlong's debut. He won the MTV Movie Award for Best Breakthrough Performance. His personal life later deteriorated severely; he has struggled with addiction since the late 1990s. Robert Patrick (the T-1000) was a relatively obscure character actor who broke through with T2.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World features a famous '8 dollars' joke when Scott pays for his movie ticket. The scene caused some misinterpretation among American audiences who didn't realize the price reflected a specific real-world fact about the source material. What's the joke about?
answer: Toronto movie ticket prices in 2010 were genuinely around $8, anchoring the story in a specific Canadian setting
choices: Toronto movie ticket prices in 2010 were genuinely around $8, anchoring the story in a specific Canadian setting
American movie tickets in 2010 were genuinely $8 in suburbs, matching Scott's apparent class status
The Canadian dollar in 2010 was at near-parity with USD, making the price internationally legible
The Honest Ed's discount theater near Lee's Palace charged exactly $8 for second-run shows
context: Scott Pilgrim is intensely rooted in Toronto-as-portrayed-by-Bryan-Lee-O'Malley. The price detail is the kind of granular accuracy that makes the comic feel like a memoir. Honest Ed's was a real discount store at Bloor and Bathurst, demolished in 2017 to make way for apartments. Lee's Palace (the inspiration for the Chaos Theatre) is still operating. The Scott Pilgrim Universe (a sketch series) and the 2023 Netflix anime expanded on the same Toronto.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, the climactic battle features Scott earning the 'Power of Love' sword by defeating Todd Ingram. The +1 sword that ends the same chapter is used against Gideon Graves. The final reveal — that Scott actually defeats Gideon using a 'Power of Self-Respect' sword — comes from a specific encounter with his Nega-Scott. What does Nega-Scott represent?
answer: Scott's repressed memories of being a terrible boyfriend, especially to Knives Chau and Envy Adams
choices: Scott's repressed memories of being a terrible boyfriend, especially to Knives Chau and Envy Adams
Scott's college-era addiction to alcohol that he'd been hiding from Ramona
Scott's subconscious Canadian guilt complex inherited from his immigrant Scottish parents
Scott's actual brother Lawrence whom Scott had repressed memories of from childhood
context: Nega-Scott is the personification of Scott's flaws he hasn't acknowledged. In the 2010 film, the encounter is brief and played for laughs ('We have a lot in common, actually'). In the graphic novels, the Nega-Scott confrontation is treated more seriously, with Scott finally taking responsibility for his past. The 2023 Netflix anime adapted both versions in different episodes.

question: In The Super Mario Bros. Movie from 2023, the villain King Bowser attacks the peaceful Snow Kingdom by rolling giant snowballs across the ice at its penguin defenders. Nintendo fans instantly noticed the move is a callback to a boss fight in Super Mario 64, the 1996 Nintendo 64 game where the plumber Mario first ran around in a full three-dimensional world. Which Super Mario 64 boss and stage is the 2023 movie's snowball attack copying?
answer: Chief Chilly's snowball attack in Snowman's Land, where the boss rolls snowballs at Mario
choices: Chief Chilly's snowball attack in Snowman's Land, where the boss rolls snowballs at Mario
Mr. Blizzard's whirling-snowball spawn in Cool Cool Mountain
Big Boo's Haunt ice-room reflection puzzle from the third star
The Bob-omb Battlefield's giant cannonball physics test from the first stage
context: Chief Chilly is the boss of Snowman's Land in Super Mario 64. The fight involves a giant snowman shooting smaller snowballs that Mario must navigate. The 2023 film's Penguin King is voiced by Khary Payton, and the Snow Kingdom sequence directly references multiple Mario games. Director Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic are reportedly huge Mario fans and overloaded the film with Easter eggs.

question: Released in 1991, T2 (Terminator sequel) shot the 'I'll be back' moment as a callback to the original 1984 film. James Cameron also wrote the screenplay with William Wisher Jr. The film's $94M budget was the largest in film history at the time, surpassing Total Recall (1990) which had held the record briefly. T2 grossed $520M worldwide — a remarkable success. Where was the iconic 'thumbs-up' final scene filmed?
answer: At the Cyberdyne Systems set in El Segundo, California, after the climactic steel-mill battle
choices: At the Cyberdyne Systems set in El Segundo, California, after the climactic steel-mill battle
On the Gainax soundstage in Tokyo as a homage to the Eva production's collapse
At a Pinewood Studios soundstage in England near Cameron's residence
At the Skywalker Ranch sound stage in Marin County, California
context: The film's steel-mill climax was actually filmed at the Kaiser Steel Mill in Fontana, California. The thumbs-up scene where the T-800 lowers himself into molten steel was one of the most-imitated movie endings of the era. Cameron has spoken about why he made the Terminator a hero in T2 — to subvert audience expectations after the original's villain reading. Sigourney Weaver was reportedly offered a role but turned it down.

question: The 1989 sci-fi comedy Back to the Future Part II sent teenager Marty McFly and mad scientist Doc Brown into the future — specifically the day October 21, 2015. Director Robert Zemeckis and writer Bob Gale filled that fictional 2015 with silly guesses: hoverboards floating over sidewalks, Nikes that laced themselves up, and the Chicago Cubs finally winning baseball's World Series. Only one of those guesses actually came true, and it stunned Gale years later. Which one?
answer: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
choices: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
Hoverboards becoming an actual consumer product (the 2015 self-balancing scooter)
Video calls with multi-channel interfaces (similar to Marty's TV-call scene)
Movies running 19+ sequels (the Jaws 19 joke poster in the film)
context: The Chicago Cubs hadn't won a World Series since 1908. Their 2016 victory broke the longest drought in major American sports. Bob Gale's screenplay had positioned the joke as the most-impossible thing about 2015. Other predictions in BTTF Part II have come partially true — video calls (FaceTime), self-tying shoes (Nike's 2016 release), Pepsi Perfect (released as Pepsi Perfect for the 2015 anniversary).

question: Released in 1989, the Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade Petra-temple sequence used the famous Al-Khazneh facade in Petra, Jordan. The interior temple was built on a UK soundstage. Steven Spielberg had previously used the Petra location for what other film concept that was never made?
answer: Spielberg considered Petra for an early Indiana Jones pitch but the location wasn't accessible until 1989
choices: Spielberg considered Petra for an early Indiana Jones pitch but the location wasn't accessible until 1989
Spielberg had attempted to use Petra for E.T. (1982) but Universal vetoed the cost
Spielberg had visited Petra for a Schindler's List location scout, ultimately rejecting it
Spielberg had filmed a Saturday morning serial pilot at Petra in 1979 that never aired
context: Petra became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985. The location had been off-limits for years before Spielberg and crew gained access for Last Crusade. The Al-Khazneh facade (carved into red sandstone, dating to the 1st century BCE Nabataean Kingdom) became one of the most-iconic film locations ever. The Petra exterior shots are 30 seconds total of screen time but among the film's most-remembered. Spielberg has spoken about the location's spiritual power.

question: The 1986 cartoon An American Tail was made by Don Bluth and Steven Spielberg. It was based on Spielberg's family history of Russian-Jewish immigration. In the story, Fievel and his family board a ship leaving Russia. What real event forced this wave of Jews to flee?
answer: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
choices: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
The Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, with Jewish refugees fleeing both conflicts
The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, when many Jewish families chose Bolshevik or anti-Bolshevik sides
The Russian Civil War of 1918-1922, fleeing the Red Army's anti-Jewish campaigns
context: The American Tail era is specifically the 1880s-1890s Russian pogroms. Spielberg's grandfather Phillip Posner emigrated around this period. The film's reference is subtle — the Mousekewitz family's flight from a wave of cats with bandanas evokes the pogroms without explicit historical detail. Fievel's separation from his family on the boat to America happens during a storm. The film's release in November 1986 was timed for the holiday season.

question: In the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon, four teenage mutant turtles named after Renaissance artists lived in the New York City sewers and fought crime for their giant rat sensei Splinter. Each turtle wore a different colored mask and used a different weapon. One turtle wore an orange mask and swung two wooden sticks joined by a chain, called nunchucks. He was the goofy, fun-loving one who yelled 'Cowabunga' whenever he did something cool. Which turtle is this?
context: The four turtles are named after Italian Renaissance masters: Leonardo (blue, katanas), Raphael (red, sai), Donatello (purple, bo staff), Michelangelo (orange, nunchucks). 'Cowabunga' became Mikey's signature exclamation through the cartoon.

question: In the 1985 cartoon ThunderCats, a group of cat-like warriors fled their dying home planet of Thundera and crash-landed on a strange world called Third Earth. Their young leader was still growing into his job, and he carried a magical weapon called the Sword of Omens that let him see far-off dangers when he shouted, 'Sword of Omens, give me sight beyond sight.' The lion-maned hero raised the sword and cried 'Thundercats, ho!' to summon his teammates. Who is this young leader?
context: Lion-O leads the Thundercats on Third Earth after fleeing the dying planet Thundera. Other team members include Panthro (panther engineer), Cheetara (cheetah speedster), Tygra (tiger), and the twin cubs WilyKit and WilyKat.

question: In the 1984 cartoon The Transformers, giant living robots from the planet Cybertron came to Earth. They could disguise themselves as regular vehicles. The good robots, called Autobots, protected humans and searched for energy. The bad robots, called Decepticons, tried to steal that same energy. The Autobot leader was a wise, brave commander who transformed into a red-and-blue Freightliner semi truck and led his team with the battle cry 'Autobots, roll out.' Who is this Autobot leader?
context: The Transformers cartoon launched in September 1984 alongside the Hasbro toy line. Optimus Prime leads the Autobots; Megatron leads the Decepticons. The tagline 'More than meets the eye' became cultural shorthand.

question: In the 1985 cartoon G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero, an elite team of American soldiers battled the evil terrorist group Cobra around the world. The Joes had famous members like the ninja Snake Eyes, the sharpshooter Duke, and the pilot Ace. Every time the team charged into action — leaping from jets or racing tanks into battle — every soldier shouted the same short two-word rallying cry together. What is the G.I. Joe team's battle cry?
context: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero ran 1985-1987 with 95 episodes. Cobra Commander led the terrorist organization Cobra alongside Destro and the Baroness. Each episode famously closed with a PSA — 'Knowing is half the battle.'

question: In the 1983 cartoon Inspector Gadget, a bumbling cyborg detective solved crimes in Metro City with the help of his clever niece Penny and his loyal dog Brain. Behind every scheme was a mysterious criminal mastermind whom viewers never fully saw. The camera showed only his big leather chair and his black-gloved hand petting his mean, growling cat named Mad Cat. Who is this hidden villain who ran the crime ring?
context: Inspector Gadget's niece Penny and dog Brain solve most of the cases while Gadget bumbles around with his cybernetic gadgets. Dr. Claw's face was never shown — viewers only saw his armored gauntlet and his white cat. The line 'I'll get you next time, Gadget — NEXT TIME' closed many episodes.

question: In 1987 Disney launched a new afternoon cartoon called DuckTales, starring the rich old duck Scrooge McDuck and his three young nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie having adventures around the world in search of gold and treasure. The show is famous for its catchy theme song. Right after the singers sing the word 'DuckTales,' the whole chorus cheers a short, punchy two-syllable sound. What is that little cheer that opens the DuckTales theme?
context: DuckTales followed Scrooge McDuck, his nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie, and a cast including Webby and pilot Launchpad McQuack. The theme song's 'DuckTales — Woo-oo!' hook lodged in a generation's heads. Scrooge's vault of gold coins, where he swam in money, was iconic.

question: In 1992 the Fox Kids channel started a Saturday-morning X-Men cartoon based on the Marvel Comics team. The X-Men are mutants — humans born with special powers like laser eyes, weather control, and claws. They lived at a big mansion in New York that was really a secret school for gifted young mutants. The school's founder was a kind, bald man in a wheelchair who could read minds and speak into other people's thoughts. Who is this X-Men leader?
context: X-Men: The Animated Series ran 1992-1997 with 76 episodes. The lineup included Cyclops, Wolverine, Storm, Rogue, Gambit, Jubilee, Beast, and Jean Grey. The opening theme by Ron Wasserman became one of the most-remembered cartoon themes ever.

question: In 1993 Warner Bros. and the film director Steven Spielberg launched an animated cartoon called Animaniacs. It followed three wacky black-and-white cartoon siblings — two brothers and a little sister — who had been locked away in a vault in the 1930s and now lived on top of the Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank, California. Their three names all rhymed and were shouted together in the theme song. What are the three Warner siblings' names?
context: Animaniacs was produced by Steven Spielberg for Warner Bros. and Amblin Entertainment. The Warner siblings shared the show with recurring segments like Pinky and the Brain (two lab mice plotting to take over the world). Dot's full name was Princess Angelina Contessa Louisa Francesca Banana Fanna Bo Besca III.

question: In 1907 a baby boy was born in Iowa and named Marion Robert Morrison. He grew up big, tall, and rugged, and eventually moved to Hollywood. Studio bosses decided 'Marion' would never do as a name for the tough cowboy heroes he was going to play.
