context: The Base Set's first print run was 'Shadowless' — no thin shadow border was added until the second print. The 'Edition 1' stamp was on the leftmost cards of the first run. A PSA 10 graded 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000 at auction. WotC's Pokemon TCG printing was managed by Carta Mundi in Belgium.

question: In 1991 Sega released the Genesis side-scrolling brawler Streets of Rage, where three police officers punched and kicked their way through a mob-controlled city. The soundtrack shocked players — pounding house and techno beats built with the Genesis sound chip that sounded like a real club mix. The composer had already scored Revenge of Shinobi in 1989 and the Super Nintendo fantasy game ActRaiser in 1990, and he became one of Japan's most famous game composers. Name him.
context: Koshiro was 24 when he scored Streets of Rage. His Streets of Rage 2 score is widely considered the greatest 16-bit OST. He used a custom Atari ST-based MIDI-tracker tool to push the Genesis FM synthesis hardware further than most thought possible. Koshiro continues composing today — Etrian dungeon-crawlers, 7th Dragon, and modern Streets of Rage 4 (2020).

question: In 1997 the Japanese composer Nobuo Uematsu wrote the final boss theme for Squaresoft's Final Fantasy 7, called 'One-Winged Angel'. It played over the fight against the silver-haired villain Sephiroth. The music mixed rock guitar, orchestra, and a Latin choir chanting the boss's name — Uematsu's first big orchestral video-game piece. He later said the terrifying choral part was inspired by one specific 20th-century classical composer's most famous work. Which composer?
context: The 'estuans interius' Latin chorus directly echoes Carmina Burana. Uematsu also cites Stravinsky and Jimi Hendrix as influences. Uematsu composed over 100 FF songs from 1987-2003, became Square's de-facto musical face, and now leads his own rock band 'The Black Mages,' which performs orchestral-rock arrangements of his game compositions.

question: In 1999, Konami released the horror game Silent Hill on the Sony PlayStation. The player controlled a father searching for his missing daughter in a foggy American town where air-raid sirens signaled that the world would shift into a rusted nightmare version of itself. The soundtrack was not orchestral — it was industrial noise, clanking metal, distorted guitars, and haunting piano. A 30-year-old Konami sound designer composed every track. What was his name?
context: Yamaoka used metal drums, factory machinery, scraping metal, and distorted electronic beats to create the Silent Hill sound. He has scored Silent Hill 1 through Silent Hill: Shattered Memories (2009) and Silent Hill f (2025). The town's foggy, alternate-dimension Otherworld with its rusted iron and bleeding walls was inspired by the films Jacob's Ladder and Eraserhead.

question: GoldenEye 007 (1997, N64) was developed by a small Rare team led by Martin Hollis. The team had no prior FPS experience and developed the multiplayer mode in the final six months of a four-year project. How many people were on the GoldenEye development team?
answer: Nine, including Hollis as project director
choices: Nine, including Hollis as project director
Seventy, the entire Rare studio at the time
context: The nine: Martin Hollis (lead), David Doak (mission designer), Steve Ellis (programmer), Karl Hilton (level artist), Mark Edmonds (programmer), Brett Jones (modeler), Duncan Botwood (level designer), Adrian Smith (modeler), and Graeme Norgate / Grant Kirkhope (music). Multiple team members later founded Free Radical Design and made TimeSplitters (2000).

question: One Sony engineer had earlier designed the SPC700 audio chip that ended up inside Nintendo's Super Nintendo (SNES) — a rare Sony chip living inside a Nintendo box. When the 1991 Nintendo-Sony CD partnership collapsed on stage in Chicago, this engineer was the one who talked Sony's bosses into striking out alone and building their very own gaming console. That console shipped in 1994 as the PlayStation. Name the engineer often called the father of the PlayStation.
context: Kutaragi was widely called 'the father of the PlayStation.' He led hardware development for PS1, PS2, PS3, and the early PSP. Sony forced him into retirement in 2007 after PS3's troubled launch. His Cell Broadband Engine processor in the PS3 was simultaneously a research achievement and a developer pain-point that hurt PS3's third-party support.

question: In 1994, the studio Shiny Entertainment released Earthworm Jim for the Sega Genesis and SNES — a bizarre platformer starring an ordinary earthworm who stumbled into a super-powered robotic space suit and became a hero. The oddball character was designed by a then-young American cartoonist and animator, the same man who would later create the cartoon Catscratch and work on Veggie Tales. Name him.
context: TenNapel sold Earthworm Jim to David Perry's Shiny Entertainment. Perry's team — Nick Bruty, Tom Tanaka, Tommy Tallarico (music) — finished the design. Tallarico's score is considered a high-water mark of Genesis FM synthesis. TenNapel later created Neverhood (1996) on PlayStation, with stop-motion claymation and Terry S Taylor music.

question: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996) was almost called 'Willie the Wombat,' but the team dropped that name to dodge a trademark fight. When artists Charles Zembillas and Joe Pearson drew Crash, which old American cartoon style did they use as a guide?
answer: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
choices: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
context: Crash's hyper-exaggerated facial expressions, eyebrow waggles, and head-snap reactions were directly inspired by Avery's wartime cartoons (Red Hot Riding Hood). Pearson and Zembillas had both come from television-cartoon backgrounds. Crash 1's 'Sony Sucks' Bandicoot Mascot Wars marketing campaign was Sony of America's deliberate jab at Sega and Nintendo.

question: For decades, American arcade legend Billy Mitchell claimed the first perfect Pac-Man score and the world's highest score on Donkey Kong. In April 2018, the score-keeping organization Twin Galaxies stripped his Donkey Kong records after a technical investigation showed the video tapes he had submitted as proof came from an arcade emulator, not a real arcade cabinet. Twin Galaxies' own CEO led that investigation. Name him.
context: Jace Hall is a Hollywood producer, founder of Monolith Productions (No One Lives Forever, F.E.A.R.), and Twin Galaxies' owner from 2014. The Mitchell investigation used reverse-engineering of arcade-board level-load patterns vs MAME's level-load patterns — a frame-by-frame signature analysis the original Twin Galaxies referees couldn't have done in 2003.

question: The first known video-game Easter egg — a hidden credit reading 'Created by Warren Robinett' — was buried in an Atari 2600 game in 1979 after Atari refused to credit designers on cartridges. The game was an adventure puzzler with a small square hero, three castles, and a dragon. What was the game called?
context: Robinett's hidden credit was placed in the Black Castle, accessible by carrying a pixel-thin 'gray dot' across multiple screens to a specific spot. Atari executives at first wanted Robinett fired for the secret, then realized players loved discovering it. The term 'Easter egg' was coined by Atari Director of Software Steve Wright in 1980 to describe the phenomenon.

question: Atari's 1982 hit Yars' Revenge — a vertical shooter with a fly-like protagonist Yar battling the Qotile cannon behind a force-field — was Howard Scott Warshaw's first big hit, predating his E.T. disaster. The game contained a famous central scrolling band of random colors and pixels called what?
context: The Neutral Zone was a randomly-painted strip of memory bytes — Warshaw used the game's ROM itself as the visual texture. The Yar character was a yellow eight-legged fly-creature; the Qotile alternated between a stationary cannon and a swirly killing-projectile called the Swirl. Yars' Revenge sold over a million copies for the 2600, an enormous hit for the era.

question: Midway released NBA Jam Tournament Edition to arcades in 1994. It let players unlock hidden basketball players by typing certain dates and initials at the title screen. The secret roster included TV stars, the developers themselves, and even sitting American politicians dunking basketballs alongside NBA pros. One of those hidden players was the person in the White House at the time. Which sitting US president was on the list?
context: NBA Jam TE's hidden characters: Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Tipper Gore, the Beastie Boys, Frank Thomas, Tonya Harding, several Mortal Kombat fighters, and the entire Midway development team. The Mortal Kombat unlocks featured stretchy-arm versions of Sub-Zero, Scorpion, and Raiden. Many cheat codes were leaked in Electronic Gaming Monthly print articles.

question: In the late 1970s, an American semiconductor company called MOS Technology released an 8-bit processor chip that was cheap, fast, and easy to program. It became the brain of the Apple II home computer, the Commodore 64, the Atari 2600, and — inside a Ricoh-manufactured version with a locked-out decimal mode — the Nintendo NES. Almost every classic home computer and console of that era ran on this same chip family. Which chip was it?
context: The 6502 was designed by Chuck Peddle's team at MOS Technology in 1975 — explicitly to compete with Motorola's 6800 at one-fifth the price. The 6502 dominated 8-bit personal computing of the late 1970s and the entire NES era. Steve Wozniak picked the 6502 for the Apple I (1976) because it was the cheapest CPU he could find — $25 vs the 8080's $359.

question: When Nintendo of America launched The Legend of Zelda in the United States on August 22, 1987, the cartridge was shiny gold instead of the standard gray plastic used for every other NES cart. It was a marketing choice — Nintendo wanted Zelda to look like buried treasure on the store shelf. The trick worked so well that Nintendo gave the same gold cart to one 1988 NES sequel. Which sequel got the gold treatment?
answer: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
choices: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
Metroid II: Samus Returns Game Boy
Kid Icarus II: Of Myths and Monsters
context: Zelda II is the only other NES game in the gold-cart treatment. The Famicom Disk System Japanese version of Zelda used a literal floppy disk in a yellow-and-blue plastic case. The Disk System's audio expansion chip allowed Koji Kondo to use FM synthesis in the original Zelda — capability the NES motherboard lacked.

question: In 1989 Sega released the Genesis, their 16-bit home console, and marketed it against Nintendo with the slogan 'Genesis does what Nintendon't.' Under the hood, its main processor was a 16-bit chip made by an American semiconductor company. The same chip family also powered the Apple Macintosh, the Commodore Amiga, and most 1980s arcade cabinets — it was the workhorse of the era. Which 16-bit chip was it?
context: The Genesis ran the 68000 at 7.6 MHz with a secondary Zilog Z80 handling audio (a leftover from the Sega Master System architecture). The SNES used the 65816 (a 16-bit 6502 successor) at 3.58 MHz — slower clock but more efficient. 'Blast Processing' was Sega's marketing for the Genesis's faster clock advantage.

question: Sega launched Sonic the Hedgehog 2 worldwide on Tuesday, November 24, 1992 — a coordinated release day the company advertised as 'Sonic 2sday.' The Genesis pack-in introduced Sonic's new sidekick: a young orange fox with two tails who follows Sonic on every stage. Everyone calls him 'Tails' because of those spinning tails. But 'Tails' is just his nickname. What is the fox's real name in the games?
context: 'Tails' is his nickname. The 'Miles Prower' = 'miles per hour' pun is a Sonic-canon-trivia gem. Tails was designed by Yasushi Yamaguchi at Sega Technical Institute. Sonic 2 was the first major game co-developed between Sega of Japan and Sega Technical Institute (Mark Cerny's team), pioneering the trans-Pacific Sega development pipeline.

question: OutRun (1986) was designed by Yu Suzuki as Sega's signature arcade racer. The game's gimmick was branching road choices at the end of each stage — letting the player pick a left or right path. What kind of cabinet hardware made the racing immersive beyond visuals?
answer: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
choices: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
Force-feedback in the steering wheel and accelerator pedal
A 3D stereoscopic LCD shutter set for a glassless 3D effect
Wraparound surround-sound speakers in the bucket headrest
context: Suzuki's 'taikan' (full-body) cabinets defined Sega arcade hardware. After Burner (1987) had a yoke that simulated jet roll. Hang-On (1985) had a motorcycle the player straddled. The OutRun cabinet's bright-red convertible Ferrari shape became an arcade icon — the deluxe version is the holy grail of arcade collectors.

question: Konami's 1997 PS1 hit Castlevania: Symphony of the Night was the franchise's pivot from linear levels to open-castle exploration. The game's protagonist was the half-vampire son of Dracula, with a name that's Dracula spelled backwards. What's his name?
context: Alucard's first Castlevania appearance was Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse (1989). Director Koji Igarashi led Symphony of the Night and made it the prototype for the term 'Metroidvania' — open exploration of a castle with item-gated traversal. Original cover art by Ayami Kojima. The opening boss fight with Dracula uses dialogue lifted directly from the SNES Dracula X intro.

question: The original 1985 NES Super Mario Bros contains a glitch in World 1-2 that lets the player enter a strange underwater level with no exit. To trigger it, the player must jump up under a specific pipe with frame-perfect timing to clip past the Warp Zone trigger. The result places Mario in a corrupted level the inventory display labels with a non-numeric tile. What did fans nickname this level?
context: The corrupted tile is interpreted by the game's level-loader as the never-finishing World 7-2 water level — Mario can swim forever but the flagpole never appears. On the Japanese Famicom Disk System, the Minus World corrupts to three different underwater glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position.

question: The opening scene of Rob Reiner's 1987 The Princess Bride shows a young Fred Savage in bed playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga personal computer while his grandfather (Peter Falk) arrives to read him a story. Production designer Norman Reynolds picked a then-current 1987 sports release from Accolade software. Name the game shown.
context: The Amiga 1000 (released 1985) was the visible hardware in the prop shot. Goldman wrote both the novel and screenplay. Reiner's daughter Tracy famously coined the practical-effects rats in the fire-swamp scene 'pretend they're not on fire.' Savage was 11 during filming; he was already cast in The Wonder Years TV pilot the same year.

question: Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly-verified perfect game of Pac-Man on July 3, 1999, at a Funspot arcade in Weirs Beach, New Hampshire — eating every dot, every fruit, every power pellet, and all four blue ghosts on every level through 255, then dying intentionally on the kill-screen Level 256. The session took just over six hours. What was the exact perfect score?
context: Mitchell played continuously for 6 hours and 6 minutes without losing a life. The score 3,333,360 is mathematically the maximum possible — 255 levels of 240 dots, 2 power pellets, all four ghosts and bonus fruit eaten on every level. Only a handful of perfect Pac-Man games have ever been verified since.

question: In a lakefront resort town in New Hampshire sits the world's largest classic-arcade museum — endless rows of original 1980s cabinets, still coin-operated. It is where American arcade legend Billy Mitchell rolled the first perfect Pac-Man score in 1999. Years later, it was where the climactic Donkey Kong showdown of the 2007 documentary King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters was filmed. Name the arcade.
choices: Pinball Hall of Fame in Las Vegas
context: Funspot was founded in 1952 by Bob Lawton. It maintains over 600 classic cabinets and is a Twin Galaxies-sanctioned official high-score recording site. The American Classic Arcade Museum within Funspot includes Pong, Computer Space, Asteroids, and dozens of working originals. The Funspot Annual Tournament has drawn world-class scorers for 40+ years.

question: The famous 'Konami Code' was first implemented by a Konami programmer who found his own game (Gradius, 1986) too hard to playtest. The code — up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A — was originally a developer cheat that gave the player full power-ups on Gradius. What was the programmer's name?
context: Hashimoto died in February 2020 at age 61. The code was supposed to be removed before retail release of Gradius but accidentally shipped. By 1988's Contra, where it gave 30 lives, it had become canon. The code appears in over 100 Konami titles plus easter-eggs across web sites, banks, and Google's old search bar.

question: In Namco's 1981 arcade shooter Galaga, dedicated players discovered a famous secret trick that makes the entire alien fleet stop shooting at you forever. To pull it off, you kill every alien on the wave except two of one specific color in one specific row, then survive about fifteen minutes without firing a single shot. After that, the aliens will never shoot again for the rest of the game. Which two aliens must you spare?
answer: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
choices: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
The two red aliens of the bottom row
The two yellow flagships of the top row
The two green dragonflies in mid-formation
context: The exploit is a collision-detection bug in Galaga's enemy-state machine — Namco's programmers later acknowledged the bug had shipped. Top scorers exploit it to grind toward the 999,990 score-display rollover before continuing. The bug only works on arcade originals; most home ports patched it.

question: In 1983, Atari secretly buried a truckload of cartridges in the New Mexico desert. A film crew dug them up on April 26, 2014. The crew's leader was Zak Penn, who made the dig documentary — and also wrote the script for which 2018 Spielberg movie packed with video-game history?
context: Penn's documentary 'Atari: Game Over' (2014) showed the excavation team finding thousands of buried Atari cartridges — including ET, Pac-Man, Centipede, Asteroids, and Defender — plus crushed manuals and console parts. The dig was sanctioned by Alamogordo NM authorities. Howard Scott Warshaw (ET's developer) attended the excavation in person.

question: Ms. Pac-Man, released to American arcades in 1982, started life as an unauthorized bootleg add-on for Namco's Pac-Man cabinet. Two students working at a small MIT-founded startup called General Computer Corporation (GCC) hacked existing Pac-Man boards to add a moustache, glasses, and longer legs to the yellow hero. Namco liked the hack so much that they later hired GCC to finish it as the official sequel. Name the two GCC engineers.
context: GCC's Macrae and Curran had already done an unauthorized speed-up hack of Missile Command (1981). They were sued by Atari and settled by becoming Atari's exclusive enhancement-kit developer. Their Crazy Otto Pac-Man hack was approached by Midway, licensed and rebadged as Ms. Pac-Man, and went on to gross over $1.2 billion in coin-drop.

question: The Polybius legend is a famous internet ghost story about arcade gaming. It said that in 1981 a mysterious black arcade cabinet named Polybius appeared in a few Portland, Oregon arcades. Teens who played it supposedly had seizures, nightmares, and memory loss, and after a few weeks men in black suits arrived to haul it away. No physical cabinet has ever been proven to exist. The story first appeared online in February 1998, dressed up like a real arcade-history entry. On which website did it first show up?
context: coinop.org's listing for Polybius cited 'unknown manufacturer' and added the conspiracy details over time. No physical cabinet, no manual, no PCB, no flyer has ever been found. The legend has been parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob,' showing a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T') and treated as creepypasta canon.

question: In 1982, the American company Williams Electronics released a two-player arcade game called Joust. Each player mashed a flap-button to fly a bird-riding knight around the screen, trying to smash the other knight from above. One knight rode an ostrich; the other rode a buzzard. The Williams designer picked those two specific birds because they were the only mounts he could imagine that could flap in midair and still 'look heroic.' Name that designer.
context: Newcomer designed several Williams classics including the dual-button flap mechanic that defined Joust. The cooperative mode where two players could fly together (and accidentally knock each other off) made Joust one of the best two-player arcade experiences of the era. The Pterodactyl appears after 70 seconds; killing it gives 1000 points.

question: In 1981, the American game maker Williams released the arcade shooter Defender. The player piloted a small ship flying sideways across an alien planet's surface, rescuing tiny humans before mutant abductors could carry them into the sky. Defender's control panel was famously brutal — reviewers said it took a solid hour of practice just to figure out what each control did, let alone survive Wave 1. How many separate physical inputs did the player have to work at once?
answer: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
choices: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
Three buttons plus an eight-direction joystick
Two buttons plus a 360-degree spinner knob
Seven buttons plus a four-direction joystick
context: Defender's controls: Reverse (flip horizontal direction), Thrust (accelerate forward), Hyperspace (teleport randomly — possibly to death), Fire (shoot horizontally), Smart Bomb (kill everything on screen). The joystick controlled vertical movement only. The complexity made Defender notoriously hard for first-time players and a beloved expertise badge for arcade veterans.

question: Konami's Frogger hit arcades in 1981 and became a smash hit worldwide. Parker Brothers, the American board-game company, licensed the game and shipped an Atari 2600 home port in 1982. The cartridge became one of the top-selling 2600 games of the year, helped along by a clever freebie packed inside every box — something a kid could carry upstairs and enjoy separately from the game itself. What did Parker Brothers give away with each copy?
answer: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
choices: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
Parker Brothers bundled it with a glow-in-the-dark frog plush
Parker Brothers added a tournament reply-card sweepstakes
Parker Brothers shipped it in a clear plastic frog-shaped case
context: The Frogger song — 'Time to hop! Look out for the cars!' — was performed by The Buckner & Garcia (also of 'Pac-Man Fever' fame) and shipped on a 45 RPM single included in the 2600 box. The track went to #57 on the Billboard Hot 100. Parker Brothers' Frogger 2600 port sold roughly 4 million units.

question: In Metal Gear Solid (1998), the boss Psycho Mantis also performs a controller-rumble feat — making the DualShock vibrate without any in-game input as a way to demonstrate his 'psychic power.' He further taunts the player with comments based on data he reads from where?
answer: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
choices: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
The CD-ROM disc's TOC, reading the user's region code
The PS1's BIOS clock, telling the player what time they last played
Sony's PocketStation if connected, reading installed mini-games
context: Mantis comments on Castlevania Symphony of the Night, Suikoden, and other Konami saves if they're on the card. If no Konami games are saved, he comments 'I see you don't have many Konami games.' Kojima's fourth-wall-breaking signature. The fight is solved by switching the controller from Port 1 to Port 2.

question: The NES used a custom Ricoh 6502-variant Central Processing Unit (CPU) and required cartridges to contain a small lockout chip to be authorized to play. The chip generated a synchronized signal that the console verified before booting. What was the chip called?
context: The 10NES chip (a Checking Integrated Circuit, or CIC) was Nintendo's region-lock and unauthorized-developer-lock. Tengen famously reverse-engineered the chip and won a US lawsuit against Nintendo in 1991 for antitrust violations. The chip is the reason why blowing on NES cartridges 'fixed' read failures — the 10NES handshake would fail on dust, then succeed on retry.

question: After the American video-game crash of 1983, when store shelves flooded with low-quality Atari cartridges and shoppers stopped trusting the label 'video game,' Nintendo of America needed a way to tell buyers which NES games were properly made. Executive Howard Lincoln at Nintendo created a small gold-and-black seal that appeared on the box of every game Nintendo officially licensed. What exact phrase was written on that gold seal?
context: The original 1985 seal said 'Official Nintendo Seal of Quality.' Nintendo dropped 'of Quality' from the seal in 1989 after lawsuits from third-party publishers (Color Dreams, Tengen) over implied quality claims. The seal then read 'Official Nintendo Seal.' Modern Nintendo Switch games no longer use the gold seal.

question: Nintendo's 1993 SNES game Star Fox was the first console game with on-cart 3D-rendering processing power. The processor — designed by British firm Argonaut Software in partnership with Nintendo — was named after a Nintendo executive's nickname for super effects. What was the chip called?
context: The Super FX was a RISC processor built into Star Fox's cartridge specifically to handle 3D polygon rendering — the SNES CPU couldn't manage it natively. Argonaut's Jez San was hired specifically to design it after demoing a working 3D game on a stock SNES. The Super FX 2 in Yoshi's Island (1995) and Doom (1995 SNES) was a faster variant.

question: When Nintendo launched the Game Boy in the US in 1989, Tetris came in the box. But Nintendo first had to win a messy legal fight for the worldwide handheld rights. Who was the Dutch-Japanese designer who flew to Moscow in 1989 to deal straight with the Soviet ELORG (Electronorgtechnica) office for Nintendo?
context: Rogers had previously published the JRPG The Black Onyx (1984) in Japan. Sega's Mirrorsoft contract for handheld Tetris rights turned out to have been invalid — only ELORG had the right to grant them. Rogers went into ELORG and won the deal. The dispute is dramatized in the 2023 Apple TV+ film 'Tetris' starring Taron Egerton.

question: The British studio Rare released GoldenEye 007 for the Nintendo 64 in 1997. It hid a set of unlockable cheats behind speed-run challenges — beat a level under a time and a cheat opens up. If you finished the very first mission, called the Dam, in under two minutes and forty seconds, you unlocked a cheat that made every character's head and hands cartoonishly oversized during play. What was that cheat named?
context: DK Mode also made characters' hands oversized. The full Dam unlock list: 2:40 = paintball mode, 2:30 = invincibility, 2:20 = DK Mode. Speedrunning the Dam to under 2 minutes was the rite of passage. Multiple GoldenEye cheats only worked if a second controller was connected during the unlock — a common Rare anti-cheat habit.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) contains a notoriously long, repetitive, dimly-lit level where Master Chief must escort Cortana's data-spike through identical hallways while waves of Flood attack. Reviewers and fans called it the 'least fun' level in the entire trilogy. What was the level called?
context: Bungie reused the Library's corridor assets repeatedly due to development crunch. The level's combat is essentially the same arena 12 times. Halo 2 (2004) and Halo 3 (2007) consciously avoided this design pattern. Bungie's Marty O'Donnell scored the Library's anti-climax with the calm 'Library Suite' — a deliberate misdirection.

question: Super Mario 64 (1996) requires exactly 70 of the game's 120 Power Stars to face Bowser in the final battle 'Bowser in the Sky.' To beat the boss, Mario must grab Bowser's tail and swing him into one of three TNT (trinitrotoluene) bombs surrounding the platform. How many times must Bowser be thrown to win?
context: Mario grabs Bowser's tail via the B-button, twirls him via the analog stick, and releases on the right rotation arc. Each successful throw triggers a cutscene where Bowser hits a bomb. After three, Bowser explodes and drops the Power Star. The post-Bowser '120 Stars' ending unlocks Yoshi on the castle roof, who gives Mario 100 lives.

question: The Soviet Tetris rights — which Nintendo had licensed for handheld via Henk Rogers — finally reverted to Tetris's original Russian programmer in 1996 after the dissolution of the USSR. Until then, the programmer had received no royalties from the game's billions in revenue. Name him.
context: Pajitnov co-founded The Tetris Company in 1996 with Henk Rogers. Pajitnov emigrated to the US in 1991 and worked for Microsoft and others before launching The Tetris Company. The 2023 Apple TV+ film 'Tetris' dramatizes Rogers' Moscow trip to wrest the rights from Robert Maxwell and Soviet apparatchiks.

question: Nintendo's Mario Kart 64 launched on the Nintendo 64 in 1996 and included a beloved battle mode where up to four players fired shells and dropped bananas until only one balloon was left. One battle arena became famous for how peaceful it looked: a flat platform suspended high in a cloud-filled sky, with four small block towers to duck around but no pits, walls, or hazards to fall from. What was that battle arena called?
context: The four MK64 battle arenas: Block Fort (four-corner blocks with ramps), Skyscraper (open platform falling to a kill-zone), Double Deck (two-layer arena with central holes), and Big Donut (ring with no center). Block Fort's relative open-ness made it the dominant tournament-mode arena from 1996 through GameCube's Mario Kart Double Dash (2003).

question: The N64 Rumble Pak was released alongside Star Fox 64 in 1997 — Nintendo's first vibration-feedback peripheral. It plugged into the back of the controller's expansion slot, but it had a specific power source that made it different from later vibration solutions. What was the power source?
answer: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
choices: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
Drew power from the controller's main circuit board
A small lithium cell rechargeable through the cartridge slot
Solar cells on the rear shell of the pack
context: Sony's DualShock (1997 Japan, 1998 US) included rumble motors directly in the controller, drawing power from the console. The N64's battery-powered Rumble Pak was widely criticized for adding weight and requiring battery replacement. Star Fox 64 was bundled with the Rumble Pak in the US — the first game to require external vibration hardware.

question: In 1999 Nintendo released Super Smash Bros on the Nintendo 64, a fighting game where their famous mascots punched each other off floating platforms. It launched with eight starting characters — Mario, Donkey Kong, Link, Samus, Yoshi, Kirby, Fox, and Pikachu — plus four extra characters you could unlock by finishing challenges. Only three of the four secret unlockables from the original Nintendo 64 game are listed below. Which listed character was never a secret unlockable in the original game?
context: Smash 64's starting eight: Mario, Donkey Kong, Link, Samus, Yoshi, Kirby, Fox, and Pikachu. The four unlockables: Captain Falcon, Ness, Jigglypuff, and Luigi. Marth debuted in Melee (2001). Smash creator Masahiro Sakurai also created Kirby (1992) at HAL Laboratory. The original Smash project was a one-off called Dragon King: The Fighting Game before Nintendo's IP was added.

question: Super Smash Bros. Melee, released for the Nintendo GameCube in 2001, exploded into a global competitive scene largely because players stumbled onto an unintended trick the developers never planned. If you air-dodged diagonally into the ground during a jump, your character kept the sliding momentum from the dodge and slid across the stage without walking. Pros used it to move faster than the game was meant to allow. What did players name this trick?
context: Sakurai never intended wavedashing — the physics emerged from how air-dodge momentum was preserved through ground contact. Smash 4 (2014) and Smash Ultimate (2018) deliberately removed it. EVO removed Melee from its 2013 main lineup; community outrage caused a fundraiser that paid to reinstate Melee within hours. Melee tournaments still draw thousands of players today.

question: Sega launched the Genesis console in North America in 1989. The music sounded unlike any other console of its era — a punchy, brassy, buzzsaw tone from a synthesis technique called FM, short for frequency modulation. You heard it in Sonic the Hedgehog's zone themes, in the funky Streets of Rage soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro, and in the sweeping Phantasy Star adventure scores. One six-channel Yamaha chip generated every note. Which chip was it?
context: The YM2612 had six FM synthesis channels plus a DAC channel for sampled sounds. The companion SN76489 (TI-licensed) provided four PSG channels for sound effects. Hidden inside the architecture: the Z80 secondary CPU handled audio playback while the Motorola 68000 ran the game. The Genesis sound architecture was a direct continuation of Sega's earlier System 16 arcade boards.

question: Super Mario 64 (1996) contains a sequence-break glitch that lets speedrunners skip large portions of the castle by repeatedly performing a specific move against a wall, building up negative speed that lets Mario clip through doors. What is the move called?
context: The BLJ exploits Mario 64's speed-clamping logic — when long-jumping backwards while running into a wall, the game accumulates negative momentum but caps positive speed. Speedrunners stack BLJ frames against the endless staircase up to Bowser, eventually clipping through. The trick lets a runner finish the game with 0, 1, 16, 50, or 70 Stars depending on what skips they perform.

question: The final boss of Squaresoft's Final Fantasy 7 (1997) fights you to a soaring choral theme called 'One-Winged Angel,' composed by Nobuo Uematsu. The Latin chorus stitches lyrics from four medieval sources. One of them is a 13th-century collection of Latin drinking songs and poems discovered in a Bavarian monastery, which the German composer Carl Orff later set to famous thundering orchestral music in 1937. What is that medieval songbook called?
context: The 'One-Winged Angel' chorus specifically pulls 'Estuans interius / ira vehementi' from Carmina Burana. Other text comes from the Latin requiem mass. Composer Nobuo Uematsu also cites Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring (1913) and Jimi Hendrix as influences. Uematsu had never written orchestral chorus music before; FF7 was his first experiment with the form.

question: In 1995 Squaresoft released the Super Nintendo time-travel role-playing game Chrono Trigger, with music by 24-year-old Yasunori Mitsuda. It was his first major game score, and he pushed himself brutally — sleeping under his desk, eating out of vending machines, and working long overnight sessions to hit the deadline. Partway through the project, Mitsuda collapsed at work and had to be rushed to a hospital in Tokyo. What medical condition put him there?
answer: A perforated stomach ulcer from overwork-induced stress
choices: A perforated stomach ulcer from overwork-induced stress
Repetitive strain injuries in both wrists
Acute exhaustion from going without sleep for four days
A car accident on his commute to Square's Tokyo studio
context: Nobuo Uematsu stepped in to write 10 of the game's 65 tracks while Mitsuda recovered. Mitsuda later said he had been working roughly 20 hours a day. The Chrono Trigger soundtrack is widely considered among the greatest in video-game history. Mitsuda went on to score Xenogears (1998) and Chrono Cross (1999) under less brutal conditions.

question: At Nintendo's Spaceworld show in 2000, they debuted a tech demo showing an adult, dark-cloaked Link swordfighting a real-looking Ganondorf on the GameCube. Fans went wild expecting a serious, gritty Zelda. Then in 2002 Nintendo released the actual game, The Wind Waker — and Link was a big-eyed, chibi-style toon rendered with cel shading that made him look drawn in a comic book. Angry fans coined a mocking nickname for the cartoony new style. What did they call it?
context: The Spaceworld 2000 'GCN Demo' showed an adult Link sword-fighting Ganondorf in photorealistic combat — generating immense hype. The reveal of Wind Waker's cel-shaded toddler-Link with floating Tetra pirates produced an internet meltdown. Eiji Aonuma later said the realistic 2000 demo had never been a real game in development — it was a tech demo only.

question: In the Halo game series, the super-soldier Master Chief carries a blue-glowing AI helper named Cortana who lives in a chip in the back of his helmet. Her creation story is unsettling. The Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI), a secret science and espionage branch of the future Navy, made her by flash-cloning a living woman's brain — a legally shaky procedure that produced a smart AI patterned on that person's own mind. Whose brain did ONI copy to make Cortana?
answer: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan-II program lead scientist
choices: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan-II program lead scientist
Captain Jacob Keyes, of the Pillar of Autumn
Admiral Margaret Parangosky, head of ONI
Dr. Eric Tobin, a Halsey research colleague
context: Halsey illegally cloned her own brain to create Cortana — flash cloning was considered black-market technology by the UNSC. This makes Cortana effectively Master Chief's surrogate mother in genetic terms, since Halsey ran the Spartan-II abduction program that took six-year-old John-117 from his family. The Halo: First Strike novel by Eric Nylund (2003) is canonical.

question: The 1984 sci-fi movie The Last Starfighter is about a trailer-park teen recruited as an alien fighter pilot after he beats an arcade high score. It had 27 minutes of computer graphics rendered on what was then the world's most powerful supercomputer, kept at Digital Productions in Los Angeles. Name it.
answer: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
choices: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
The CDC Cyber at the Argonne Lab
context: Digital Productions installed a Cray X-MP/22 in 1983 specifically for rendering The Last Starfighter and Tron 2 (which was never made). The X-MP could render approximately one frame per 5-10 minutes. Despite the technical achievement, the film grossed only $28M against a $14M budget. Director Nick Castle later made The Boy Who Could Fly (1986) and Major Payne (1995).

question: Stranger Things Season 3 (2019) introduces Steve Harrington's Scoops Ahoy ice-cream-parlor colleague Robin Buckley — a bilingual genius who decodes Russian transmissions for Dustin and Steve. The actress playing her is the daughter of two A-list Hollywood actors. Name her.
context: Maya Hawke is the daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman. She debuts as Robin in Season 3 — the dynamic between Robin, Steve (Joe Keery), and Dustin (Gaten Matarazzo) became one of the show's best comedy trios. The Stranger Things Palace Arcade scenes were filmed at a real Atlanta reproduction arcade with period-accurate cabinets.

question: Disney's Wreck-It Ralph (2012) features cameos from real video-game characters in the 'Bad Anon' support-group scene. Of the listed real cameos, only one character lost his identifying voice — Disney could not get the licensing for the voice actor. Whose voice was missing?
answer: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed
choices: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed
M. Bison (Street Fighter) — Capcom wouldn't license Raul Julia's late voice
Bowser (Mario) — Nintendo wouldn't license Charles Martinet's vocals
Robotnik (Sonic) — Sega withheld the Jim Cummings voicework
context: Wreck-It Ralph director Rich Moore confirmed Disney secured Bowser, Robotnik, Zangief, Clyde, Cyril, Kano, and M. Bison appearances directly. Kano's voice in the meeting is original to the film. The film's villain Turbo / King Candy was the longest-original character — voiced by Alan Tudyk. The Pac-Man ghost in the meeting is Clyde, not Blinky.

question: The 1982 CBS-TV movie Mazes and Monsters — based on Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel inspired by the 1979 James Dallas Egbert III disappearance — starred a then-25-year-old actor in his first major TV role. The film was a centerpiece of the satanic-panic moral campaign against Dungeons & Dragons. Who starred?
context: Hanks played Robbie Wheeling, a college student whose D&D-like 'Mazes and Monsters' game blurred with reality during a delusional episode. The 1979 Egbert disappearance — a Michigan State University prodigy who vanished in steam tunnels — was misreported as D&D-related. Hanks went on to Splash (1984), Big (1988), and the modern Hollywood A-list shortly after.

question: In director John Badham's 1983 movie WarGames, a teenage American hacker named David Lightman accidentally dials into a Pentagon supercomputer at NORAD (North American Aerospace Defense Command) that controls nuclear war simulations, and nearly starts World War III. From his bedroom in Seattle, David types on a real 1970s home microcomputer with a distinctive metal front panel covered in red toggle switches. What model of home computer is he using?
context: The IMSAI 8080 (released 1975) was an early S-100-bus microcomputer built by IMS Associates. It used an Intel 8080 CPU and shipped as a kit or assembled. Director Badham picked it for its dramatic front-panel of toggle switches and red LEDs. The WHOPPER supercomputer at NORAD was played by Cray-style cabinetry; the actual line 'shall we play a game?' came from an Apple-II text-to-speech card.

question: In 1938 the American publisher DC Comics printed Action Comics #1, a ten-cent comic book with a shocking new cover — a strong man in a blue suit and red cape lifting a whole car over his head. He was an alien baby rocketed from the dying planet Krypton and raised on an Iowa farm by Jonathan and Martha Kent as their son Clark. This character invented a whole new kind of story: the superhero. Who was he?
context: Created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, both teenagers from Cleveland. The first issue cost ten cents; a pristine copy sold for $6 million in 2024.

question: One year after Superman appeared, DC Comics gave readers a very different hero in Detective Comics #27, published in May 1939. He wasn't an alien — he was a rich Gotham City heir whose parents had been shot dead in an alley in front of him when he was a boy. He grew up training his mind and body, then dressed as a giant bat to hunt criminals by night. Who is he by day?
context: Bob Kane is credited as creator but writer Bill Finger contributed the cape, cowl, and detective elements; DC formally added Finger's credit in 2015.

question: In March 1941, months before America even entered World War II, the young Jewish creators Joe Simon and Jack Kirby put out Captain America #1 at Timely Comics. The cover was pure defiance: the star-spangled hero Steve Rogers, a scrawny kid turned super-soldier, leaping through a Nazi bunker and throwing a right hook straight at the jaw of a real living dictator. Simon and Kirby got death threats for that cover. Who was Cap punching?
context: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby created Cap nine months before Pearl Harbor. The cover drew angry letters from American Nazi sympathizers; NYC mayor Fiorello La Guardia personally called the publisher to offer police protection.

question: In August 1962, Marvel writer Stan Lee and artist Steve Ditko needed a hero for the last issue of a struggling magazine called Amazing Fantasy. They tried something new — a shy, brainy high-school kid from Queens, New York, who visits a science demonstration and gets bitten by a radioactive spider. The bite gives him spider-strength, wall-crawling, and lightning reflexes. What is the boy's name?
context: Written by Stan Lee, drawn by Steve Ditko. Publisher Martin Goodman thought spiders were creepy and gave Spider-Man only one issue to fail. Sales were so good Spidey got his own title four months later.

question: In November 1961 Marvel Comics kicked off what fans now call the Silver Age of superheroes with Fantastic Four #1 — four astronauts hit by cosmic rays who come home with strange new powers: Reed's stretching, Sue's invisibility, Johnny's flame, and Ben's rocky orange hide. The writer was a New York huckster with a knack for slang; the artist was a Brooklyn-born powerhouse who drew like every panel might explode. Who were the two creators?
context: Lee wrote, Kirby drew. The team — Mr. Fantastic, Invisible Girl, Human Torch, Thing — got their powers from cosmic-ray exposure on a rocket flight.

question: Wolverine, real name James 'Logan' Howlett, is the short, gruff, cigar-chewing Canadian mutant of Marvel's X-Men. Long ago the shadowy Weapon X program strapped him to a table and grafted an unbreakable silver metal onto every bone in his body, including the retractable claws that pop from between his knuckles. His mutant healing factor is the only reason he survived. What is that metal called?
context: Wolverine debuted in Incredible Hulk #181 in 1974. The adamantium-bonding was done forcibly to Logan by the Weapon X program. Vibranium is Captain America's shield metal.

question: In 1941 the American writer William Moulton Marston, a Harvard-trained psychologist, dreamed up a new comic-book heroine — Princess Diana of Themyscira, a warrior Amazon who leaves her hidden island to fight for peace in the world of men. He named her Wonder Woman and armed her with a golden lasso that forced anyone caught in it to tell the truth. In his day job, Marston invented a real machine that read blood pressure and pulse to detect lies. What did he build?
context: William Moulton Marston also lived with two women in a polyamorous relationship that informed his ideas about female-led utopian societies. Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth is a direct nod to the polygraph.

question: Stan Lee, born Stanley Lieber in New York in 1922, was the writer and editor at Marvel Comics who co-created Spider-Man, the X-Men, the Fantastic Four, the Hulk, Iron Man, Thor, and Daredevil across the 1960s. In every letter column, every editor's note, and later every cameo he made in Marvel movies, Lee signed off with the same booming Latin word that means 'ever upward.' What was his catchphrase?
context: Lee used 'Excelsior' from the Latin for 'ever upward' — also the New York State motto. He'd often close his Stan's Soapbox columns with it. Lee died in 2018 at 95.

question: Jack Kirby, born Jacob Kurtzberg in a poor New York tenement in 1917, drew the Fantastic Four, the X-Men, the Avengers, the Hulk, Thor, and Captain America at Marvel through the 1960s. His action panels crackled with cracked pavement, cosmic energy, and impossible machinery — no artist drew like him before, and everyone imitated him after. Other comic-book artists gave him a one-word nickname of respect. What did they call him?
context: Kirby is widely considered the most influential American comics artist of all time. He also co-created Captain America in 1941 with Joe Simon. His dynamic 'Kirby Krackle' visual style for cosmic energy is still imitated.

question: In Marvel's X-Men comics, mutants are people born with a genetic quirk that gives them powers — laser eyes, weather control, telepathy, healing — and makes ordinary humans fear them. A bald, gentle, wheelchair-bound Oxford-trained telepath opened a private school for mutant children at his family mansion in Westchester, New York, so young mutants could learn to control their gifts in safety. What is his name?
context: Xavier and Magneto's friendship-turned-rivalry was loosely modeled by Stan Lee on Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The school is at the Xavier Institute in Salem Center, New York.

question: Peter Parker, the teenage Spider-Man, was raised in Queens, New York, by his gentle Uncle Ben and Aunt May after his parents died. When Peter first got his spider-powers, he used them selfishly — for wrestling prize money and TV fame. Then one night a robber Peter had refused to stop shot Uncle Ben in the back. Ben's dying words became the moral rule Peter has carried as Spider-Man ever since. What is the phrase?
answer: With great power comes great responsibility
choices: With great power comes great responsibility
Never let your guard down against true evil
The strong have a duty to protect the weak
A hero's job is to never stop trying his best
context: The line appears in the closing caption of Amazing Fantasy #15. Uncle Ben's death — Peter failing to stop a burglar who later kills Ben — is the moment that launches Spider-Man's career.

question: In Marvel Comics, Thor is the Norse thunder god adapted from ancient Viking myth. He is the son of Odin, king of the shining realm of Asgard, and he can fly, summon lightning, and shatter mountains — but only when he wields the enchanted war-hammer forged in the burning heart of a dying star. Only those judged truly worthy can even lift it. What is the hammer called?
context: Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83 in 1962. Only the worthy can lift Mjolnir. Stormbreaker is a separate hammer wielded by Beta Ray Bill.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, wizard children across Britain get their acceptance letter at age eleven, board a scarlet steam engine at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters in London's King's Cross Station, and travel up to a hidden castle in the Scottish Highlands to learn magic. The castle has moving staircases, a Great Hall with a starlit ceiling, and four ancient student houses. What is the full name of the school?
answer: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
choices: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
context: Hogwarts is in the Scottish Highlands. Beauxbatons is French and Durmstrang is Northern European — both featured in Goblet of Fire. Author JK Rowling wrote the first book in Edinburgh cafés.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, the greatest dark wizard of the age is a pale, snake-faced sorcerer who split his own soul into hidden objects called Horcruxes to make himself immortal. When Harry was a baby, this dark lord murdered Harry's parents and tried to kill Harry too, leaving him with a lightning-shaped scar. Most wizards are so afraid of him that they refuse to say his name and call him only 'You-Know-Who.' What is his name?
context: His birth name was Tom Marvolo Riddle, an anagram of 'I am Lord Voldemort.' Most characters call him 'You-Know-Who' or 'He Who Must Not Be Named.' Harry's distinctive lightning-bolt scar comes from Voldemort's failed killing curse in 1981.

question: At Hogwarts, J.K. Rowling's magical school, every new student sits under an ancient Sorting Hat that reads their heart and calls out one of four student houses: brave Gryffindor, cunning Slytherin, clever Ravenclaw, or loyal Hufflepuff. When the Hat sat on Harry Potter's head, it whispered that Slytherin could make him great — but Harry begged for a different house and the Hat gave him the one he asked for. Which house did Harry join?
context: The Sorting Hat almost places Harry in Slytherin but listens to his preference. Gryffindor was founded by Godric Gryffindor; its colors are scarlet and gold, its animal a lion.

question: In 1990 a British woman was riding a delayed train from Manchester to London when the idea of a scrawny orphaned boy who discovers he is a wizard hit her all at once. She spent the next several years writing the first book on scraps of paper in Edinburgh cafés, often broke and raising a baby daughter alone on welfare. When the London publisher Bloomsbury finally put out Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997, she became one of the best-selling authors in history. Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
context: Joanne Rowling famously wrote much of the first book as a single mother on welfare. The publisher added the 'K' (for her grandmother Kathleen, a name she never had) so the books would appeal to boys.

question: When Harry Potter turns eleven, the huge half-giant Rubeus Hagrid takes him shopping in the wizard alley called Diagon Alley for his school supplies. In a magical pet store, Hagrid buys Harry a beautiful pure-white snowy owl as a birthday present — the first birthday present Harry has ever received. The owl carries his mail, sleeps in his dormitory, and later saves his life. What is her name?
context: Hagrid buys Hedwig for Harry as an 11th birthday gift in Diagon Alley. Errol is the Weasleys' owl, Pigwidgeon is Ron's, Crookshanks is Hermione's cat.

question: For most of J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, Hogwarts is run by an ancient, kindly wizard with half-moon spectacles, a long silver beard tucked into his belt, and a twinkle in his blue eye. He once defeated the dark wizard Gellert Grindelwald in a legendary 1945 duel, and he was the only man the Dark Lord Voldemort truly feared. He becomes Harry's guide and protector at school. What is his name?
context: Dumbledore's full name is Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore. He defeated the dark wizard Grindelwald in 1945 and is considered the greatest wizard of his age.

question: At Hogwarts, Harry Potter's two closest friends are Ron Weasley — a tall, red-haired boy from a big, poor, loving pure-blood wizard family — and a bushy-haired Muggle-born girl who scores top marks in every class, memorizes textbooks before term even starts, and constantly reminds the boys to do their homework. Without her research and quick thinking, Harry would never have survived his first year. What is her name?
context: Hermione is a Muggle-born witch and the top student in their year. The trio meets on the Hogwarts Express in 1991. Hermione's name is pronounced 'her-MY-oh-nee.'

question: Quidditch is the wizarding sport in J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter, played on flying broomsticks around two towers of goal-hoops. Each team has seven players in four roles: Chasers throw the leather Quaffle, Keepers guard the hoops, Beaters swing bats to knock away heavy iron Bludgers, and one player alone chases a tiny golden winged ball called the Snitch — catching it ends the game and scores 150 points. Harry rides a Nimbus Two Thousand for that fourth job. Which position does he play?
context: The Seeker chases the Golden Snitch — a tiny winged ball worth 150 points. Catching it usually ends the match. Harry becomes the youngest Seeker in a century when he joins the team as a first year.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter, an enormous, shaggy-bearded half-giant works as gamekeeper and Keeper of the Keys at Hogwarts. He lives in a wooden hut on the school grounds, adores dangerous magical creatures like dragons and three-headed dogs, and drinks his tea from bucket-sized mugs. When Harry turns eleven and the Dursleys try to hide him from his acceptance letter, this half-giant kicks down the door of the shack where they're hiding and hands Harry the letter in person. What is his name?
context: Hagrid was expelled from Hogwarts as a student in 1943 but allowed to stay as gamekeeper through Dumbledore's intervention. He raises everything from acromantulas to dragons.

question: A Patronus is a silvery guardian spirit a wizard conjures to fight off dementors, the soul-sucking prison guards of Azkaban. The Patronus takes the shape of the animal that best fits the caster's spirit. Harry Potter's father James was an unregistered Animagus who could turn himself into an antlered animal, earning the nickname 'Prongs' among his four friends. The first time Harry casts a full Patronus at age thirteen, it comes out as that same animal — and Harry breaks down crying. What shape did it take?
choices: A wolf, like his mentor Lupin
A doe, like his mother Lily
An owl, like his pet Hedwig
context: James Potter was an unregistered Animagus at Hogwarts, transforming into a stag — earning him the Marauder nickname 'Prongs'. His three best friends were Sirius Black (Padfoot, a dog), Remus Lupin (Moony, a werewolf), and Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail, a rat). Harry's Patronus inheriting the stag form ties him to his father even though James died when Harry was a baby. Lily's Patronus was a doe; Snape's was also a doe, in memory of her.

question: In May 2008, Marvel Studios released the very first film of what fans now call the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Directed by Jon Favreau on a modest budget, it starred a comeback-era Robert Downey Jr. as a genius billionaire weapons designer who is kidnapped by Afghan warlords, builds a rocket-boot armored suit in a cave to escape, and comes home determined to be a hero instead of an arms dealer. Which Marvel character did Downey play?
context: Jon Favreau directed the 2008 Iron Man. The casting of Downey — then still recovering from drug-related arrests — was a massive gamble that set the MCU's wisecracking tone for over a decade.

question: In 2011 Marvel Studios released Captain America: The First Avenger, then followed it with The Avengers, two Cap sequels, and Avengers: Endgame in 2019. Across all those films a Boston-born actor played Steve Rogers, the scrawny Brooklyn kid turned super-soldier who wields a round vibranium shield. He shares his first name with three other action stars — Hemsworth, Pratt, and Pine — which is why the choices below all look the same. Which actor was it?
context: Evans had previously played the Human Torch in the 2005 Fantastic Four films. He almost turned down Captain America: The First Avenger before agreeing to a multi-film contract.

question: In April 2018 Marvel Studios released Avengers: Infinity War, the nineteenth film of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and the biggest crossover in comic-book movie history. A giant purple warlord from the moon of Titan sets out to collect the six Infinity Stones, each an object of god-like cosmic power. He believes wiping out half of all life in the universe with a single gauntlet-snap will bring the survivors balance. What is this villain's name?
context: Thanos is played by Josh Brolin via motion capture. His name comes from Thanatos, Greek god of death. He first appeared in Marvel Comics in 1973 created by Jim Starlin.

question: In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, actor Chris Hemsworth has starred in nine films as a mighty Asgardian warrior who wields a magical hammer called Mjolnir. The character comes from Norse mythology, where he is the god of thunder and storms. Which Norse warrior god does Hemsworth play in the movies?
context: Hemsworth was nearly cut from auditions; his brother Liam read for the part before Chris's mother pushed him to try again. Kenneth Branagh directed the 2011 Thor.

question: In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, British actor Tom Hiddleston has played a horned Asgardian villain across many films. The character is the adopted brother of Thor and is based on a trickster god from Norse mythology — a sly shape-shifter who loves mischief and clever schemes. Which Norse trickster god does Hiddleston play?
context: Hiddleston originally auditioned for Thor before being cast as Loki. Loki is Thor's adopted brother — actually a Frost Giant raised in Asgard by Odin. He invades New York with the Chitauri in 2012's The Avengers.

question: In 2014, Marvel Studios released a film about a rag-tag team of misfit space heroes who protect the galaxy from cosmic threats. The team is led by Peter Quill, a human raider who calls himself Star-Lord, and includes a talking raccoon named Rocket and a walking tree named Groot. What is this team called?
choices: The Inhumans Royal Family of Attilan
context: Directed by James Gunn. The team includes Star-Lord (Chris Pratt), Gamora, Drax, Rocket Raccoon, and Groot ('I am Groot'). The soundtrack of 1970s pop hits became iconic.

question: In 2018, Marvel Studios released a film set in the hidden African kingdom of Wakanda — a technologically advanced nation powered by a rare metal called vibranium. The hero-king wears a suit of vibranium-lined black armor styled after a jungle cat. What is this Marvel film called?
context: Chadwick Boseman starred as T'Challa. The film grossed over $1.3 billion and received seven Oscar nominations including Best Picture — a first for a superhero film. Boseman died of cancer in 2020.

question: The Hulk is a Marvel hero: a giant, green, super-strong monster born when a mild-mannered scientist was blasted with gamma radiation. Edward Norton played him in 2008, and Mark Ruffalo took over the role in The Avengers (2012). When the scientist is calm, he goes by his ordinary human name. What is that civilian name?
context: Eric Bana played Banner in 2003's Hulk before Norton's 2008 version and then Ruffalo's. Banner's transformation is triggered by anger; he becomes the green-skinned Hulk after a gamma-radiation accident.

question: In October 1956, DC Comics rebooted The Flash in an anthology comic called Showcase #4. The original Flash from the 1940s was a college student named Jay Garrick who wore a metal helmet. DC replaced him with a brand-new speedster: a red-and-yellow-suited hero with a scientific day job and no ties to the old character. Comics historians say that single issue launched the 'Silver Age' of superhero comics. What was the new Flash's civilian name and job?
answer: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
choices: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
Wally West, Barry's nephew and protégé
Bart Allen, the speedster from the future
Jay Garrick, the original 1940s Flash returning
context: Barry's costume — red with yellow lightning — was designed by Carmine Infantino. He was struck by lightning and doused in chemicals in his crime lab. Wally West would take over the mantle decades later after Crisis on Infinite Earths in 1985.

question: In 1959, DC Comics rebooted an old hero for the Silver Age of comics. Test pilot Hal Jordan found a crashed alien named Abin Sur, who gave him a glowing green power ring before dying. The ring lets Hal create anything he can imagine — swords, shields, giant fists — as long as he has willpower. It also links him to a huge team of ring-wearing peacekeepers from every corner of space. What is that intergalactic organization called?
context: The Corps is a force of 7,200 intergalactic peacekeepers run by the Guardians of the Universe on the planet Oa. Hal Jordan was a test pilot when the dying Abin Sur passed him the ring. The Corps oath: 'In brightest day, in blackest night...'

question: In 1963, Marvel writer Stan Lee and artist Jack Kirby created a team of teenage mutants — humans born with strange powers — who train at Professor Xavier's school for gifted students. The five original X-Men each had one signature power. The team's field leader wore a special visor because he could not turn off his eyes, which fired blasts of red force. Which original X-Man led the team?
context: Scott Summers can't control his optic blasts, so he wears a ruby-quartz visor or glasses. The five original X-Men were Cyclops, Marvel Girl (Jean Grey), Angel, Beast, and Iceman. The team was repeatedly cancelled and revived until Giant-Size X-Men #1 in 1975.

question: Daredevil is a Marvel hero created by Stan Lee and Bill Everett in 1964. As a boy in New York City, Matt Murdock pushed a stranger out of the path of a truck carrying toxic waste. The chemicals splashed his eyes and blinded him, but they sharpened his other senses — hearing, touch, smell, taste — to superhuman levels. By night he fights crime in a red devil suit. What is his day job when he isn't in costume?
answer: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
choices: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
context: Matt Murdock practices law with partner Foggy Nelson at Nelson & Murdock. Created by Stan Lee and Bill Everett, Daredevil first appeared in Daredevil #1, April 1964. Frank Miller's late-1970s/early-1980s run redefined the character.

question: In 1966, Stan Lee and Jack Kirby introduced comics' first major black superhero in Fantastic Four issue 52. He is the king of Wakanda, a hidden African nation richer than any Western country because it sits on the world's only supply of vibranium. He wears a sleek suit styled after a jungle cat and leads a warrior guard called the Dora Milaje. Who is this Wakandan king?
choices: Storm of the Mau Mau kingdom
Luke Cage of Harlem's hero scene
context: The Black Panther Party in California formed independently around the same time. Marvel briefly renamed the character 'Black Leopard' in 1972 to avoid confusion before reverting. T'Challa rules a technologically advanced, vibranium-rich nation.

question: The Marvel Comics mutant Wolverine first appeared as a Hulk enemy in 1974 and joined the new team of X-Men in Giant-Size X-Men #1 in 1975. He was created by writer Len Wein and artist John Romita Sr., and became famous for being short, angry, and having a healing factor plus retractable bone claws in his fists. His street nickname is 'Logan,' but he has a real birth name too. What is his full real name?
context: Wolverine first appeared in Incredible Hulk #181, October 1974, fighting both Hulk and Wendigo. His real name was revealed gradually — 'Logan' became canon in Uncanny X-Men, the full 'James Howlett' came in the 2001 Origin miniseries.

question: American comics writer Chris Claremont wrote Marvel's Uncanny X-Men from 1975 to 1991 — a record-setting 16-year run that defined every version of the team since. Working with artist John Byrne in 1980, he told his most famous story: the X-Men's telepath Jean Grey is corrupted by a cosmic firebird entity that turns her into a world-devouring destroyer, and her teammates must choose between saving her and stopping her. What is that story arc called?
context: Dark Phoenix ran in Uncanny X-Men #129–137. Editor Jim Shooter required Claremont and Byrne to change the original ending — Phoenix's destruction of an inhabited solar system mandated her death. Byrne later left the book.

question: In 1986, British writer Alan Moore and artist Dave Gibbons published Watchmen, a twelve-issue comic that reimagined superheroes as flawed and often dangerous people. One small object becomes the story's signature symbol — you see it on the cover of issue 1, and it keeps returning throughout the tale as a reminder of a murdered hero named the Comedian. What is that famous image?
answer: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
choices: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
A red rose held by a costumed vigilante in silhouette
A black silhouette of a clock with hands at midnight
A blue silhouette of a man against a glowing red moon
context: The smiley face belongs to the murdered Comedian (Edward Blake), whose death opens the series. Dave Gibbons drew the entire 12 issues. The smiley face is also used in Watchmen's nine-panel grid system, the Doomsday Clock, and Mars sequences.

question: In 1986 the American comic-book writer and artist Frank Miller drew a four-part story for DC Comics that changed superhero comics forever. Set in a dark, near-future Gotham City, it showed a gray-haired, 55-year-old Bruce Wayne — long-retired from crime fighting — pulling the cape and cowl back on to face street gangs, a fascist government, and a final duel with Superman. What was Miller's landmark four-issue series called?
context: Miller followed up in 1987 with Year One (Batman's first year, with David Mazzucchelli). The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen, both from 1986, are often cited as the start of the 'mature' comics era. Miller's older Batman fights a returning Joker, a Reagan-allied Superman, and the Mutant gang leader.

question: British writer Neil Gaiman's comic series Sandman ran for 75 issues from 1989 to 1996. It followed Dream, also called Morpheus, the pale lord of every story ever told. Dream is one of seven immortal siblings older than the gods, called the Endless — each rules over one part of existence. The eldest of the Endless is Dream's older sister, a cheerful young woman with dark eyeshadow and an ankh necklace, whom the other Endless respect but rarely see. Who is she?
context: The seven Endless: Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair, and Delirium (formerly Delight). Death appears as a cheerful young goth woman with an Egyptian ankh necklace. The series won 26 Eisner Awards and the World Fantasy Award for short fiction in 1991.

question: In 1993 the American comic artist Mike Mignola created a new comic-book character for Dark Horse Comics. His hero was a bright-red-skinned demon summoned to Earth by Nazi occultists during the Second World War but raised by a kind American professor to fight evil. Adult-sized with sawed-off horn stubs, a giant right hand made of stone, a fat cigar, and a big revolver, he works as a paranormal detective for a secret US agency. What is he called?
context: Hellboy was summoned to Earth by Nazi occultists in 1944 but raised by Allied paranormal researcher Trevor Bruttenholm. He works for the Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense (BPRD). Guillermo del Toro directed the 2004 and 2008 films starring Ron Perlman.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon ran Preacher from 1995 to 2000 at DC's Vertigo imprint. The hero is a small-town Texas pastor who gains a divine voice that can command obedience. His traveling companions are his on-and-off girlfriend Tulip and what Irish vampire?
context: Jesse Custer, the preacher, hosts an entity called Genesis — offspring of an angel and a demon. The trio crosses America hunting God Himself, who has abandoned creation. AMC adapted the comic into a four-season TV series in 2016–2019.

question: In 1997 the British author J.K. Rowling published the first book in her Harry Potter series in the United Kingdom. It followed an orphaned eleven-year-old boy who learns he is a wizard, and it launched a global fantasy franchise. When the American publisher Scholastic released the same book in 1998, they changed the title, worried kids would think 'Philosopher' sounded too dry — so US copies use a different subtitle. What was the original British title of the very first book?
answer: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
choices: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
Harry Potter and the Magic Stone
Harry Potter and the First Year
context: US publisher Scholastic insisted on changing 'Philosopher's' to 'Sorcerer's' for the 1998 American release, worried 'philosopher' sounded too academic. The Philosopher's Stone is a real alchemical concept tied to Nicolas Flamel, a real 14th-century French alchemist who features in the book.

question: In J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter novels, one Hogwarts teacher hates Harry from the very first Potions class and seems cruel and petty for years. He is the greasy-haired, black-cloaked head of Slytherin house who brews potions in the school dungeons. In the final book we find out he had loved Harry's mother Lily and had been secretly serving Dumbledore against Voldemort the whole time — a heartbreaking double agent. Who is this Potions Master?
context: Snape is head of Slytherin House. He famously taunts Harry from the first day of Potions class. Alan Rickman played him in all eight films; Rickman knew Snape's full arc from Rowling earlier than the cast or readers did.

question: In J.K. Rowling's third Harry Potter novel, Prisoner of Azkaban, thirteen-year-old Harry learns that a dangerous convict has just escaped from Azkaban, the wizard prison guarded by soul-sucking dementors. Harry is told the man wants to kill him — but the truth turns out to be very different. The convict is actually Harry's own godfather, framed years ago for a crime he did not commit. Who is he?
context: Sirius can transform into a large black dog, his Animagus form. He was framed for betraying Harry's parents by Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail). Sirius dies in Order of the Phoenix (book five), killed by Bellatrix Lestrange and falling through the Veil in the Department of Mysteries.

question: In Prisoner of Azkaban, Harry Potter is given the Marauder's Map — an enchanted parchment made by his father and three friends when they were students at Hogwarts. Tap it with a wand and it reveals the location of every person moving inside the castle. But it only works if you speak the correct opening phrase, and you must speak a matching closing phrase to hide it again. What are those two magic phrases?
answer: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
choices: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
'Show me what is hidden' / 'Concealed once more'
context: The Map was made by the Marauders: Moony (Remus Lupin), Wormtail (Peter Pettigrew), Padfoot (Sirius Black), and Prongs (James Potter). Fred and George Weasley give it to Harry in Prisoner of Azkaban after stealing it from Filch's office.

question: In Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, the giant Hogwarts gamekeeper Hagrid gets promoted to teach the Care of Magical Creatures class. For his very first lesson he leads the students out to the paddock and brings out a rare flying beast — half giant eagle up front, half horse in back, with sharp claws and a huge orange beak. Hagrid warns the class the creature is proud and dangerous, and Harry has to walk forward slowly and bow deep before it will let him near. What magical creature is it?
context: A Hippogriff has the front half of an eagle and the back half of a horse. Buckbeak is sentenced to death after attacking Draco Malfoy (who didn't bow). Harry and Hermione later use Hermione's Time-Turner to rescue Buckbeak.

question: In Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, three wizarding schools — Hogwarts, Beauxbatons, and Durmstrang — each send a champion to compete in the Triwizard Tournament, a dangerous three-task contest. In the final task, Harry and the Hogwarts co-champion Cedric Diggory race through a magical hedge maze and decide to grab the Triwizard Cup together as joint winners. The moment they touch it, the whole story turns dark. What happens next?
answer: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
choices: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
They are dropped into a flooded chamber to face a sea giant
They are sent back to Hogwarts where the Cup explodes
They are transported to the Forbidden Forest for a centaur trial
context: Cedric Diggory is killed by Peter Pettigrew on Voldemort's orders. Voldemort uses Harry's blood for his resurrection. Mad-Eye Moody (actually Barty Crouch Jr. on Polyjuice) had turned the Cup into a Portkey. Robert Pattinson played Cedric in the 2005 film.

question: In the Harry Potter books, Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry is split into four houses. Each house is named after one of the four wizards who founded the school a thousand years ago. Slytherin House prizes cunning and ambition, and its emblem is a green serpent. Which of the four founders started Slytherin House?
context: Slytherin valued cunning and pure-blood ancestry, leading to his split with the other founders. He sealed a basilisk in the Chamber of Secrets — discovered by Tom Riddle in 1942 and reopened in 1992. Slytherin's symbol is a serpent; house colors are green and silver.

question: In Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, students at Hogwarts have been turning up petrified — frozen solid as stone — after a giant serpent called a basilisk has been slithering through the school's pipes. Down in the hidden Chamber under the castle, Harry stabs the monster through the roof of its mouth with the sword of Gryffindor and kills it. Then he grabs one of its poisonous fangs and drives it into the enchanted object that a memory of the young Tom Riddle had been using to possess Ginny Weasley. What object was it?
context: The diary is the first Horcrux destroyed — Harry stabs it with the basilisk fang. The seven Horcruxes total: diary, ring, locket, cup, diadem, Nagini, and an unintended one Harry only learns about in book seven.

question: Alfonso Cuarón is a Mexican filmmaker known for Y Tu Mamá También and later Gravity and Roma. In the early 2000s he took over the Harry Potter film series from Chris Columbus and gave it a darker, more grown-up look — colder colors, tighter camera work, real weather in every scene. Every Potter film after his imitated that style. Which Harry Potter movie did Cuarón direct?
answer: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
choices: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (2001)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005)
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2007)
context: Chris Columbus directed the first two; Cuarón did Azkaban; Mike Newell did Goblet of Fire; David Yates directed the last four films. Cuarón's work on Azkaban led to his later acclaim for Children of Men (2006), Gravity (2013), and Roma (2018).

question: In the Harry Potter novels, Headmaster Albus Dumbledore keeps a pet phoenix in his office at Hogwarts. The bird is named Fawkes after Guy Fawkes, the man behind the 1605 Gunpowder Plot in England. A phoenix bursts into flame when it dies and is reborn from its own ashes. Fawkes's feathers match the fire he keeps returning from. What color are they?
answer: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
choices: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
Silver and white with platinum-tipped wings
Black and purple with iridescent feathers
context: Fawkes is named for the English Catholic conspirator Guy Fawkes (Gunpowder Plot, November 5, 1605). The phoenix's tears heal Harry's basilisk wound in Chamber of Secrets. Phoenix tail feathers are wand cores — Harry's and Voldemort's wands both contain feathers from Fawkes.

question: In 2008, Marvel Studios released Iron Man, the first film in what would become the Marvel Cinematic Universe. In a hidden scene after the credits rolled, a one-eyed government agent named Nick Fury, played by Samuel L. Jackson, appeared in Tony Stark's mansion. Fury told Stark he wanted to talk about assembling a team of extraordinary heroes. What did Fury call that team-building program?
context: Samuel L. Jackson played Fury based on his depiction in Mark Millar's Ultimate Marvel comics, which had drawn Fury as Jackson. The scene was added late and cost Jackson a one-day shoot to film. The Avengers (2012) arrived four years later.

question: In 2014, Marvel released Captain America: The Winter Soldier — a spy-thriller superhero movie about Steve Rogers uncovering a Nazi secret group hidden inside Marvel's own intelligence agency.
