It came with the 1980 World of Greyhawk Folio and grew in the 1983 boxed set. A TSR mapmaker painted it. Her first name became a shorthand for the whole D&D map style of that era. What was her name?
answer: Darlene Pekul, credited as simply 'Darlene' on the published maps
choices: Darlene Pekul, credited as simply 'Darlene' on the published maps
Diesel LaForce, credited as just 'David Diesel' or 'D.D.'
Stephen Sullivan, credited as 'S.D. Sullivan' in TSR's catalog
Dennis Kauth, credited as 'D. Kauth' in art reviews
context: Darlene Pekul (1947-) joined TSR as a cartographer in the late 1970s. Her Flanaess map's distinct color palette (muted greens, browns, blues) and hand-lettered nation names became visual shorthand for 1980s D&D campaign settings. The map was reissued in poster form and remains a collector's item. Darlene also produced the maps for the 1983 World of Greyhawk hardcover boxed set and many TSR adventure modules. She returned to TSR/WotC for the 2007 Living Greyhawk Gazetteer.

question: After Gary Gygax was pushed out of TSR in 1985, he wrote a set of new sword-and-sorcery novels. The hero was a Greyhawk street thief who grew, book by book, into a strong adventurer. He was Gygax's own favorite character, and the novels (1985-1987, from New Infinities Productions) drew right from his home Greyhawk game. What was the hero's name?
answer: Gord the Rogue, of the City of Greyhawk
choices: Gord the Rogue, of the City of Greyhawk
Mordenkainen the Wizard, of the Circle of Eight
Robilar the Fighter, of the Bandit Kingdoms
Bigby the Hand, of the Greyhawk Academy
context: Gord the Rogue novels: Saga of Old City (1985), Artifact of Evil (1986), Sea of Death (1987), Night Arrant (1987), City of Hawks (1987), Come Endless Darkness (1988), Dance of Demons (1988). The series ends with Gord destroying the multiverse and being reborn as a new god — Gygax's literal authorial revenge on TSR for taking the world away from him. The Gord novels remain in print as PDFs through various small presses. Gygax's later original RPG settings (Dangerous Journeys, Lejendary Adventure) never reached the same audience.

question: T1 The Village of Hommlet (1979) shows a deceptively simple frontier town hiding an evil cult. The local cleric of Saint Cuthbert, the smiling Brother Calmert, and one other Hommlet authority figure are secretly cultists. Careless players often befriend them as allies. The most famous hidden traitor, shown as a young friendly priest, secretly serves which demonic patron?
answer: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders, through her terrestrial mortal cult
choices: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders, through her terrestrial mortal cult
Iuz — the cambion demigod of the northern Flanaess
Zuggtmoy — the demon queen of fungi, beneath the Temple
Asmodeus — the lord of the Nine Hells of Baator
context: The young priest is Brother Calmert (sometimes also a deeper-cover NPC named Lareth the Beautiful) — Lareth serves Lolth, drawn from the D-series modules. Hommlet was published before the full T1-4 supermodule explained the larger cult; the original module hinted at Zuggtmoy and Iuz being involved but didn't name them as the central villains. The 2001 Return to the Temple of Elemental Evil and 2003 Troika CRPG fleshed out the Elemental Evil cult's relationship to all four demon lords.

question: The 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement added psionics to D&D, a second magic system built on mental powers and the 'astral' plane rather than the magical planes. Many DMs hated it and left it out. Gygax himself went back and forth: he dropped psionics from the 2nd Edition core, then let them back in with The Complete Psionics Handbook (1991). What is the classic D&D psionic monster, a brain with bug-like legs that stalks dungeons and eats minds?
answer: The Intellect Devourer — a brain-shape with four crab-like legs
choices: The Intellect Devourer — a brain-shape with four crab-like legs
The Ulitharid — a giant elder-form mind flayer
The Cerebrilith — a demon-form psionic predator from the Abyss
The Thought Eater — an etherial creature that eats memorized spells
context: The Intellect Devourer was created for Eldritch Wizardry (1976) alongside the mind flayer. The two creatures are tied together: mind flayer larvae sometimes mature into intellect devourers if they hatch in non-humanoid hosts. In D&D 5e, intellect devourers also evolved into the Stranger Things-inspired 'mind flayer-larva' visual aesthetic. The 2016 Out of the Abyss adventure features them prominently as Underdark hazards.

question: Gary Gygax's 1978 D&D module Vault of the Drow describes a huge cavern. Its ceiling is so high it looks like a night sky, dotted with jeweled stalactites and glowing fungus. Gygax later said he was trying to match a 1968 fantasy novel he loved. Whose 'Land of Faerie' inspired him?
answer: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
choices: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
Lord Tennyson, of 'Idylls of the King' Arthurian poetry
Lord Macaulay, of 'Lays of Ancient Rome' historical poetry
Lord Byron, of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' Romantic poetry
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) was the godfather of secondary-world fantasy. His 1924 novel The King of Elfland's Daughter is the canonical depiction of Faerie as an alien-beautiful realm with skies of unearthly light. Gygax cited Dunsany in the original DMG Appendix N. The Vault of the Drow itself, as a place, became an iconic image: the dark elves' city, beautiful and corrupt, lit by an artificial gem-and-fungus 'sky.' Players who have visited the Vault in the original D3 often remember the scene better than any combat encounter.

question: From 1986 to 2003, the publisher TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) printed Dragon Magazine, the official Dungeons and Dragons magazine, and ran a monthly rules Q&A column called 'Sage Advice' in every issue. Players wrote in with tricky rules questions and one TSR staff designer answered them almost the entire seventeen-year run — grappling, spell components, monster stats, every edge case gamers could invent. He became the D&D rules oracle for a whole generation and later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D. Who was he?
answer: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
choices: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
Roger E. Moore, who edited Dragon Magazine through the same era
Kim Mohan, who edited Dragon Magazine in the 1980s
Bruce Heard, of the Voyage of the Princess Ark Mystara column
context: Skip Williams joined TSR in the early 1980s and became the company's rules-arbitration specialist. He co-authored the 2000 D&D 3rd Edition Monster Manual with Jonathan Tweet and Monte Cook. Williams' Sage Advice column was infamous for both authoritative rulings and occasional reversals — letters would prompt re-rulings months later. The column resumed in 5e under Jeremy Crawford, but the classic-era Sage Advice with Williams remains the iconic version.

question: TSR's 1989 Spelljammer cosmology placed D&D solar systems inside vast crystal spheres, floating in a strange medium called the phlogiston. Ships travel the phlogiston using a magical helm, a chair-shaped device that turns the pilot's spell energy into ship motion. Helms range from cheap minor helms to powerful major helms. Who built the high-end major helms in canonical Spelljammer lore?
answer: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
choices: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
The Mercane — the canonical Spelljammer name for a different blue-skinned race
The Neogi — spider-slavers who manufacture helms via dark magic
The Giff — Napoleonic hippopotamus-mercenaries who fabricate helms
context: The Arcane are 15-foot tall blue-skinned humanoids with too-long limbs. They speak with their own dialect of the Auld trade tongue and value gold above all other commodities. They monopolize the helm market across all of crystal-sphere space. The 2022 5e Spelljammer reboot renamed them 'Mercane' (canonically a related but distinct species) due to a Tasha-era sensitivity-read concern about the term 'Arcane' being already overloaded. Spelljammer purists prefer the original name and lore.

question: Before Ravenloft (1983), Tracy Hickman wrote a trilogy of 1982-1983 modules called the Desert of Desolation series, set in a fictional Arabian-inspired desert region of the Forgotten Realms. The three modules are I3, I4, I5. The middle module sends the PCs into a pyramid tomb of a long-dead Pharaoh, ultimately confronting his lich form. What was the lich-pharaoh's name?
answer: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
choices: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
Set-Anu, the Lord of the Black Lands of Athas
Khepri-Atum, the Sun Pharaoh of the lost dynasty
Imhotep-Ra, the Architect-King of the great pyramid
context: The Desert of Desolation trilogy: I3 Pharaoh (1982), I4 Oasis of the White Palm (1982), I5 Lost Tomb of Martek (1983). The series was popular enough that TSR compiled it as a single supermodule in 1987. The 'Pharaoh's Box' magic item from I3 is iconic among TSR collectors. Tracy Hickman has cited the modules as his proving-ground writing exercises before tackling Dragonlance and Ravenloft. The Egyptian-inspired Mulhorand region of the Forgotten Realms eventually absorbed the setting.

question: After WotC bought TSR in 1997, the company launched a major rules overhaul in 2000 called D&D 3rd Edition. It was built around a unified d20 mechanic and an Open Game License that let third-party publishers freely use the rules. The lead designers were Jonathan Tweet, Monte Cook, and Skip Williams. Which 1995-2000 D&D-adjacent system did the 3rd Edition d20 mechanic most directly come from?
answer: Roll-over d20 vs target number, evolved from Alternity (1998) and basic d20 mechanics in many TSR products
choices: Roll-over d20 vs target number, evolved from Alternity (1998) and basic d20 mechanics in many TSR products
Roll-under d20 vs attribute, used in the BRP-based Call of Cthulhu and RuneQuest games
Pool of d10s, similar to Vampire the Masquerade's Storyteller system
Roll 3d6, used in GURPS and Champions (Hero System) games
context: The d20 System Reference Document (SRD) launch in 2000 under the Open Game License was revolutionary — it let companies like Paizo (publishers of Dungeon Magazine post-2002) create products built on D&D's chassis. The OGL was responsible for the indie-RPG boom of the 2000s and ultimately Paizo's 2009 Pathfinder, which used a modified d20 chassis. WotC tried to revoke the OGL in 2023 — sparking a major backlash that resulted in the OGL 1.0a being permanently released to the public domain.

question: Mordenkainen's apprentice in Gygax's Greyhawk campaign was a wizard whose "hand" spells became iconic. They include Bigby's Interposing Hand, Grasping Hand, Forceful Hand, Crushing Hand, and Clenched Fist. Bigby was actually the personal campaign character of one of TSR's earliest employees. Whose home-campaign character was Bigby?
answer: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and TSR co-founder
choices: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and TSR co-founder
Tim Kask, the original editor of Dragon Magazine
Brian Blume, Gygax's TSR business partner
James Ward, of Metamorphosis Alpha fame
context: Rob Kuntz (1955-) co-DM'd the Greyhawk campaign with Gygax from 1972 onwards. His main character Robilar (a fighter) and his second character Bigby (a wizard) both became iconic Greyhawk NPCs. Robilar famously joined Mordenkainen and others in the Citadel of Eight (later the Circle of Eight). Kuntz worked at TSR from 1976 until the late 1980s as a designer. He has spent decades documenting his Greyhawk-era home-game material and writing his own systems.

question: The visual identity of classic Dungeons and Dragons was established by a small group of staff artists at TSR in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The most distinctive style, psychedelic and weird and slightly Gothic, belonged to one artist whose creature illustrations in the 1977 Monster Manual and 1981 Moldvay Basic rulebook defined the aesthetic. Who was the artist?
choices: David Trampier — DMG and Monster Manual interior art
Jeff Easley — covers of 1983-1989 AD&D hardcovers
context: Erol Otus (1956-) joined TSR in 1979 and left around 1982 for freelance work. His distinctive bold-color compositions and weirdly-proportioned monsters became visual shorthand for early-1980s D&D. Otus illustrated the Moldvay Basic D&D rulebook cover (1981) and many beloved Monster Manual interior pieces. The other major staff artists were David Trampier (DMG cover, MM interior), Jeff Dee (the Underworld and Wilderness Adventures box art), Larry Elmore (later 1980s covers, Dragonlance), Jeff Easley, and Clyde Caldwell. Each had a distinct visual style.

question: Rob Kuntz's home-campaign fighter Robilar became infamous in Greyhawk lore for breaking into Castle Greyhawk, Gygax's home-campaign mega-dungeon. Robilar slaughtered most of its monsters and traps during mid-1970s play. In a 1975 session, Robilar and Mordenkainen together explored the deepest level. They confronted its most powerful demonic ruler. Which demon-lord did they face?
answer: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
choices: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders
Demogorgon, the Prince of Demons himself
Iuz, the cambion demigod of the Flanaess
context: Zuggtmoy was first mentioned in Gygax's Greyhawk play sessions in 1973-1975 before her formal publication in the 1985 Temple of Elemental Evil. Robilar and Mordenkainen 'defeated' her in the deepest level of Castle Greyhawk — though Gygax later said the encounter ended with the demon being imprisoned rather than destroyed, setting up her later return as the central villain of T1-4. The 'Castle Greyhawk' dungeon itself was the original D&D megadungeon, and Gygax's home-campaign play notes (later somewhat published) are sought-after collector's items.

question: Chaosium's 1981 Call of Cthulhu RPG translated Lovecraft's cosmic horror into a tabletop format with the iconic 'Sanity Score' mechanic. A character's Sanity points decrease as they witness cosmic horror; reach zero and the character goes permanently insane. The system spawned over 40 years of supplements and remains one of the longest-running RPGs ever. Who designed it?
answer: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
choices: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
Steve Perrin, the original RuneQuest fantasy-game system designer
Greg Stafford, the legendary creator of the Glorantha setting
Ken St. Andre, the irascible Tunnels and Trolls designer
context: Sandy Petersen (1955-) is a deeply religious Mormon designer who somehow became the world's foremost interpreter of cosmic-horror gaming. After Call of Cthulhu, he designed RuneQuest III and worked on id Software's Doom (1993) and Quake (1996). The 'level designer' role he pioneered at id influenced first-person shooter design forever. He returned to tabletop in the 2010s with his own company, Petersen Games, making Lovecraftian and historical board games.

question: Chaosium's 1978 RuneQuest was set in a Bronze Age fantasy world. It had cult-based religion, dragon-newts, dwarves who were living machines, talking ducks, and warring Lunar and Solar empires. Chaosium's founder made the whole setting. Who created Glorantha?
answer: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
choices: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
Steve Perrin, the RuneQuest rules designer
Sandy Petersen, the Call of Cthulhu designer
Lynn Willis, the Chaosium editor and designer
context: Greg Stafford (1948-2018) built Glorantha as a personal worldbuilding project starting in the 1960s — like Ed Greenwood with Forgotten Realms, but with a deeper anthropological framing. Glorantha drew on Eliade's Patterns in Comparative Religion as a structural inspiration. Stafford spent his entire life refining the setting; HeroQuest, Pendragon (1985), and the more recent 13th Age in Glorantha all drew on his core lore. Stafford was inducted into the Origins Awards Hall of Fame in 2013. He died in 2018.

question: Game Designers' Workshop published the sci-fi RPG Traveller in 1977, designed by Marc Miller, and it established many conventions of science-fiction roleplaying. Its character generation was famous for one specific innovation. Characters served careers (Navy, Marines, Scouts, Merchants, Army, Other) for four-year terms, gaining skills but risking death. If you "died" during chargen, you actually rolled up a new character. What was this signature mechanic called?
answer: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
choices: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
Reincarnation tables — death meant a new body but the same character
Critical career failure — death meant career change, not actual death
Random aging effects — repeated terms reduced physical stats but not death
context: Traveller's death-during-chargen mechanic became famously controversial — some saw it as adding gritty realism, others as just frustrating. Later Traveller editions made the rule optional. The game's setting, the Third Imperium, has been a constantly-developing universe since 1977. Marc Miller still oversees the line, now published as Mongoose Traveller (2008+). Traveller is considered one of the most influential RPGs ever, alongside D&D, RuneQuest, and Call of Cthulhu.

question: Hero Games' 1981 superhero RPG Champions was the first big game built on 'point-buy' character creation. Players spent points to design custom powers, perks, and drawbacks. The same rules were later used for fantasy, spy, and sci-fi games. What was the shared system called?
answer: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
choices: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
The GURPS System, the Steve Jackson Games universal mechanic
The Storyteller System, the White Wolf World of Darkness mechanic
The FATE System, an early Fudge-derivative game
context: The Hero System reached its definitive form in 4th Edition (1989), with revisions through 6th Edition (2009). The system's signature feature is the granularity of power design — every superpower or magical effect could be deconstructed into 'mechanics' bought separately. Champions itself remains in print as the flagship Hero System game. Hero Games' tabletop RPG The Champions of New Olympus has appeared in superhero-RPG canon since 1981 alongside Mayfair Games' DC Heroes and TSR's Marvel Super Heroes.

question: West End Games' 1984 dystopian-comedy RPG Paranoia was designed by Greg Costikyan, Dan Gelber, and Eric Goldberg. It satirized Cold War paranoia through a future totalitarian complex run by an insane AI Computer. Players are Troubleshooters, whose job is finding traitors while being traitors themselves. Each carries a clearance color (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet, Ultra-Violet). What was the player handbook's notorious cover slogan?
answer: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
choices: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
'You Are Safe! The Computer Is Your Friend! Report Everything!'
'Welcome To Alpha Complex! Have A Nice Day! Don't Die!'
'Service The Computer! Report All Mutants! Watch Out For Communists!'
context: Paranoia's tone was deliberately satirical — Costikyan was a libertarian-leaning author whose intent was a comedic critique of authoritarianism (the Computer thinks it's helping; the players are forced to lie and betray to survive). The game spawned multiple editions through Mongoose Publishing (2004 onwards). Greg Costikyan went on to write extensively about game design theory. The phrase 'The Computer is your friend' became a tongue-in-cheek meme outside the gaming hobby.

question: Gygax's 1978 S1 Tomb of Horrors module contains a famously specific trap involving the demilich Acererak's final form. After the PCs defeat his minions and pass through the tomb's puzzles, they reach Acererak's burial chamber. His skull rests on a pile of gems. When approached, the demilich rises and attacks. The skull has six gems set in its eye sockets, with very specific effects. What happens when a player tries to take one of the gems?
answer: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
choices: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
Each gem is a sphere of annihilation in disguise; touching disintegrates the PC instantly
Each gem is a wish-spell trapped in physical form; touching grants the wish but kills the PC
Each gem is an alternate timeline of the PC; touching merges the PC with the alternate, causing alignment loss
context: Acererak's gems include diamond, ruby, jet, fire opal, large opal, and emerald. Each represents a different soul-trapping mechanism — touching one drains levels, another forces a saving throw vs death, another permanently traps the PC's soul. The demilich form is a skull animated by the lich's residual willpower; it can only be defeated by destroying the gems AND the skull. Some 1e modules and later 5e adaptations have player characters who unsealed an Acererak gem decades earlier returning to the game as freed (but missing-souled) characters.

question: American writer Fritz Leiber and his college friend Harry Otto Fischer invented two sword-and-sorcery heroes back in 1934: Fafhrd, a giant northern barbarian with red hair, and the Gray Mouser, a small thief-magician of the city. The two friends kicked the characters around in letters for five years. Then in August 1939 the very first published Fafhrd-and-Mouser story finally appeared in the pulp magazine Weird Tales, launching one of fantasy's foundational series. What was the title of that first-published 1939 story?
answer: 'Two Sought Adventure' — the original 1939 Weird Tales publication title
choices: 'Two Sought Adventure' — the original 1939 Weird Tales publication title
'The Jewels in the Forest' — the second-published Fafhrd-Mouser story
'Ill Met in Lankhmar' — the Hugo-winning 1970 novella
context: 'Two Sought Adventure' (1939) was retitled 'The Jewels in the Forest' for later collections. Leiber wrote Fafhrd-Mouser stories continuously from 1939 until his death in 1992, eventually filling seven collected volumes. 'Ill Met in Lankhmar' (1970) won the Hugo and Nebula awards for Best Novella — the only Fafhrd-Mouser story to win major awards. The collection 'Swords and Deviltry' compiled the earliest stories chronologically. Lankhmar itself, the city of Black Toga, is the most-developed city in classic sword-and-sorcery.

question: Gary Gygax's original home-campaign mega-dungeon, Castle Greyhawk, was the playtesting ground for D&D from 1972 onwards. The dungeon had multiple levels — Gygax himself ran it for years with his home group. The exact level count varies in different sources. According to Gygax's own 1979 Dragon Magazine retrospective and his later Castle Zagyg series, how many levels did Castle Greyhawk have in its mature form?
answer: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
choices: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
Ten levels of identical 20-by-20 hex rooms, with no significant deeper sections
Twenty-five themed levels, including elemental zones and a Far Realm gateway
Seven levels matching the classical seven-planet medieval astrology
context: Castle Greyhawk's design was idiosyncratic, with thematic levels (the Magic-User Level, the Trap Level, the Demonic Level), multiple stairways between levels, and dimensional pockets. The infamous 'Tomb of Tsojcanth' was one such pocket. Gygax began publishing partial Castle Greyhawk material via his post-TSR company Troll Lord Games in 2005 — Castle Zagyg (Yggsburgh + The East Mark of the Flanaess) before his 2008 death. The full mega-dungeon material was eventually published in 2008-2011 by Troll Lord, but the Gygax estate has restricted later printings.

question: R.A. Salvatore introduced Drizzt Do'Urden as a last-minute addition to The Crystal Shard (1988) — his editor Mary Kirchoff had asked for a 'sidekick' for the human ranger protagonist. Salvatore offered a renegade drow as a placeholder, expecting Kirchoff to reject the idea. The novel hadn't been pitched with Drizzt at the front, but he stole the entire trilogy and went on to anchor over thirty more Salvatore novels. Salvatore later wrote a separate prequel trilogy giving Drizzt's full origin in Menzoberranzan. What's that prequel trilogy called?
answer: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
choices: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
The Legacy Trilogy: Legacy, Starless Night, Siege of Darkness (1992-1994)
The Cleric Quintet: Canticle, In Sylvan Shadows, Night Masks, Fallen Fortress, Chaos Curse (1991-1994)
The Hunter's Blades Trilogy: Thousand Orcs, Lone Drow, Two Swords (2002-2004)
context: The Dark Elf Trilogy is widely considered Salvatore's best work and the definitive depiction of drow society. Homeland (1990) showed Drizzt's youth in House Do'Urden in Menzoberranzan; Exile (1990) showed his banishment into the Underdark wilderness; Sojourn (1991) showed his journey to the surface and the early friendship with the blind ranger Montolio DeBrouchee. Salvatore's portrayal of Menzoberranzan as a matriarchal drow city-state — with its noble houses, the Academy, and the constant intrigue against Lolth — became iconic Forgotten Realms canon.

question: Jack Chick's 1984 evangelical tract 'Dark Dungeons,' the most-distributed anti-D&D pamphlet of the Satanic Panic era, depicts a fictional teenage girl named Debbie being recruited into a D&D group by a 'Dungeon Master' named Ms. Frost. The group plays a session where Debbie's character earns levels of magic. Frost then invites Debbie to a real witchcraft circle, where she learns 'real spells.' One specific spell Debbie casts on her father is named in the tract. What does she cast on him?
answer: A 'Mind Bondage' spell that puts him in a hypnotic state
choices: A 'Mind Bondage' spell that puts him in a hypnotic state
A 'Charm Person' spell directly copied from D&D
A 'Cause Disease' spell that makes him fall ill
A 'Curse of Failure' spell that destroys his business
context: The Mind Bondage spell in the tract was Jack Chick's invention, not drawn from any actual D&D spell-list. The tract ends with Debbie's friend Marcie killing herself after her D&D character 'died' (echoing the Patricia Pulling narrative), Debbie repenting and accepting Christ, and the tract burning her D&D books. The 2014 indie film 'Dark Dungeons' (directed by JR Ralls, written by Tim Skubick) adapted the tract as a deadpan straight-faced comedy with the original pamphlet's dialogue preserved verbatim. Jack Chick (1924-2016) produced hundreds of tracts on various 'evils' from rock music to Catholicism.

question: The 1982 CBS made-for-TV movie Mazes and Monsters starred Tom Hanks as a college student named Robbie Wheeling, who loses touch with reality while playing the fictional Mazes and Monsters game. It was Hanks' first leading role. The climax sends Robbie's character "Pardieu the Holy Man" on a magical leap from a great height as part of his fantasy ritual. From what New York City landmark does Robbie plan to leap?
answer: The top of the World Trade Center, before being talked down
choices: The top of the World Trade Center, before being talked down
The Statue of Liberty's torch, in a foggy night sequence
The Brooklyn Bridge, during a sunrise confrontation
The Empire State Building observation deck, during midnight
context: Pardieu the Holy Man's fictional last 'task' in the game is to leap from a tall tower to reach the Two Towers of Belderak. Robbie's fantasy delusion sends him to the World Trade Center's observation deck. His friends find him at the brink. The scene's emotional climax is intercut with the parents and friends realizing what's been happening to him. Tom Hanks said in a 2018 interview that he was 'mortified' to learn the film was now considered a Satanic Panic artifact, when at the time he just thought it was a serious-issues TV movie. Mazes and Monsters has become an ironic cult favorite at retro tabletop conventions.

question: In the Pokemon world, Charmander is the small orange lizard starter Pokemon. Its most distinctive feature is a small flame that burns forever on the tip of its tail. According to the Pokedex (the trainer's Pokemon encyclopedia), if the flame ever goes out, what happens to Charmander?
choices: Charmander loses the ability to use Fire moves
context: The flame burns brighter when Charmander is healthy or excited and dims when he is weak or sick. Trainers shelter the tail from rain. It is the most iconic life-force symbol in the franchise.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a trainer's little orange lizard Charmander grows up in two steps — first into the sturdier Charmeleon, then into the huge dragon-like Charizard, wings flared and tail blazing. Charizard's Pokedex entry lists two types, and one of those types is Fire. What is Charizard's other type?
context: Charizard is the only fully evolved Kanto starter with dual typing. Despite his dragon appearance, he was never Dragon-type until Mega Charizard X (Pokemon X/Y, 2013) granted him a Fire/Dragon alternate form.

question: In the Pokemon games for the Nintendo Game Boy, a young trainer walks through tall grass and suddenly runs into a wild creature like a Pikachu. To catch it, the trainer plucks a small red-and-white ball from their belt and throws it — the ball snaps open in a burst of light and pulls the Pokemon inside to become part of the trainer's team. What is this red-and-white capture ball called?
context: The standard Pokeball is the baseline catch device. The Master Ball is the rarest, with a 100% catch rate, and is famously given once in each main-line game.

question: In the 1997 Japanese anime Pokemon, a ten-year-old trainer named Ash Ketchum sets off with his Pikachu to catch monsters and become a Pokemon Master. He leaves his home in Pallet Town, battles gym leaders in Pewter City and Cerulean City, and finally competes in the Indigo League tournament — all inside one starting region modeled on real east-central Japan. What is this region called?
context: Kanto is the original 151-Pokemon region from Pokemon Red and Blue. Each later generation introduced a new region: Johto (Gold/Silver), Hoenn (Ruby/Sapphire), and so on.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, scientists on Cinnabar Island found a fossilized eyelash of Mew, an ancient myth Pokemon, and used its DNA to clone a new life-form in their secret lab. The result was a tall purple psychic Pokemon far more powerful than the original. He escapes, retreats to the Unknown Dungeon cave, and becomes the post-game boss the trainer must fight after beating the Elite Four. Name him.
context: Mewtwo's origin lore is told in journals scattered through the abandoned Cinnabar Island Mansion. He escapes captivity, destroys the lab, and is later found in Cerulean Cave by trainers who have already beaten the Elite Four.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a young trainer from Pallet Town journeys across the Kanto region battling city Gym Leaders like Brock of Pewter City, Misty of Cerulean City, and Erika of Celadon City. Every leader they defeat hands over a shiny metal Gym Badge. Only trainers who collect the full set of Kanto Gym Badges are allowed to travel to the Indigo Plateau and challenge the Elite Four. How many badges must a Kanto trainer earn to reach the Indigo League?
context: The Kanto gym badges, in order, are: Boulder (Brock), Cascade (Misty), Thunder (Lt. Surge), Rainbow (Erika), Soul (Koga), Marsh (Sabrina), Volcano (Blaine), and Earth (Giovanni).

question: In the Pokemon TV cartoon, Team Rocket is a bumbling trio of villains chasing Ash Ketchum's Pikachu. The three members — Jessie, James, and a talking cat Pokemon named Meowth — always show up reciting a rhyming motto together before every fight. What two-word phrase does Jessie use to open the motto?
context: The full opening is 'Prepare for trouble! / And make it double!' James follows Jessie, then they introduce themselves and Meowth caps it. The motto became one of the most recognizable bits of dialogue in 90s anime dubbing.

question: In February 1996 the tiny Japanese studio Game Freak released Pokemon Red and Green for the Nintendo Game Boy handheld console, ending six years of quiet development. Each Pokemon in the Kanto region got its own numbered entry in the trainer's Pokedex encyclopedia — starting with the grass-lizard Bulbasaur at number 001 and ending with the rare psychic legend Mew at the final slot. How many Pokemon appeared in that first Kanto Pokedex?
context: The 151 became the cultural canon. Mew was added in development as an Easter egg by programmer Shigeki Morimoto with only days left before the master disc shipped. The number 151 was later memorialized by the Pokerap.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a starter Charmander grows through experience points earned by winning battles against wild Pokemon and other trainers. When a Charmander hits a set level, it glows white and reshapes itself into the tougher Charmeleon, and eventually into the huge winged Charizard. Every Pokemon species has an evolution level fixed in its stats. At what level does a Charmander first evolve into Charmeleon?
context: Charmander reaches Charmeleon at level 16 and the final-form Charizard at level 36, matching the other Kanto starters' evolution levels. Most players grind through Mt. Moon and Cerulean to hit level 16 before challenging Lt. Surge.

question: In an early first-season episode of the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum and his friends Misty and Brock are hiking through a heavy rainstorm when they find a wild Charmander — the little orange fire-lizard whose life depends on the flame burning on the tip of his tail. The Charmander is huddled on top of a rock, desperately trying to shield his tail flame from the raindrops. His original trainer had told him to wait on that rock, then abandoned him there with a cruel lie. What was the original trainer's name?
context: Damian told Charmander to wait on the rock and would come back, knowing he would not. The Pokemon was too loyal to leave. Ash takes Charmander in, and the dynamic that produces Ash's most famous Pokemon arc begins right there in the rainstorm.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum challenges the seventh Kanto gym leader — a bald old showman named Blaine who loves puzzles and stage-magic gags. In the deciding match Ash's newly evolved Charizard defeats Blaine's ace Magmar, and Ash walks away with the Volcano Badge. Blaine's home city, the entrance to his gym, and his Pokemon's element all match one very specific theme. Which Kanto gym leader is Blaine?
answer: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
choices: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
The Saffron City psychic gym leader of Silph Co. fame
The Fuchsia City poison gym leader who trains ninjas
The Vermilion City electric gym leader, an American soldier
context: Blaine's gym is hidden inside the Cinnabar Mansion through a secret-passage door requiring riddles to open. The mansion is also where Mewtwo was cloned. Blaine's iconic Pokemon are Magmar, Ninetales, and Rapidash.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Brock is the rock-type gym leader of Pewter City — the first city Ash Ketchum ever reaches on his Kanto journey, and the first gym he ever challenges. Ash loses to Brock on his first attempt. On his second try, Ash's Pikachu triggers the gym's overhead sprinklers, drenching Brock's ace Pokemon. That ace is a giant rock snake made of chained boulders, and once wet it becomes vulnerable to electricity — Pikachu zaps it and Ash finally earns the Boulder Badge. Name that rock-snake Pokemon.
context: Brock travels with Ash for most of the original anime as a cook and aspiring Pokemon breeder. He has many younger siblings whom he raises in Pewter City after his father Flint leaves. Brock's signature gag is fainting over every Nurse Joy and Officer Jenny he meets.

question: In the very first episode of the Pokemon anime, a wild Pikachu jolts a red-haired girl who is passing by on a two-wheeled vehicle, frying the vehicle to a smoking wreck. That girl is Misty, the water-type gym leader of Cerulean City, and she ends up traveling with Ash Ketchum as his first companion in the whole show. Across the early episodes she keeps chasing him and demanding he replace the vehicle her Pikachu incident ruined. What is the item Misty wants Ash to pay her back for?
context: Misty's flooded bike is the running gag of the early series. Pikachu fried it with a Thundershock that scared off a flock of Spearow chasing Ash and him. Misty follows them for repayment and never collects.

question: Pokemon Red and Green launched in Japan on February 27, 1996 as a pair of Game Boy cartridges. Nintendo re-released them worldwide as Red and Blue about two and a half years later, in September 1998 in North America. Each version's box cover features one of Kanto's three starter Pokemon in its fully-evolved form: Red shows the fire lizard, Green shows the plant dinosaur, and Blue shows the water starter — a giant blue turtle with cannons mounted on its shell. Name the fully-evolved Water starter that appears on the North American Blue cover.
context: Pokemon Red and Blue launched in the US on September 28, 1998 for the Game Boy. The English version was based on the Japanese Pokemon Blue revision, with the original Japanese Red and Green's color pair swapped to Red and Blue for the Western market.

question: In 1999, a special anime-tie-in version of Pokemon Red and Blue released in the US. It started the player with a Pikachu instead of one of the three Kanto starters, and Pikachu followed the player around outside its Pokeball. What was the game called?
context: Pokemon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition launched in Japan on September 12, 1998 and in the US on October 19, 1999. Jessie, James, and Meowth replaced certain Rocket grunts. All three Kanto starters could be obtained over the course of the game.

question: The first Pokemon movie, released in 1998 in Japan and 1999 in the US, tells the origin of the lab-cloned Mewtwo. Mewtwo escapes the lab in a fit of psychic rage and broods about who he is. What rebuilt place does he blast to rubble before his big speech?
answer: The Cinnabar Island laboratory where Dr. Fuji cloned him
choices: The Cinnabar Island laboratory where Dr. Fuji cloned him
Team Rocket's Saffron City Silph Co. headquarters
Professor Oak's research lab in Pallet Town
The Indigo Plateau Pokemon League stadium
context: Dr. Fuji's journals (found in the abandoned Cinnabar Mansion in the games) describe the cloning experiment. The film's most famous moment is the climactic clone-versus-original showdown, halted by Ash leaping between Mewtwo and Mew and being turned to stone.

question: Pokemon Gold and Silver launched in Japan in 1999 and in North America in October 2000, on the Game Boy Color. They were the second generation of the Pokemon series and added 100 brand-new Pokemon to the original 151. Gold and Silver also introduced a real-time in-game day-and-night cycle, powered by the Game Boy Color cartridge's internal clock — the sky and the wild Pokemon really changed as the actual hours passed. Most importantly the games opened up a brand-new region located just west of Kanto. What is the name of that new region?
context: Johto introduced breeding via Day Care couples, the Pokegear watch device, and 16 gym badges (Johto's eight plus the original Kanto eight in the post-game). Crystal (2000-2001) added a female protagonist option named Kris.

question: In 2019, Warner Bros released Detective Pikachu, the first live-action Pokemon feature film. It stars American actor Justice Smith as Tim Goodman, a young man whose detective father has mysteriously vanished in Ryme City. Tim finds his father's Pikachu partner and, to Tim's shock, discovers the little electric mouse can suddenly talk to him — in the deadpan wisecracking voice of an adult man. That voice belongs to a Canadian-American actor best known for playing Deadpool. Who was the voice actor?
context: Detective Pikachu was directed by Rob Letterman, based on the 2016 Japanese 3DS spinoff game. It became the highest-grossing live-action video-game film at release. Reynolds's Pikachu drinks coffee, wears a deerstalker hat, and snarks his way through Ryme City's mysteries.

question: On July 6, 2016, Niantic launched a mobile augmented-reality game that turned real-world parks and landmarks into Pokemon hunting grounds. People walked into traffic, climbed fences, and gathered in parks at 2 a.m. by the thousands. What was the game?
context: Niantic had built the GPS-walking framework with their earlier game Ingress (2013). Pokemon GO hit 500 million downloads in its first eight months. The cultural sensation included serious news coverage of Lapras and Snorlax sightings in Central Park.

question: As a boy growing up in Machida, Japan, in the 1960s and 70s, Satoshi Tajiri obsessively collected beetles and stag beetles in the fields near his home — which decades later gave him the idea for a game about catching creatures. In 1989 he founded the game studio Game Freak in Tokyo with a talented young illustrator he had been co-publishing a Japanese fanzine with. Ever since Pokemon Red and Blue in 1996, that co-founder has personally drawn the concept art for every main-series Pokemon monster. Who is Tajiri's Game Freak co-founder?
context: Ken Sugimori is the lead character designer who has drawn the canonical art for every Pokemon since 1996. Junichi Masuda became the music director. Tsunekazu Ishihara runs The Pokemon Company, the licensing arm. Shigeru Miyamoto greenlit the project at Nintendo when no one else would.

question: Pokemon X and Y launched worldwide on the Nintendo 3DS in October 2013 as the sixth generation of the Pokemon series. Its headline new mechanic was Mega Evolution — a temporary in-battle super-form each Pokemon could enter if its trainer held the matching Mega Stone. Charizard was so popular the developers gave him two different Megas. Mega Charizard Y keeps his original Fire and Flying typing. But Mega Charizard X drops the Flying type entirely, turning his scales pitch black and his flames electric blue as he shifts into a completely new dual type. What is Mega Charizard X's dual typing?
context: Mega Charizard X was a fan-service nod to the long-running argument that Charizard 'should have been' Dragon-type. It exclusive to Pokemon X. Mega Charizard Y, exclusive to Pokemon Y, keeps the Fire/Flying typing and grows much larger wings. Both share a Charizardite stone.

question: In January 1999, the American game company Wizards of the Coast — the same publisher that already ran Magic the Gathering — released the English-language Pokemon Trading Card Game Base Set, a starter run of exactly 102 cards including sixteen holographic rares. The rarest, most valuable card in the whole set is the holographic Charizard, which schoolyard kids traded for lunch money and still trade for real money today. Collectors identify it by its exact slot in the numbered checklist. What is the Charizard card's number in the 102-card Base Set?
context: The Base Set is numbered alphabetically by Pokemon name within rarity groups, so Charizard's 4/102 reflects 'C-h-a-r' placement. The Base Set is the most reprinted TCG set in history. The card's 1st Edition Shadowless variant is the most valuable, currently selling at auction for hundreds of thousands of dollars.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum's mother Delia lives back in Pallet Town while Ash travels the world. She keeps a strange helper around the house — a tall pink-haired clown Pokemon who cleans the house, cooks meals, and weeds the garden. What species is this Pokemon?
context: The Pokemon's nickname is Mimey. Delia adopts him after Ash and friends help out in an early-season episode. Mr. Mime's Pokedex skill is to project invisible walls, which Delia uses to keep dust out of the house. He is a household staple in the Ketchum home for the rest of the anime.

question: In the Pokemon anime's Charizard disobedience arc, the turning point comes when Ash and Charizard fight a wild Magmar in a deep freezing snowstorm. Charizard is left exhausted and nearly frozen to death. Ash refuses to abandon him and shelters him through the night. When morning comes, Charizard does what to save Ash's life in return?
answer: Warms Ash with his tail flame held against Ash's chest
choices: Warms Ash with his tail flame held against Ash's chest
Carries Ash on his back to the nearest Pokemon Center
Burns the surrounding ice to start a warming fire
Hatches a Vulpix egg using his own body heat to keep them warm
context: The tail-flame-on-Ash moment is the emotional payoff of the entire disobedience arc. After this episode, Charizard finally trusts and obeys Ash without question. The Charizard line's mythology — flame as life force — becomes literal here: Charizard shares his life force with Ash.

question: After Ash Ketchum finishes the Indigo League and moves on into the Johto region in the Pokemon anime, he decides his loyal Charizard needs to become stronger before he can rely on him in real fights. Ash leaves Charizard in a hidden mountain valley in Johto — a valley filled with dozens of wild Charizards flying, fighting, and sunning themselves. A stern older Charizard trainer named Liza watches over the valley and supervises the training matches Ash's Charizard has to win. The valley's name is a pun made from the species itself. What is that valley called?
context: Charicific Valley appears in the Johto saga of the anime. The matron is named Liza, an expert in raising Charizards. She rides her own Charizard, identifiable by a heart-shaped scar on its chest. Ash's Charizard occasionally rejoins Ash for major battles like the Battle Frontier finale.

question: Ash's Charizard developed a signature finishing move in the anime that he uses to knock out (KO) opponents from giant Onix to Articuno. He grabs the opponent in his front claws, soars high, and slams them spinning back into the ground. What is the move called?
context: Seismic Toss is a Fighting-type move in the games and would not normally be in a Charizard's learnset, but the anime's broader 'rule of cool' lets Charizard use it freely. The Articuno match was the climactic Battle Frontier showdown at Noland's Pyramid in 2006.

question: Ash's Charmeleon evolves into Charizard in the Pokemon anime during a dramatic rescue mission. A wild fossil Pokemon revived by Team Rocket has snatched Ash from a cliff and is flying him away. Charmeleon evolves mid-pursuit to save him. What fossil Pokemon was the kidnapper?
context: Aerodactyl, the prehistoric Flying/Rock-type, was revived from an Old Amber fossil by Team Rocket on Grampa Canyon. Charmeleon's mid-air evolution into Charizard, slashing Aerodactyl with newly grown claws, is one of the most-replayed evolution scenes in the original anime.

question: In the Pokemon anime, Ash Ketchum's Charmander evolves into Charmeleon and later, during the dramatic Aerodactyl rescue on Grampa Canyon, evolves once more into a full Charizard. Charmander had adored Ash — Charmeleon was already stubborn — but the fully-evolved Charizard stops obeying Ash altogether for a long stretch of episodes, sleeping in the middle of battles and roasting Ash with flamethrower for laughs. The anime gives one clear in-universe reason for why the evolution flipped his loyalty. What is that reason?
answer: Charizard sees Ash as too weak to command a fully evolved Pokemon
choices: Charizard sees Ash as too weak to command a fully evolved Pokemon
Charizard misses his original trainer Damian and resents Ash
Charizard has been corrupted by exposure to Aerodactyl's primal aura
Charizard requires a higher-tier Pokeball than Ash's standard one
context: In Pokemon lore, a Pokemon may stop obeying a trainer below its level if the trainer lacks the appropriate gym badges. The anime adapts this into Charizard's pride: he tests Ash by sleeping through gym battles or burning him with Flamethrower until Ash earns his respect.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, the town of Lavender has a multi-story building where people go to remember their deceased Pokemon. Ghost Pokemon appear on every floor. Team Rocket has occupied the upper floors when Red arrives. What is the building called?
context: The Pokemon Tower includes the ghost of a Marowak killed by Team Rocket while defending her child Cubone. Red can only see and battle the ghosts after acquiring a Silph Scope from Saffron City. The Marowak ghost is the most haunting NPC encounter in the original Kanto games.

question: In the original Pokemon Red and Blue Pokedex, one small ground-type Pokemon named Cubone is nicknamed 'the Lonely Pokemon.' Cubone stands upright on two legs, carries a bone as a club, and wears an oversized animal skull like a helmet that hides his face. The Pokedex entry explains that beneath the mask Cubone is always crying — he is in constant mourning for one specific person, and the skull he wears on his head is a relic from the dead. Whose skull is Cubone wearing?
choices: A defeated rival's skull from his first battle
The skull of an Aerodactyl ancestor
A ceremonial mask handed down through Cubone generations
context: Pokemon Red's Pokedex entry: 'Wears the skull of its deceased mother on its head. Its cries echo inside the skull and come out as a sad melody.' The lore ties directly to the Marowak ghost on the Pokemon Tower's seventh floor. This is one of the darkest pieces of canon in the entire franchise.

question: Lt. Surge is the electric-type gym leader of Vermilion City, styled like an American army veteran. His ace Pokemon is the evolved form of Pikachu. He brags about evolving his Pikachu the moment he caught it, before it could learn key moves. What is Lt. Surge's signature Pokemon?
context: In the anime, Ash refuses to evolve Pikachu — even with a Thunder Stone offered in episode 14 — because of Lt. Surge's gloating about Raichu losing access to Pikachu-tier moves. Pikachu remains unevolved for the entire series. The lesson became one of the show's defining moral arcs.

question: In one of the most emotional Pokemon episodes of the first season, Ash releases his Butterfree at the end of a story where the species migrates across the ocean to find mates. The episode aired in 1997. Its title is a farewell phrase. What is the episode called?
choices: The Path to a Pokemon Master
context: Butterfree had been Ash's first wild catch as a Caterpie on Route 1. The Hurricane Migration episode shows him meeting a pink-furred shiny Butterfree. Ash lets him go to follow her across the ocean. Many adult viewers cite this episode as their introduction to Pokemon-anime tear-jerker storytelling.

question: On December 16, 1997, a Pokemon episode titled Electric Soldier Porygon aired in Japan at 6:30 in the evening. The flashing red lights on screen caused seizures in many children, and 685 were sent to the hospital. The Pokemon at the center of the episode was banned from the show for good. Which one?
context: Ironically, Porygon was banned despite the seizure-inducing effect coming from Pikachu's Thunderbolt explosion, not from Porygon itself. The incident, dubbed 'Pokemon Shock,' delayed the anime's return by four months and led to Japanese broadcast standards reducing strobe-cut rates. Porygon, Porygon2, and Porygon-Z have not appeared in the anime since.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, a famous glitch lets a player encounter a corrupted-data Pokemon called Missingno. To trigger it, you talk to a specific non-player character and then surf along a coast. That character tells a story about catching Pokemon before walking back to a building. Where do you meet this character?
answer: On the docks of Viridian City, the Old Man who demonstrates catching
choices: On the docks of Viridian City, the Old Man who demonstrates catching
In the Celadon Game Corner, the rocket grunt at slot machines
On Cinnabar Island, in front of the Pokemon Mansion's main door
In the Pewter City Museum, the curator with the Old Amber
context: The Old Man demonstrates the catching tutorial, which writes the player's name to a buffer used to load wild Pokemon when surfing. Surfing the Cinnabar Coast — east edge of the island — then loads garbage data as the species, summoning Missingno. The glitch duplicates the player's sixth-slot item by 128, the famous Master Ball / Rare Candy duplication exploit.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, Team Rocket is a criminal syndicate in matching black uniforms that steals Pokemon across the Kanto region. Its secret boss turns out to be a man named Giovanni. Giovanni is also, in public, the eighth Kanto gym leader — he runs his gym in Viridian City as a legitimate cover, and it's the very last gym Ash must beat before he can enter Victory Road and challenge the Elite Four. Giovanni's declared type specialty at his Viridian gym is the Ground type. What is the badge his gym awards to trainers who defeat him?
context: Giovanni's identity as Team Rocket's leader is revealed during the Silph Co. raid. He keeps his Mewtwo cloning project secret. Red defeats him at Silph Co., then again at Viridian Gym for the Earth Badge. Giovanni's signature Pokemon is Rhydon, the very first Pokemon ever designed by Game Freak.

question: During the late 1990s peak of the Pokemon anime, a song played at the end of every episode. It named all 151 original Pokemon in rapid-fire rhymes over rotating animations. American kids memorized the entire song and the order of the names. What was the song called?
context: The Pokerap aired at the end of US episodes during the Kids' WB Saturday morning lineup. It was split into four parts, each cycling a quarter of the Pokemon. Adult Pokemon fans can still recite the order from memory, especially the climactic Mew-ending of the fourth and final segment.

question: Sabrina is Saffron City's psychic-type gym leader. In one of the early anime's most surreal episodes, she telekinetically turns Ash, Misty, and Brock into living dolls displayed in her dollhouse. The lore explains her cold powers as the result of a childhood trauma. Who lives in her gym as her family?
answer: Her father and a doll inhabited by her childhood-self psyche
choices: Her father and a doll inhabited by her childhood-self psyche
Her trainer-mother and twin sister, both also psychic gym leaders
Her grandmother and a Mr. Mime who acts as a butler
Her brother Sabri, a younger non-psychic challenger
context: Sabrina's father explains that her powers grew so strong that her emotional side split off into a doll. Ash defeats her thanks to a wild Haunter who makes the cold Sabrina laugh for the first time in years, breaking the psychic shield protecting her gym. The episode's atmosphere remains one of the eeriest in 90s kid TV.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, three legendary bird Pokemon roam the Kanto region as a trio — Zapdos the electric bird, Moltres the fire bird, and Articuno the ice bird. Each of them waits in a specific hidden dungeon somewhere on the Kanto map, and every trainer who wants to catch one has to find that lair. Articuno waits at the bottom of a multi-floor frozen ice-cave labyrinth at the southwestern tip of the region, an island cave system reached by Surfing south from Fuchsia City. What is the name of Articuno's frozen lair?
choices: Victory Road on the way to Indigo Plateau
context: Articuno (Seafoam Islands), Zapdos (Power Plant outside Cerulean), and Moltres (Victory Road, later Mt. Ember in remakes) form the legendary bird trio. Each can be caught at level 50 and is famously hard to keep awake long enough to throw a Pokeball without first running out of them.

question: In the 2006 Pokemon: Battle Frontier season, Ash's Charizard returns from training at Charicific Valley to challenge a Frontier Brain in a legendary 1-vs-3 match. The Frontier Brain is a former military pilot who runs the Battle Pyramid and uses a single Articuno as his ace. Charizard's Seismic Toss takes Articuno down. Name the Frontier Brain.
choices: Brandon (Pyramid King of Snowpoint, alternate continuity)
context: Brandon is actually the Pyramid King; Noland runs the Battle Factory. Ash's Charizard-vs-Articuno match was Noland's Battle Factory. The fight ended with Charizard collapsing seconds after his win, and the moment is generally cited as the peak of Ash's Charizard's anime career. The Frontier Brains spanned seven specialist battle facilities in Kanto.

question: Pokemon Yellow (1998 Japan, 1999 US) introduced a feature where the player's lead Pokemon walks behind the player on the overworld. In Yellow, only one Pokemon could do this. The next mainline game to fully bring back overworld-following was a Johto-region release that allowed any Pokemon to follow. What game?
answer: Pokemon HeartGold and SoulSilver (2009 Japan, 2010 US)
choices: Pokemon HeartGold and SoulSilver (2009 Japan, 2010 US)
context: HeartGold and SoulSilver, the DS remakes of Gold and Silver, brought back Pikachu-style overworld-following for every Pokemon in the player's lead slot. Each Pokemon had a unique sprite and special interaction lines. The Pokewalker pedometer accessory shipped with the game, letting you 'walk' Pokemon real-world distances.

question: In Pokemon Red and Blue, the player eventually explores the abandoned Cinnabar Mansion — a once-grand three-story house on Cinnabar Island, half burnt, full of locked doors, hidden switch statues, and stray Pokemon. Scattered across the mansion's four floors are four handwritten journal pages. Read in order, they tell the story of a Pokemon research team's expedition to Guyana, the discovery of a mysterious new Pokemon named Mew in the deep jungle, and the cloning experiment on Cinnabar Island that produced Mewtwo. The final journal page names the scientist who wrote the diary. Who is he?
context: Dr. Fuji also appears as the doctor at the Pokemon Tower in Lavender Town, working to revive a Marowak ghost. His full backstory expands in Pokemon Adventures manga and the first Pokemon movie, where his daughter Ai's death is the original motivation for cloning research. Mewtwo's resentment toward humans grew from understanding he was built to replace a dead child.

question: Richie is the Ash-lookalike trainer Ash faces at the Indigo League conference. Richie's team mirrors Ash's at the time of the match, including a nicknamed counterpart of Ash's Charmander. Richie's Pikachu is named Sparky. What does he name his Charmander?
context: Richie's team mirrors Ash's: Sparky (Pikachu), Zippo (Charmander), Happy (Butterfree, mirroring Ash's released Butterfree), Cruise (Pidgeotto), Rose (Bulbasaur, later Ivysaur). Richie's nicknaming habit contrasts with Ash, who never nicknames any of his Pokemon. Richie advances further in the tournament after Ash loses to him in the round of 16.

question: In 1999, Nintendo released a first-party Pokemon game on the Nintendo 64 that was not a battle RPG. Instead, the player rides an automatic tracked buggy called the Zero-One through six wildlife courses across Pokemon Island, photographing wild Pokemon in their natural habitats so that Professor Oak can grade the photos back at the lab. The player character is a young Pokemon photographer whose family name — Snap — is literally the game's title verb. What is the photographer's name?
answer: Todd Snap (Todd in the West, Tōru in Japan)
choices: Todd Snap (Todd in the West, Tōru in Japan)
Mark Roll (Mark in the West, Maaku in Japan)
Lance Click (Lance in the West, Ransu in Japan)
Chase Shutter (Chase in the West, Chesu in Japan)
context: Pokemon Snap launched on the N64 in 1999 (Japan March, US June). Todd reappears in the Pokemon anime as a recurring character in the Orange Islands and Johto arcs. McDonald's in 1999-2000 famously ran a Pokemon Snap promotion where you could print your photos at in-store kiosks — a primitive cultural moment for digital photography.

question: Pokemon Stadium arrived in 1999 in Japan and 2000 in America on the Nintendo 64. A peripheral called the Transfer Pak let you import your Pokemon directly from Game Boy cartridges into 3D battles. Between battle cups, the game offered a set of minigames. The most beloved was a thump-the-button rhythm minigame starring a specific Pokemon. Name the minigame.
answer: Clefairy Says (a Simon-says color-pattern rhythm game)
choices: Clefairy Says (a Simon-says color-pattern rhythm game)
context: The Stadium minigames were the social heart of every kid's sleepover. Clefairy Says ran from short patterns to staggering long sequences. Other classics: Magikarp's Splash, Run Rattata Run, Sushi-Go-Round, Snore War, Ekans Hoop Hurl, Dig! Dig! Dig!. Mewtwo was the post-game superboss of the R-2 Round 2 cup, available only after defeating the entire game.

question: In 1998 and 1999, American elementary-school kids passed around a rumor that a hidden 151st Pokemon — Mew — could be caught in Pokemon Red and Blue with one specific glitch trick. The trick, they whispered, required first riding the S.S. Anne cruise ship out of Vermilion City harbor so the ship left the dock, and then using Surf to sneak back over the water to a very specific empty spot on the now-deserted dock. Mew, supposedly, was hiding underneath a vehicle parked in that spot. Where was Mew rumored to be waiting?
answer: Under the parked truck near the S.S. Anne dock
choices: Under the parked truck near the S.S. Anne dock
Behind the Pokemon Center counter in Pewter City
Inside the Pokemon Tower's third floor pillar in Lavender Town
Beneath the bicycle in the Saffron City Silph Co. lobby
context: The truck legend was the most pervasive Pokemon urban legend of the late 90s. Mew is genuinely there in the game data — but you cannot catch him via the truck. The real glitch path involves Cinnabar Coast surfing combined with specific Trainer Fly setup. Mew was officially distributed via Nintendo events; the very first event was at Toys R Us in Hawaii, May 1999.

question: Pokemon Sword and Shield (2019) for the Switch broke a longstanding franchise tradition. For the first time, the National Pokedex was not fully included. Hundreds of Pokemon from earlier generations were left out, sparking a fan backlash that trended worldwide for weeks. What did fans nickname this exclusion?
choices: The Galar Cut, after the UK-inspired game region
context: Game Freak director Junichi Masuda explained the cut as necessary to give each remaining Pokemon higher-quality 3D models and animations. Fans were not satisfied. Many cut Pokemon returned via the Crown Tundra and Isle of Armor DLCs in 2020. The full National Dex has not yet returned to a mainline game as of the most recent releases.

question: Inside Lavender Town's Pokemon Tower, an enraged ghost blocks the player's path on the upper floors. The player cannot identify, fight, or move past it until obtaining a specific Team Rocket invention from Silph Co. in Saffron City. What is the item?
context: The Silph Scope reveals ghost-type Pokemon as their true species. With the Scope equipped, the ghost is revealed as a Marowak who died defending her child Cubone from Team Rocket. Red defeats her and lays her spirit to rest. Then he climbs to the top and rescues Mr. Fuji, who gifts the Poke Flute, which wakes Snorlax on Routes 12 and 16.

question: Team Rocket's bumbling trio of Jessie, James, and Meowth carry different names in the original Japanese anime. The names were chosen by Pokemon anime writers as nods to two famous samurai-era figures. Jessie is Musashi and James is Kojiro in Japanese. These were the rivals of which historical figure?
answer: Miyamoto Musashi (whose duel-rivals included Sasaki Kojiro)
choices: Miyamoto Musashi (whose duel-rivals included Sasaki Kojiro)
Toyotomi Hideyoshi (and his retainer Ishida Mitsunari)
Oda Nobunaga (and his rival Takeda Shingen)
Tokugawa Ieyasu (and his vassal Honda Tadakatsu)
context: Miyamoto Musashi (1584-1645) fought Sasaki Kojiro at Ganryujima in 1612 in one of Japan's most famous duels; Musashi won using a wooden sword carved from a boat oar. Pokemon writers reused Musashi/Kojiro for the Rocket trio. The third Rocket character Nyarth (Meowth in English) keeps a name pattern from a Japanese cat-onomatopoeia, distinct from the samurai pair.

question: Charizard's first appearance in Super Smash Bros came in 2008, as the third Pokemon on a swap-tag character called Pokemon Trainer. The Trainer cycles through three Kanto-starter Pokemon mid-match. Squirtle plays the speed role; Ivysaur the ranged poker. Charizard plays the heavy. The Trainer's three Pokemon are explicitly the Kanto starter trio at three stages of evolution. What sub-detail did director Masahiro Sakurai add to the Trainer's animation specifically tying him to Pokemon Red and Blue?
answer: The Trainer wears the iconic backwards-cap outfit of Red, the silent protagonist of the original Game Boy Pokemon games
choices: The Trainer wears the iconic backwards-cap outfit of Red, the silent protagonist of the original Game Boy Pokemon games
The Trainer is voiced by Veronica Taylor, the original English voice actress for Ash Ketchum in the Pokemon anime
The Trainer's victory animation includes a Pokeball-toss synced to the anime's catch-sound effect from Indigo League season one
The Trainer's idle stance includes a Pikachu following behind, in a homage to the Pokemon Yellow Pikachu-follows mechanic
context: Pokemon Trainer's three forms exhausted differently on his 2008 Smash debut, with a stamina system urging the player to swap. Charizard split off as his own standalone character in Smash 4 (2014). The Trainer returned with all three Pokemon in Super Smash Bros Ultimate (2018), this time with a stamina-free swap. Charizard's Final Smash is Mega Charizard X, the black-dragon Fire/Dragon form introduced in Pokemon X/Y.

question: In January 1998, the Japanese magazine CoroCoro Comic ran a one-of-a-kind Pokemon illustration contest. The winners received a holographic Trainer card unlike any other Pokemon card in print: it depicted Pikachu holding a paintbrush and the card's type symbol was a painter's palette, not the standard Lightning energy symbol. About 39 copies were ever produced. The card has sold at auction for over $900,000. What is the card called?
context: Pikachu Illustrator is the rarest Pokemon card in the world. Each was hand-signed by manga artist Atsuko Nishida, the original Pikachu designer at Game Freak. One PSA 10 sold for $900,000 in 2021 to Logan Paul, who wore the card around his neck in a clear pendant during his 2022 WrestleMania appearance. Pikachu Illustrator is generally considered the 'Black Lotus' of Pokemon TCG.

question: Pokemon Red and Blue have a Safari Zone glitch. You save inside the zone, restart, leave, and re-enter at just the right moment. That drops you into a broken map of scrambled tiles, frozen in dialog with no way out until you save and reload. What did fans call this corrupted place?
context: Glitch City's exact layout depends on the player's coordinate buffer at the moment of corruption. Some instances let you walk through Saffron's Silph Co. building diagonally as a single-tile city block; some place a Pokemon Center inside Mt. Moon with no exit. The Safari Zone trick relies on the step counter being cached separately from the world-loading routine. Pokemon Adventures manga adapted Glitch City as the prison housing Mewtwo's clone Pokemon.

question: The Cinnabar Coast Missingno glitch in Pokemon Red and Blue spawns Missingno at a level set by your rival's stored name. Most Missingnos show up at the same level, thanks to the letter codes that your rival's name writes into memory. What is the most common Missingno level?
context: Missingno's level depends on the OT name letters interpreted as Pokemon-species ID bytes by the Cinnabar Coast wild-Pokemon loader. Catching a Missingno scrambles the Pokemon storage box but otherwise leaves the game stable. The famous side effect — sixth-slot item duplication by 128 — was the only known way to amass infinite Master Balls or Rare Candies, allowing speedy completion of the Pokedex.

question: The original Pokemon games released in Japan in February 1996 as Red and Green, not Red and Blue. A third version called Blue came out later as an enhanced port with updated sprites, bug fixes, and the data the West would eventually receive. The Japanese covers featured the three starters' final evolutions, one per version. Which final-form Pokemon was on the Japanese Pokemon Blue cover?
context: Japanese Pokemon Red had Charizard; Green had Venusaur; Blue had Blastoise. For the Western release, the localization team used Blastoise's Blue version's improved code base and renamed the second version 'Blue' with Blastoise on the cover, replacing the Japanese 'Green/Venusaur' pairing. Pokemon Green eventually did appear in the West as bonus content via the Red/Blue Virtual Console release decades later.

question: The 1999 English Pokemon Trading Card Game (TCG) Base Set was printed by Wizards of the Coast in multiple successive print runs distinguishable by tiny printing tells. The very first printing has the rarest 'shadowless' card frame — no shadow on the right side of the artwork box — combined with a small black circle in the lower-left corner stamped 'EDITION 1.' What did collectors nickname this combination?
context: The Shadowless print run was the first 2,000-card Wizards run of the English Base Set in late 1998 through early 1999 before the more economical 'shadowed' template was adopted. The 1st Edition stamp marks the very first print group. The 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard #4/102 in PSA 10 condition is among the most valuable Pokemon cards ever sold, fetching over $400,000 at auction.

question: The Pokemon Red Pokedex entry for Charizard describes a striking altitude at which it can fly for long stretches. Later official entries have echoed the same figure, often paired with the claim that its breath can melt boulders. What altitude does the Red entry give for Charizard's maximum flight?
context: Pokemon Red's exact Pokedex entry: 'Spits fire that is hot enough to melt boulders. Known to cause forest fires unintentionally.' Pokemon Blue adds: 'When this Pokemon expels a blast of superhot fire, the red flame at the tip of its tail burns more intensely.' Later games scaled the altitude. Charizard's wingspan is given as 7 feet, weight 200 pounds in standard Kanto form.

question: Pokemon Stadium (1999 Japan, 2000 US) on the N64 contains a famously brutal post-game superboss available only after defeating Round 1 of all four cups and then Round 2 of all four cups — a feat requiring near-perfect IV-trained imported Pokemon from a Game Boy cartridge. The final fight is a 1-on-1 against a specific level-100 ace. Who is the Stadium R-2 final boss?
choices: The Elite Four leader Lance with his Dragonite
Professor Oak with his unrevealed full team
context: Stadium's Mewtwo is a level-100 with full-stat investment. Beating him unlocks the alternate Game Boy Tower color palettes for the entire Pokemon Red/Blue/Yellow cartridges plus a special Mewtwo-themed certificate background. The cup structure (Pokeball, Great Ball, Ultra Ball, Master Ball) culminates in the Master Ball cup at Round 2, with Mewtwo as the final fight after that.

question: Pokemon Gold and Silver (1999 Japan, 2000 US) introduced a real-time day/night cycle, time-of-day Pokemon spawns, and special events tied to days of the week. The system worked via a small clock battery hidden inside each Game Boy Color cartridge. About 15 years later, fans worldwide began rediscovering that the battery had died, breaking the time-sensitive events. Where exactly is the clock battery located?
answer: Soldered to the cartridge PCB, behind the back-cover screw, requiring a Tri-wing or homemade screwdriver to access
choices: Soldered to the cartridge PCB, behind the back-cover screw, requiring a Tri-wing or homemade screwdriver to access
Glued underneath the cartridge ROM chip, requiring complete disassembly of the cart shell
External to the Game Boy in a separate clock-pak peripheral, easily replaced
Inside the Game Boy Color console itself, shared across all Gen-2 carts
context: The Tri-wing screw was Nintendo's standard cartridge security from the SNES era forward. Modders use Game Boy Color screwdriver sets to replace dead CR1616 batteries. Pokemon Crystal added a feature where the player could only get certain shiny Pokemon and the Celebi event-trigger via working clock data, so dead-battery Crystal cartridges still play but lose half their late-game content.

question: Mew was data-locked in Pokemon Red and Blue, meant to be handed out only at official Nintendo events in stores and at conventions. The very first US Mew event ran at one major retailer's Pokemon promotional tour starting in May 1999. The download was cabled into your Game Boy at a kiosk. Which retailer hosted that first event?
answer: Toys R Us (the 'Mew giveaway' Pokemon League tour, May 1999 onward)

context: The Toys R Us 'Pokemon League' tour ran across US cities and let kids cable their Game Boys into a Nintendo Power station; staff downloaded a level-5 Mew with the moves Pound and Transform onto the cart. After the official events ended, schoolyard rumor and the Mew-under-the-truck legend filled the gap for kids who missed the live distribution.
